chef_bio.background: A back-alley oyster izakaya near the Tatemachi tram stop in central Hiroshima, with the dining room on the second floor. The house specializes in Hiroshima oysters and Seto Inland Sea seafood, built around its signature 'bucket platter' of steamed and raw oysters served in a metal bucket.
chef_bio.philosophy: Each dish is prepared to order after it is requested (一品一品オーダーを受けてから), emphasizing freshly cooked seafood.
chef_bio.specialty: Oysters in roughly 50 preparations, anchored by the bucket platter of steamed and raw oysters, with fried oysters, butter-grilled oysters, oyster gratin, and oyster ajillo; also anago and small sardines.

anecdotes.text: The oysters are sourced from Miyamoto Kaisan in Etajima, and the menu also features Hiroshima specialties such as kone (whale skin/コーネ).
The signature raw-oyster bucket platter (生食用カキ 鬼 バケツ盛り, 6 pieces) is a centerpiece of the menu, with a wide range of oyster dishes made one by one to order.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: hotpepper/tabelog listings confirm the shop offers 約50種類 of oyster dishes, sources its oysters directly from 江田島の宮本海産, features the 鬼 バケツ盛り (6-piece raw / 8- and 16-piece steamed buckets) and Hiroshima コーネ (whale), sits on the 2nd floor a 3-min walk from the Tatemachi tram, and cooks each dish to order.

hiro_okonomiyaki_junia.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The specialty Fuchu-yaki uses beef-fat mince, and okonomiyaki here typically includes egg, pork, and fish-based dashi/bonito plus a wheat-soy okonomiyaki sauce. No vegan options are documented.

chef_bio.background: A long-standing, individually run okonomiyaki shop in central Hiroshima, tucked near the Tatemachi tram stop behind the Nomura Securities building. The owner-chef cooks every order himself on the first-floor teppan counter, with sofa private rooms upstairs.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop describes its approach as keeping to old-fashioned cooking methods and ways of eating, and takes particular pride in its premium hand-pulled noodles, which it says even the noodle maker has full confidence in.
chef_bio.specialty: Fuchu-yaki, a regional style that uses beef-fat mince rather than the usual pork; the result is crisp on the outside and fluffy inside, with the sweetness of the cabbage playing against the sauce. The shop also serves classic Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, teppan dishes, and even hamburgers.

anecdotes.text: Regulars describe the owner as extremely shy and quiet, soft-spoken rather than gruff, and ultimately a very kind gentleman behind the griddle — as the shop itself notes, '店主は人見知りが激しく愛想も無く無口ですが怒っているわけではございません。とても優男です。'
The shop is known for being crowded with lines forming regularly, but locals say the wait is worth it.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site places Junia at 中区立町3-21 (1F-2F), one minute from the Tatemachi tram behind Nomura Securities, with the owner-chef cooking each order on the 1F teppan and sofa private rooms upstairs; it highlights Fuchu-yaki and premium hand-pulled noodles and carries the verbatim note that the proprietor is very shy but a kind man (とても優男).

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Okonomiyaki and Fuchu-yaki are finished with a standard sweet okonomiyaki sauce, which is wheat-and-soy based; the dishes are also built on wheat batter and wheat noodles.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: Sauce and noodles are documented as present, but nothing on the site states either is wheat- or soy-based, so the gluten assertion is inference presented as sourced. cultural_comfort.note: A small, traditional counter-style okonomiyaki shop where the chef cooks in front of you; little to no English is documented, so basic Japanese or a translation app helps, but pointing at the menu works fine for a relaxed casual meal.

hiro_mikazuki.gf_detail: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki is built on a wheat-flour crepe batter and layered with wheat noodles (そば) or udon, then finished with a wheat-soy-based okonomi sauce. The core dishes here are inherently not gluten-free, and there is no documented gluten-free preparation.

chef_bio.background: A small, owner-run okonomiyaki shop in a quiet residential pocket of Naka Ward near Funairicho, southwest of the Peace Memorial Park, open since 2011 with just about a dozen counter-and-table seats. It keeps a deliberately narrow menu, focusing on doing the classic meat-and-egg okonomiyaki well rather than offering a long list of variations, and has been named to Tabelog's Top 100 Okonomiyaki list.
chef_bio.philosophy: A traditional Hiroshima technique of pressing the okonomiyaki down with a weight on the griddle, using fine boiled noodles griddled to a crisp, fragrant finish on a meticulously maintained teppan.
chef_bio.specialty: The house standard is 肉玉そば (meat, egg, and noodles), with an udon version also available; cheese and double-egg are among the few simple add-ons.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen presses the okonomiyaki with a weight while it cooks and uses fine-textured boiled noodles griddled until crisp, giving a noticeable toasted-wheat aroma that regulars single out.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog lists ミカヅキ in Naka Ward near Funairicho/Kakomachi (加古町) as owner-run, open since Sept 2011, 12 seats, a Tabelog Top 100 Okonomiyaki 2023 selection, with 肉玉そば (¥880), udon substitution and cheese/double-egg add-ons, weight-pressed on a well-kept griddle with crisp noodles (麺はパリ).

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki is finished with a standard okonomi/Worcester-type sauce that is wheat- and soy-based.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a tiny family-run okonomiyaki counter where ordering is simple (point to 肉玉そば or 肉玉うどん) but little to no English is likely, so basic Japanese phrases or a translation app will help.

There is no documented gluten-free menu or wheat-free dashi/soy-sauce alternative, so this is not a suitable destination for strict gluten-free diners.
hiro_taiko_udon_nakamachi_ten.vegan_detail: The Nakamachi branch has a dedicated vegan menu that uses no animal ingredients at all — notably soy-milk tantan udon and a no-soup (dry) tantan udon, available only at this location. The vegan dashi is made 100% from plant materials (kombu, vegetables, fruit) after extensive in-house research, and plant-based tempura is fried in a separate pot and oil kept apart from other orders. Note the standard (non-vegan) dashi uses bonito/mackerel/anchovy and wheat-containing soy sauce, so you must order from the vegan menu specifically. Foreign-language menus are available, which helps when specifying vegan needs.

chef_bio.background: Taiko Udon opened this central Hiroshima location in 2016 as its second shop, set in the city's downtown business and tourism district within easy walking distance of the Peace Memorial Park and Hondori shopping street. By day it is a handmade-udon restaurant; in the evening it shifts into an izakaya-style spot known as 'Udon-mae Taiko' (饂飩前太閤), serving small plates built around local seasonal ingredients alongside the noodles.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen uses no chemical seasonings (mukacho) and emphasizes carefully selected, safe, local seasonal ingredients. The shop went to unusual lengths for plant-based diners, developing a 100% plant dashi from kombu, vegetables and fruit and keeping a separate fryer and oil for plant-based tempura.
chef_bio.specialty: Handmade udon made from a blend of three domestic wheat flours and mineral-rich salt water, given a two-stage rest and made over a full day so it can be served freshly cut and freshly boiled. Signature dishes include the house-favorite ojiya udon and a creative carbonara udon.

anecdotes.text: The shop offers a free 'baby udon' made only with white dashi for families dining with infants ('白だしだけで作った赤ちゃんうどんは無料でお出ししています').
On the last day of each month the shop runs a daytime-only ramen service ('Taiko Ramen').

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official Nakamachi page states the shop opened in 2016 as the 2号店 in central Hiroshima, becomes 饂飩前太閤 (izakaya style) at night, offers a free white-dashi 赤ちゃんうどん, and names ojiya udon (当店一番人気) and carbonara udon as signatures; vegewel confirms 無化調, a 100% plant vegan dashi from kombu/veg/fruit, a separate fryer and oil, three domestic wheat flours, and month-end daytime 太閤ラーメン.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The udon noodles are made from a blend of three domestic wheat flours, and tempura uses wheat batter; no gluten-free option is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The standard dashi uses Marushima soy sauce from Shodoshima (a conventional wheat-based shoyu) along with bonito, mackerel and anchovy, so the regular broth is neither vegan nor wheat-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: For plant-based tempura and fried items, the shop prepares a dedicated oil and pot used only for plant-based items, kept separate from other customers' orders.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Foreign-language menus and a clearly marked vegan menu are available, and the vegan dishes are explicitly stated to contain no animal-derived ingredients.

positives.text: The vegan dashi is made 100% from plant materials (kombu, vegetables and fruit) after extensive in-house research.
Dedicated separate oil and pot are used for plant-based tempura to avoid cross-contact with animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: Foreign-language menus, free Wi-Fi, and counter power outlets make this an easy, welcoming stop for a foreign student, and staff can point vegan diners to the dedicated plant-based menu.

No vegan menu or plant-milk option is documented, so a vegan should ask about dairy-free milk before ordering.

chef_bio.background: Founder Keisuke Sasaki is from Asaminami Ward in Hiroshima City. As a university student he and three friends launched a venture pulling rickshaws on Miyajima, which led him to study the island's history and culture to answer tourists' questions, before turning toward the world of coffee. In 2006 he opened his first self-roasted-coffee cafe at age 23, keeping it open until midnight in a back-alley spot with few customers. By 2009 he had opened a second cafe, sarasvati, as Japan's appreciation for specialty coffee grew.
chef_bio.philosophy: He aims for an 'unnoticed specialty' (意識されないスペシャルティ): he is happiest when people enjoy his coffee without consciously thinking about how special it is, letting it blend naturally into a quiet moment of their day.
chef_bio.specialty: Specialty coffee that he roasts himself on the island, using only the roughly 5% of beans in the market that qualify as 'specialty', alongside a popular specialty-coffee soft serve.

anecdotes.text: He describes the early years bluntly: 'barely surviving, starting in an alley where almost no one came, so we did not get many customers, staying open until midnight' ('やっぱり生きていくのに精一杯。路地裏の、誰も来ないような場所で始めたので、お客さんもそんなに来なくて、夜12時まで開けていました').
The shop is the only place self-roasting specialty coffee on Miyajima, a UNESCO World Heritage island, set in a renovated old-house-style (古民家風) building near the shrine approach.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The note.com interview gives Sasaki's Asaminami-ku origin, the student rickshaw venture with three friends, the 2006 self-roast cafe at 23, the verbatim alley/midnight struggle quote, and the 意識されないスペシャルティ ideal; the official site confirms Itsuki as the only self-roasting specialty shop on Miyajima, ~5% specialty-grade beans, soft serve, a renovated old-house building, and sarasvati (2009).

positives.text: An English menu is available, which helps travelers communicate basic preferences when ordering.

cultural_comfort.note: An English menu is available and ordering is casual cafe-style, so a foreign student can visit comfortably; note that credit cards are not accepted (electronic money and QR payments only).

hiro_hiroshima_tsukemen_benke.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The signature tsukemen is topped with char siu (pork) and served with a soy-chili dipping sauce, and the tantanmen is meat-and-sesame based. No vegan option is documented.
hiro_hiroshima_tsukemen_benke.notes: [Mom & Pop] A veteran Hiroshima tsukemen shop that has been a fixture of the Nagarekawa nightlife street for more than ten years, marked by a red noren curtain near the Billy the Kid bar.

chef_bio.background: A veteran Hiroshima tsukemen shop and longtime fixture of the Nagarekawa nightlife street, run under the Billy the Kid group and marked by its red noren curtain by the Billy the Kid bar.
chef_bio.philosophy: Make-it-your-own bowls: diners choose their noodle portion and toppings and dial the spice level up or down to taste, with a squeeze of lemon to brighten the dip.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style tsukemen: chewy noodles served cold with crisp shredded cabbage, julienned daikon, and char siu, dipped in a bright, refreshingly tangy and spicy sauce; also a Hiroshima specialty soup-less tantanmen.

anecdotes.text: Open from late night into the early morning in the heart of the drinking district, it is a favorite spot to round off a night out with a bowl of noodles.
Marked by a red noren on Hiroshima's Nagarekawa street by the Billy the Kid bar, it is a long-loved tsukemen shop.
The tsukemen has a refreshing sour edge, comes piled with cabbage, shredded daikon and char siu, and lets you adjust spice and portion; adding lemon makes it even more refreshing.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog places 弁慶 in Nagarekawa (open into the early morning, 11:30-14:30 and 19:00-07:00), operated under Billy the Kid Inc. (est. 1994), serving cold Hiroshima tsukemen with cabbage/daikon/char siu, an adjustable tangy-spicy dip finished with lemon, plus a soupless tantanmen; retty corroborates the toppings and customizable spice/portion.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core dishes are wheat-based (wheat tsukemen/ramen noodles and a soy-sauce-based dip), so a shared kitchen makes gluten avoidance impractical.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Hiroshima tsukemen is dipped in a soy-sauce-and-chili sauce; standard Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes are built on pork char siu and meat/sesame-based tantanmen, so animal products are central and shared.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, no-frills local noodle counter in a nightlife alley with no reservations and a mostly Japanese-speaking, late-night crowd; pointing at the menu and choosing your noodle size and spice level works fine, but expect little to no English.

hiro_torii.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The signature dishes — fried oysters (wheat-flour batter and breadcrumbs), tempura-style items, udon/soba/ramen noodles, and grilled/simmered seafood glazed with standard Japanese soy sauce (which contains wheat) — all rely on gluten. There is no documented dedicated fryer or gluten-free menu, so cross-contamination from the shared fry oil and soy-based sauces is likely. The parent company notes it can discuss food allergies in general, but no celiac-safe protocol is documented.
hiro_torii.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The menu is built around oysters, anago (conger eel), and other Setouchi seafood; set meals include chawanmushi (egg custard) and dashi-based soups, and dishes are seasoned with fish stock and soy sauce. No documented plant-based or vegan options.
hiro_torii.notes: [Miyajima] A seafood dining hall on the island of Miyajima, set among the shops on the approach near Itsukushima Shrine and Senjokaku Hall, where oysters are grilled out front to draw in passers-by. (Map pin approximate — Omotesandō; use the Maps link for exact spot.)

chef_bio.background: A seafood dining hall on the island of Miyajima, set among the shops on the approach near Itsukushima Shrine and Senjokaku Hall, where oysters are grilled out front to draw in passers-by.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house aims to be a place to enjoy the flavors of the Seto Inland Sea and to serve a taste that stays in your memory, choosing ingredients and cooking with care.
chef_bio.specialty: Fried-oyster and Miyajima set meals (anago rice paired with oyster fry), anago (conger eel) dishes, and front-of-shop charcoal-grilled oysters, alongside Setouchi seafood, donburi, and noodles.

anecdotes.text: Oysters are grilled at the storefront, a classic Miyajima sight, with the seasonal Setouchi lemon soft serve and strawberry shaved ice (spring-autumn) offered alongside the seafood.
Seating spans two floors, including window-side counter seats and tatami zashiki rooms upstairs, making it comfortable for families and groups visiting the shrine.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: toriiya.co.jp describes とりい as a Setouchi seafood dining hall on Miyajima with storefront charcoal-grilled oysters (6 for ¥1,650), a Miyajima Set (¥2,500) of anago rice + oyster fry, donburi/udon/soba/ramen/curry, seasonal fresh-strawberry shaved ice (Apr-Oct), and two floors with counter and tatami zashiki seating (~115 seats).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Signature fried oysters use wheat-flour batter and breadcrumbs, and the kitchen also serves udon, soba, and ramen, so the shared fry oil and prep surfaces present a high gluten cross-contamination risk.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Grilled and simmered seafood and donburi are glazed/seasoned with standard Japanese soy sauce, which normally contains wheat; no wheat-free tamari is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The menu is seafood-centered (oysters, anago) with egg-based chawanmushi and dashi/soy seasoning throughout, so there is no separation from animal ingredients.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The affiliated company's site states food-allergy inquiries can be accommodated, but no celiac- or vegan-specific protocol is documented for the dining hall.

cultural_comfort.note: A bustling, tourist-friendly seafood dining hall right by the shrine where pointing at picture menus works fine, but staff may have limited English and there is no vegan or gluten-free provision, so a guide or translation help is useful for anyone with strict dietary needs.

hiro_takaya_jizodori_honten.gf_detail: This is a Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki shop. The okonomiyaki itself is built on a wheat-flour batter (crepe layer), is layered with udon or soba noodles, and is finished with okonomiyaki sauce — all of which contain wheat/gluten. There is no indication of any gluten-free menu or accommodation, so it is not suitable for a strict gluten-free diet.
hiro_takaya_jizodori_honten.vegan_detail: The core dish is a "meat and egg" (肉玉) okonomiyaki containing pork, egg, and noodles, and the standard sauce/preparation are not plant-based. No vegan options are documented. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
hiro_takaya_jizodori_honten.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30-15:00 (L.O. 14:30); Dinner 17:00-22:30 (L.O. 22:00). Closed Tuesdays; also closed 1st and 3rd Mondays (holiday hours may vary).
hiro_takaya_jizodori_honten.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, owner-run okonomiyaki counter tucked along Hiroshima's historic Jizo-dori in Fujimi-cho. chef_bio.background: A small, owner-run okonomiyaki counter tucked along Hiroshima's historic Jizo-dori in Fujimi-cho. The proprietor has spent roughly three decades devoted to okonomiyaki, grilling each one personally and one at a time right in front of guests at the 12-seat counter.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop is proud of being a 'seitoha' (orthodox) Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki — authentic, traditional preparation done meticulously. The owner changes the cabbage variety with the seasons and pays close attention to how the vegetables are cut and grilled so their natural sweetness comes through, finished with a house sauce made with plenty of vegetables that is clean and not overly sweet.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki with a meat-and-egg base, customized with your choice of udon or soba; the noodle layer is grilled until distinctively crisp, and the seasonal cabbage and house vegetable-rich sauce are the signatures.

anecdotes.text: You eat straight off the teppan griddle using only a metal spatula — no chopsticks — which feels intimidating to newcomers but becomes part of the charm once you get the hang of it.
The cabbage is swapped by season and the vegetables are cut and grilled with care to draw out their sweetness, paired with a clean, not-sweet house sauce.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ttcbn describes 貴家。地蔵通り本店 as a 12-seat counter on Jizo-dori in Fujimi-cho where the owner-chef of roughly three decades grills each okonomiyaki to order, serves orthodox (正統派) meat-egg okonomiyaki with udon/soba and a crisp noodle layer, and has diners eat off the teppan with a spatula (no chopsticks); tabiiro corroborates the seasonal cabbage and clean, not-sweet vegetable-rich sauce.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Okonomiyaki is cooked on a shared teppan griddle where wheat batter, wheat noodles, and wheat-containing sauce are all prepared, making cross-contact with gluten effectively unavoidable.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Standard okonomiyaki contains pork, egg, and noodles cooked on a shared griddle alongside other meat dishes; no separate vegan preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny counter-only local spot where the owner grills in front of you and you eat straight off the hot griddle with a metal spatula (no chopsticks) — charming but with its own etiquette, so some basic Japanese or a willingness to follow along helps.

Several signature items are inherently wheat-based: okonomiyaki batter, ramen noodles, tempura/karaage batter, katsu breading; and standard soy sauce typically contains wheat. Gluten-sensitive diners should ask directly about specific dishes and cross-contamination before ordering.
hiro_jogesayu.vegan_detail: Fully vegan. 100% plant-based and alcohol-free across all dishes and desserts, with no animal-derived ingredients used anywhere in the kitchen.

chef_bio.background: JoGeSaYu opened in May 2025 in central Hiroshima (Otemachi) as a fully plant-based, alcohol-free restaurant. Its food is overseen by Katsumi Kusumoto, the chef behind Saido, which the international vegan platform HappyCow named the world's best vegan restaurant in 2019, while the desserts are guided by award-winning pastry chef Hironobu Tsujiguchi. The kitchen turns Japanese comfort food such as sushi, okonomiyaki, tempura bowls and karaage into entirely plant-based versions.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name (up, down, left, right) expresses acceptance of every direction, value, and form of diversity. The team set out to create a single table where people of any background — religion, allergies, dietary practice — can share a meal together, and to prove that plant-based food need not lack flavor.
chef_bio.specialty: Plant-based renditions of Japanese classics: vegan sushi, okonomiyaki, tempura bowls and karaage, alongside refined vegan desserts such as parfaits and lemon cake.

anecdotes.text: The name was chosen to symbolize openness to all directions and forms of diversity, reflecting its goal of a table where everyone can eat together regardless of dietary restriction.
Culinary direction comes from Katsumi Kusumoto of Saido, named the world's best vegan restaurant by HappyCow in 2019, with desserts by pastry chef Hironobu Tsujiguchi.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site states outright that culinary director Katsumi Kusumoto is the chef of Saido (HappyCow world's best vegan restaurant 2019), sweets are by patissier Hironobu Tsujiguchi, and 上下左右 symbolizes acceptance of all directions and diversity; Balcom (料理監修は…世界1位に輝いた) and fooddiversity corroborate the leadership, the May 2025 Otemachi opening, 100% plant-based/alcohol-free food, and dishes including vegan sushi, okonomiyaki, tempura bowls, karaage, lemon cake and parfaits.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No information published on whether the soy sauce or seasonings used are gluten-free or wheat-free; standard soy sauce typically contains wheat. Confirm directly if avoiding gluten.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The entire kitchen is 100% plant-based with no animal products or alcohol used anywhere, so there is no animal-ingredient cross-contact risk.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The menu is described as built to accommodate diverse backgrounds including religious dietary rules and allergies, so diners with and without restrictions can eat together.

positives.text: 100% plant-based and alcohol-free across the whole menu, making it a fully safe choice for vegans and vegetarians.
Vegan versions of Japanese favorites such as sushi, okonomiyaki, ramen, curry, tempura and karaage, plus vegan parfaits and lemon cake.
Official website available in English, Japanese, and Chinese, easing communication for international diners.

cultural_comfort.note: The restaurant's own website is offered in English, Japanese, and Chinese with an English contact option, so a foreign student should feel comfortable communicating here.

chef_bio.background: A small, tucked-away okonomiyaki shop in a back alley near the Tsuchihashi/Tokaichimachi trams, only about an eight-minute walk from the Peace Memorial Park and A-Bomb Dome. Despite being off the main tourist routes, it has been a neighborhood favorite for many years, run intimately by the cook and his wife.
chef_bio.philosophy: Let the vegetable lead and finish each okonomiyaki with care. The cook works the griddle by reading its different temperature zones to cook precisely, a hands-on craft at a counter that seats only a handful of people.
chef_bio.specialty: Cabbage-forward Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki. The name plays on 甘藍 (kanran, classical Japanese for cabbage), signaling that cabbage is the true star; the shop even offers a double-vegetable ('倍ヤサイ') option.

anecdotes.text: The cook is described as a true craftsman, deftly using the different heat zones across the iron griddle to finish each okonomiyaki carefully.
Though traditionally eaten straight off the hot griddle, the shop will serve okonomiyaki on a plate for visitors who prefer it, a small kindness toward travelers.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: onetabi.com documents the husband-and-wife operation, the griddle heat-zone technique, the 甘藍 (cabbage) name origin, the 倍ヤサイ double-vegetable option, roughly 7 counter seats plus a couple of tables, and plate service for visitors; it locates the shop about 8 minutes from the Peace Park near the Tsuchihashi/Tokaichimachi trams.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Single shared iron griddle (teppan) used for wheat batter, wheat noodles, pork, and egg, so heavy gluten cross-contact is inherent.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes are finished with okonomiyaki sauce, which is wheat-and-soy based; standard for Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Everything is cooked on one griddle shared with pork and egg, so no dish can be considered free of animal-product cross-contact.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a tiny owner-run counter shop where ordering and chatting happen mostly in Japanese, though the cook is used to visitors and will plate your okonomiyaki rather than serve it straight off the griddle if you prefer.

chef_bio.background: Vegan Fruits Cafe Tamaru is part of TAMARU, a Hiroshima fruit business that grew out of a small fruit vendor near Hiroshima Station with roughly 70 years of history. In 2022 the downtown Kamiyacho location reinvented itself, turning its entire menu plant-based to introduce locals and visitors to vegan food.
chef_bio.philosophy: To show that vegan dessert can be genuinely delicious by building everything around high-quality fruit and grains rather than animal products or refined white sugar.
chef_bio.specialty: Fruit-forward vegan parfaits and sweets made without eggs, dairy, or white sugar; signature parfaits pile on whole bunches of seasonal fruit such as Shine Muscat, alongside vegan sandwiches and fruit oatmeal with almond milk.

anecdotes.text: The cafe is an offshoot of a long-running family fruit vendor near Hiroshima Station that has been selling fruit for about 70 years, so the parfaits are built on a deep fruit-sourcing pedigree.
The Kamiyacho branch renovated and switched its entire menu to vegan, eliminating eggs, dairy, and white sugar.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: restaurant-guide.jp confirms the Kamiyacho shop's all-vegan menu (no eggs, dairy, or white sugar), the fruit oatmeal with almond milk, parfaits and vegan sandwiches, and its ties to the TAMARU fruit business; japantravel documents the ~70-year fruit-vendor origin near Hiroshima Station, and the Shine Muscat parfait is documented across guides. The exact renovation month (April 2022) could not be traced, so it is stated only as 2022.

positives.text: The entire menu is plant-based, made without eggs, dairy, or white sugar, so vegan diners do not need to scrutinize individual dishes.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, welcoming fruit cafe in a busy downtown shopping area; menus are mostly in Japanese with lots of photos, so a few basic phrases and pointing will get you by comfortably.

hiro_kaki_to_kaisen_sakaba_um.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is advertised. As an izakaya, fried/tempura oysters use wheat batter and most dishes rely on wheat-based soy sauce; no dedicated GF preparation indicated.
hiro_kaki_to_kaisen_sakaba_um.vegan_detail: An oyster and seafood izakaya — the menu centers on oysters, sashimi and fish, with wheat-soy-sauce seasonings. No vegan offerings indicated.
hiro_kaki_to_kaisen_sakaba_um.hours_raw: Mon-Thu 17:00-01:00 (next day), Fri 17:00-02:00 (next day), Sat 16:00-02:00 (next day), Sun 17:00-01:00 (next day) (official site). Note: reservation aggregators list earlier midday openings on some days; official site hours used here.
hiro_kaki_to_kaisen_sakaba_um.notes: An oyster-and-seafood izakaya in the heart of Nagarekawa, central Hiroshima's largest nightlife quarter, serving oysters and seafood bought from local Hiroshima suppliers.

chef_bio.background: An oyster-and-seafood izakaya in the heart of Nagarekawa, central Hiroshima's largest nightlife quarter, serving oysters and seafood bought from local Hiroshima suppliers.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima oysters served many ways — creamy raw oysters by the piece, fragrant grilled oysters, oyster tempura, fried oysters and sake-steamed oysters with butter — alongside sashimi platters and a deep lineup of Hiroshima local sake such as Kamotsuru, Ugo no Tsuki and Kirei.

anecdotes.text: Set in a modern, black-toned interior with atmospheric lighting and fully private rooms with sunken-floor seating, it pairs market-fresh oysters with regional sake.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site confirms oysters bought from local Hiroshima suppliers and served raw by the piece, grilled, as tempura, fried and sake-steamed with butter, plus a Hiroshima local-sake list (Kamotsuru, Ugo-no-Tsuki, Kirei) and private sunken-floor rooms in the Nagarekawa nightlife quarter.

cultural_comfort.note: A lively local izakaya in the Nagarekawa nightlife district where some basic Japanese or a translation app will help, as menus and staff are oriented to Japanese guests.

Effectively every dish here contains gluten, and there is no documented gluten-free preparation.

hiro_yagenbori_hassho.hours_raw: Tue-Sat 16:00-22:30 (L.O. 22:30); Sun & holidays 16:00-21:00 (L.O. 21:00). Closed Mondays, and the 1st and 3rd Tuesday of each month.
hiro_yagenbori_hassho.notes: [Mom & Pop] Yagenbori Hassho is the original, owner-run shop tucked into the Yagenbori district of central Hiroshima, around the corner from the Hatchobori entertainment area and within walking distance of Hondori. chef_bio.background: Yagenbori Hassho is a celebrated, owner-run shop tucked into the Yagenbori district of central Hiroshima, around the corner from the Hatchobori entertainment area and within walking distance of Hondori. It has been grilling Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki for roughly four decades and is regarded as one of the city's defining okonomiyaki houses.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen takes its time, cooking each okonomiyaki slowly over about 20 to 30 minutes so the cabbage steams down sweet and the layers meld, prizing careful technique and good ingredients over speed.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, with the soba-niku-tama (noodle, pork and egg) okonomiyaki as the signature; oysters appear on the griddle in winter.

anecdotes.text: Each okonomiyaki is grilled patiently for about 20 to 30 minutes, a deliberately slow approach that is part of the shop's reputation.
The house favorite is the soba-niku-tama okonomiyaki, layering wheat noodles, cabbage, pork and egg.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official gorp site states 創業40年 (established 40 years), names soba-niku-tama as the top seller made with 'twin eggs', and notes the ~20-30 minute cook time; Tabelog confirms seasonal winter oysters and consistent Tabelog-100 okonomiyaki selection. Whether this is the very first Hassho shop is not documented, so that claim was removed.

cultural_comfort.note: An English menu is available and the counter is welcoming, but it is a small, busy, cash-only neighborhood shop, so a friendly greeting and patience during the long cook time go a long way.

hiro_sarashina.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The traditional batter and broth lean on bonito (katsuo) and tororo-kombu dashi flavor, the signature dish includes pork and egg, and dishes are cooked on a shared teppan with meat and seafood. No vegan version is documented.

chef_bio.background: Sarashina has been making Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki since 1951, having started in the post-war years and grown into one of the long-running stalls that became part of Okonomimura, the multi-floor okonomiyaki complex in the Shintenchi district just east of the Peace Memorial Park.
chef_bio.philosophy: An unhurried, careful approach: the cook grills each okonomiyaki slowly and asks each guest about preferences such as whether to add red pickled ginger, tailoring the dish to the person in front of the counter.
chef_bio.specialty: Traditional griddle-cooked okonomiyaki layered with cabbage, pork, egg and noodles; the kitchen is known for generously folding in bonito flakes and tororo-kombu (shaved kelp) for a deep, gentle umami that defines its old-school flavor. The most-ordered plate is the classic nikutama-soba (pork, egg and noodles).

anecdotes.text: The shop dates to 1951 and is part of Okonomimura, the okonomiyaki food theme park near Hatchobori; it has kept the same tororo-kombu-and-bonito tradition for decades.
Staff take the time to ask guests about toppings like benishoga (red pickled ginger) so each okonomiyaki matches the customer's taste.

chef_bio.background: Chiichan is one of the oldest shops in Hiroshima's Okonomi-mura, the famous building stacked with okonomiyaki stalls. It was opened by Shozaburo Furuta, who became the very first 'village head' of Okonomi-mura when the collective of food stalls was organized in December 1965 — and whose own nickname, 'Chiichan', gave the shop its name. It has been passed down within the family and is now carried on by the second generation, keeping a single griddle counter of about 18 seats going for over half a century.
chef_bio.philosophy: Cooking centered on local Hiroshima ingredients while keeping salt and oil to a minimum, prizing the soft-runny egg and the fragrant crispness of the griddled noodles.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style negiyaki piled with sweet locally grown green onion (negi) and a trademark soft, runny half-cooked egg; seafood-and-oyster negiyaki in winter is a draw, alongside classic Hiroshima okonomiyaki and teppanyaki.

anecdotes.text: Chiichan's founder, Shozaburo Furuta, was the first 'village head' (shochou) of Okonomi-mura when the stall collective was formed in December 1965, and the shop — named after his nickname — has operated for over 50 years, carried on by the next generation.
The shop is known for negiyaki using sweet Hiroshima-grown green onion and a signature runny half-cooked egg, with winter Hiroshima oysters among its seasonal highlights.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Japanese Wikipedia states Okonomi-mura was established in December 1965 and its first village head was 古田正三郎 (Shozaburo Furuta), nicknamed 'ちいちゃん' — the source of the shop's name. Guides confirm the shop is now run by the second generation, seats about 18, and is known for Hiroshima green-onion negiyaki with a creamy half-cooked egg.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Okonomiyaki and negiyaki are cooked on a single shared teppan griddle and built from wheat batter and wheat noodles, so heavy gluten cross-contact is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes are finished with a wheat-based okonomiyaki/Worcestershire-style sauce, which contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The shared griddle is used for pork, egg, seafood and oysters; specialties prominently feature egg, so vegan separation is not feasible.

positives.text: Small two-person family operation cooking at the counter, so you can watch your dish made and speak directly with the cook about ingredients.

cultural_comfort.note: A friendly, family-run counter griddle shop inside the tourist-familiar Okonomi-mura; a few words of Japanese and pointing at the griddle go a long way, and staff are used to visitors.

hiro_susumu.gf_detail: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki is built on a wheat-flour crepe batter and layered with wheat-based okonomiyaki sauce, plus typically yakisoba/udon noodles. This is not a gluten-free-friendly dish or venue and there is no indication of gluten-free accommodation.

anecdotes.text: Susumu sits on the 2nd floor of お好み共和国 ひろしま村 with roughly 26 seats, and its most-ordered dish in reviews is the nikutama-soba.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny family-run teppan stall inside the bustling Okonomimura food building; staff are used to tourists but English is limited, so a few words of Japanese and pointing at the griddle go a long way.

hiro_bunchan.gf_detail: This is a traditional Hiroshima okonomiyaki shop. The okonomiyaki crepe base, the savory sauce, and the noodles all contain wheat, and there is no indication of any gluten-free preparation or dedicated equipment. Not suitable for a strict gluten-free diet.
hiro_bunchan.vegan_detail: Hiroshima okonomiyaki is built around egg, pork, and a layer of fried noodles, finished with a savory sauce and bonito; the menu centers on these. There is no documented vegan option, so this is not a suitable destination for vegan or vegetarian diners.

hiro_hiroshima_kara_tsukemen_.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The signature spicy dipping broth is built on seafood (oyster and scallop adductor), and toppings include squid tempura and other animal-based items. No vegan option is documented.
hiro_hiroshima_kara_tsukemen_.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small late-night noodle counter in Hiroshima's Yagenbori district that opened in April 2022, sitting just south of the Nagarekawa and Hatchobori nightlife and drawing diners looking for a satisfying bowl to cap off an evening out.

chef_bio.background: A small late-night noodle counter in Hiroshima's Yagenbori district that opened in April 2022, sitting just south of the Nagarekawa and Hatchobori nightlife and drawing diners looking for a satisfying bowl to cap off an evening out.
chef_bio.philosophy: Standing out from the crowd: the shop leans into unusual, original ingredients rather than copying the standard local tsukemen template.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style spicy tsukemen (dipping noodles) with a seafood-forward broth made using oyster and scallop, served with curly dry noodles and distinctive toppings like lemon-scented squid tempura and mushroom duxelles; oil-based abura soba is also on the menu.

anecdotes.text: A local food writer remarked he had never seen Hiroshima tsukemen differentiated this far, calling out ingredients not found at other shops.
The shop is open only at night and is widely treated as a go-to spot for a finishing bowl after drinking in the nearby entertainment district.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The modokimaru blog confirms the April 2022 opening in Yagenbori, the night-only hours (18:00-03:00), the oyster-and-scallop seafood broth with curly dry noodles, the lemon-scented squid tempura and mushroom-duxelles toppings, the abura soba, roughly 14 seats, and the writer's remark that he had never seen Hiroshima tsukemen differentiated this far.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat noodles are the base of both the tsukemen and abura soba, so the kitchen handles wheat throughout; no gluten-free preparation is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth uses a soy-style seasoning typical of Hiroshima tsukemen, which is normally wheat-based; no wheat-free tamari is mentioned.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: The cited article never mentions soy sauce; it describes the tare as oyster-and-scallop dashi. The soy inference is imported from the generic Hiroshima-tsukemen style, not from this source. Say so, or cite a Hiroshima-tsukemen reference separately — do not attribute it to this blog.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The dipping broth itself is seafood-based (oyster and scallop), so it is not separable from animal ingredients.

cultural_comfort.note: A small late-night local counter where ordering is in Japanese and the vibe is a post-drinking noodle stop; a foreign student comfortable pointing at the menu or with basic Japanese will do fine.

hiro_shoryuken.gf_detail: This is a Hakata Nagahama-style tonkotsu (pork-bone) ramen shop. The noodles are wheat-based and the broth and tare contain wheat-derived soy sauce, so the core menu is not gluten-free. No gluten-free options are documented and there is no indication of allergen accommodation.
hiro_shoryuken.vegan_detail: The signature ramen is built on a long-simmered pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth with chashu pork, egg, and back-fat. The broth itself is animal-based, so the menu is not suitable for vegans or vegetarians and no plant-based bowl is documented.
hiro_shoryuken.hours_raw: 19:00-07:00 daily (Tabelog). Other listings give 20:00-05:00 (next day). Late-night ramen shop; hours can vary, confirm before visiting.
hiro_shoryuken.notes: [Mom & Pop] A tiny late-night ramen counter tucked into Hiroshima's Yagenbori/Nagarekawa nightlife quarter in Naka Ward, Shoryuken caters to the after-drinking crowd, staying open through the small hours when most of the city has closed. chef_bio.background: A tiny late-night ramen counter tucked into Hiroshima's Yagenbori/Nagarekawa nightlife quarter in Naka Ward, Shoryuken caters to the after-drinking crowd, staying open through the small hours when most of the city has closed. It operates as a sister shop of the Hakata ramen house Nagahama No. 1 (長浜ナンバーワン), run by the elder brother while the younger runs Nagahama No. 1.
chef_bio.specialty: Hakata Nagahama-style tonkotsu ramen: a rich pork-bone broth served with thin, firm noodles you can order to your preferred firmness, soft chashu, plenty of green onion, and a half boiled egg, finished with a touch of back-fat. Free-to-add toppings like takana (pickled mustard greens) and red pickled ginger are on the counter, and tsukemen and spicy versions are also offered.

anecdotes.text: Shoryuken is run as a sister shop of the Hakata ramen house Nagahama No. 1, reflected in its Nagahama-style thin-noodle tonkotsu bowls.
It is known locally as a go-to spot for a satisfying late-night bowl after a night out in the Nagarekawa district.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shop's own Instagram (@syour_yuken) is titled '長浜ナンバーワン姉妹店 昇龍軒', confirming it is the sister shop of Hakata's 長浜ナンバーワン (elder brother runs Shoryuken, younger brother runs Nagahama No.1). Reviews confirm the Nagahama-style thin-noodle tonkotsu finished with back-fat and tabletop takana/benishoga/sesame; listings confirm the late-night 20:00-05:00 hours in Yagenbori (~13 seats).

soy_sauce_wheat.text: As a tonkotsu ramen shop, the broth tare uses standard wheat-based Japanese soy sauce and the noodles are wheat; gluten is unavoidable in the core menu.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The base broth is pork-bone (tonkotsu); there is no animal-free broth, so even noodles-only orders are cooked in and around animal-based products.

cultural_comfort.note: A small late-night counter ramen shop in a nightlife district where ordering is in Japanese and there is no English menu, so a few basic phrases or a translation app will help; pointing at the menu works fine for a simple bowl.

hiro_niwa_cafe_miyama.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is documented. The menu centers on home-style set meals, sweets/coffee, and a wagyu beef steak set; sauces and seasonings typically contain wheat-based soy sauce, and no dedicated gluten-free preparation is advertised. A celiac diner would need to ask directly and should not assume safe options.
hiro_niwa_cafe_miyama.vegan_detail: Not a vegan or vegetarian establishment. The set lunch includes home-style side dishes (obanzai) and miso soup, and a signature dish is Hiroshima wagyu beef; miso soup and dashi-based dishes commonly contain fish stock. A few vegetable sides may be available, but there is no documented vegan menu, so ask in advance.
hiro_niwa_cafe_miyama.hours_raw: Sources conflict: an earlier listing shows Lunch 11:00-14:00 / Cafe 14:00-17:00 / Dinner 17:00-20:30 with Tuesday closed; a more recent listing shows Mon/Fri/Sun 17:00-20:30, Sat 11:00-20:30, and Tue/Wed/Thu closed. Confirm directly before visiting.
hiro_niwa_cafe_miyama.notes: [Mom & Pop] Niwa Cafe Miyama opened in April 2020 on Machiya-dori, a quiet lane that runs parallel to Miyajima's busy Omotesando shopping arcade, away from the crowds that fill the island's main street. It occupies a traditional townhouse, and visitors reach it down a narrow alley

chef_bio.background: Niwa Cafe Miyama opened in April 2020 on Machiya-dori, a quiet lane that runs parallel to Miyajima's busy Omotesando shopping arcade, away from the crowds that fill the island's main street. It occupies a traditional townhouse, and visitors reach it down a narrow alley and through a garden courtyard before stepping inside.
chef_bio.philosophy: The cafe is built around its rare garden setting, offering a calm, unhurried place to eat at your own pace rather than the rushed, crowded experience common at tourist spots on the island.
chef_bio.specialty: Home-style daily set lunch with seasonal vegetable sides, miso soup and pickles, plus a Hiroshima wagyu beef steak set; coffee and sweets in the afternoon.

anecdotes.text: Having a cafe with its own garden is unusual on Miyajima, and the spot is known as a hidden retreat reached through a quiet courtyard off the main lane, with views of the garden from inside.
It was announced as a newly opened dining spot on Miyajima's machiya street in April 2020.
anecdotes.source: https://hg-nishichugoku.co.jp/グランドオープン　庭カフェ御山/

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: hg-nishichugoku announced the grand opening on 13 April 2020 on Miyajima's Machiya-dori; co-trip confirms the rare garden setting reached via a back alley, the family-style daily set lunch with seasonal vegetables, miso soup and pickles, and an A5-grade Hiroshima-wagyu steak set, with coffee and sweets.
sources: https://hg-nishichugoku.co.jp/グランドオープン　庭カフェ御山/

cultural_comfort.note: A small, locally run Japanese cafe off the tourist path; some basic Japanese (or a translation app) will help, though the relaxed garden setting is welcoming to visitors.

hiro_sassou_bettei.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The core dishes are wheat-noodle ramen (汁なし担々麺, 台湾まぜそば, 油そば) and the sauce/tare is soy-sauce based, so wheat is present in both the noodles and the seasoning. No gluten-free menu, noodle, or preparation is documented.
hiro_sassou_bettei.vegan_detail: Not vegan. Documented ingredients include pork mince (豚ミンチ) in most dan dan noodles, raw egg (生卵) on the Taiwan mazesoba, a chicken-bone broth, and bonito/tuna katsuobushi (マグロ削り節) used in the broth and tare. Peanuts appear in one oil-noodle dish. No vegan options are documented.
hiro_sassou_bettei.hours_raw: 11:00-20:00 (until sold out). Some sources list 11:00-20:30. Closed Wednesdays (official/Tabelog); some articles list Thursday instead.
hiro_sassou_bettei.notes: [Mom & Pop] This is the second shop ('Bettei', meaning annex) of Menya Sassou, which owner Masanobu Miyafuji opened in Saijō, Higashi-Hiroshima in 2016 and built into a local favorite for brothless dan dan noodles. He opened this central Hiroshima location on September 2, 2022, in

chef_bio.origin: Higashi-Hiroshima (Saijō); opened this central Hiroshima branch behind Hiroshima PARCO
chef_bio.background: This is the second shop ('Bettei', meaning annex) of Menya Sassou, which owner Masanobu Miyafuji opened in Saijō, Higashi-Hiroshima in 2016 and built into a local favorite for brothless dan dan noodles. He opened this central Hiroshima location on September 2, 2022, in a clean, stylish, wood-grain café-like space with a counter and open kitchen, deliberately designed to be easy to enter for women dining alone and welcoming to international visitors.
chef_bio.philosophy: Miyafuji emphasizes balance over heat — prioritizing aroma rather than spiciness. He makes his own chili oil tuned for fragrance, lets diners adjust heat themselves with a five-spice chili oil, fruit vinegar, and sansho pepper on the table, and recommends level 1 heat for newcomers. The tare is a soy-sauce base with sesame paste (芝麻醬) and vinegar; the pork mince is salt-stir-fried then simmered in pure-rice sake to render out oil and water; the chicken broth is built up with plenty of aromatic vegetables and sweetened with tuna katsuobushi; the noodles come from a maker in Higashi-Hiroshima.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style brothless dan dan noodles (汁なし担々麺), alongside Taiwan mazesoba and abura soba

anecdotes.text: After opening during the COVID period the central Hiroshima shop was initially quiet, but word of mouth grew from about three months in and it now has a loyal regular following.
Miyafuji describes his approach as balance-focused, prioritizing fragrance over heat, with a house-made chili oil and a tare built on soy sauce, sesame paste and vinegar.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site confirms the central Hiroshima branch opened on 2 September 2022; Chugoku Shimbun confirms owner 宮藤正信, the 2016 Saijō original (麺屋颯爽), the aroma-over-heat philosophy, house-made chili oil, the soy/sesame-paste/vinegar tare, the sake-simmered pork mince, the chicken-and-katsuobushi broth and the Higashi-Hiroshima noodles; e-tomato describes the clean, wood-grain café-style space welcoming to solo women and the post-opening word-of-mouth growth.

gf_cross_contamination.text: All main dishes are wheat noodles prepared in a shared noodle kitchen, so cross-contact with wheat is unavoidable; no gluten-free preparation is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tare (sauce) is described as soy-sauce based with sesame paste and vinegar; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes use pork mince, raw egg, chicken broth and tuna/bonito katsuobushi; animal products are central to the menu with no vegan items documented.
The chicken-bone broth is sweetened with tuna katsuobushi and the pork mince is simmered in sake, so fish and meat are integral even to the base components.

positives.text: The official menu lists specific allergen notes per dish (pork mince in most dan dan noodles, raw egg in Taiwan mazesoba, peanuts in the junk oil noodles), which helps diners identify what to avoid.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, stylish counter noodle shop with a PayPay-enabled ticket machine that is comfortable for solo diners and described as welcoming to international visitors, though ordering is mostly in Japanese, so a few basic phrases help.

hiro_yuki_tei.gf_detail: The core dishes are tsukemen and dandan noodles made with wheat flour noodles, plus char siu pork and a chili-based dipping sauce that typically uses wheat-containing soy sauce. There is no gluten-free option and no indication of allergen accommodation.
hiro_yuki_tei.vegan_detail: Dishes are built around wheat noodles topped with char siu pork, and the dipping/seasoning sauce is meat- and likely fish/soy-based. No vegan or vegetarian options are documented.
hiro_yuki_tei.hours_raw: New Yagenbori location (reopened 2026-03-01) does not publish exact hours on its listing; mobile-order system. Prior operating pattern: Mon-Sat 18:00-03:00 (some listings 17:30-03:30), closed Sundays and holidays (also Obon and New Year).
hiro_yuki_tei.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, independent late-night noodle shop in central Hiroshima's nightlife district, specializing in Hiroshima-style tsukemen (cold dipping noodles) and chili-driven dandan noodles. chef_bio.background: A small, independent late-night noodle shop in central Hiroshima's Nagarekawa nightlife district, specializing in Hiroshima-style tsukemen (cold dipping noodles). After years near Kochi-cho/Ginzan-cho, the shop relocated a short distance to a counter-only (L-shaped counter) space in Yagenbori, reopening on March 1, 2026.
chef_bio.philosophy: An unfussy, noodle-first approach: well-textured noodles and a clean dipping sauce that lets the chili and the noodles speak rather than heavy seasoning.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style tsukemen: firm, springy wheat noodles served cold with cucumber, green onion, boiled cabbage and soft char siu, dipped into a chili-based sauce whose heat can be customized up to 20x.

anecdotes.text: A regular described the dipping sauce as pleasantly simple and not over-seasoned, with heat that starts mild and builds gradually as you eat; staff steady customers by suggesting a starting spice level (around 3x for chili fans).
The noodle prep is something of a spectacle: after boiling, the cook drains and flips the noodles in a large colander dozens of times (reportedly 40-50) to firm up their texture before plating.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog lists the current Yagenbori shop (胡町からの移転、2026年3月1日オープン、L字カウンターのみ); HotPepper confirms tsukemen with spice adjustable up to 20倍 and ~19 seats; an Ameblo review documents the 3x-recommended heat and the repeated 麺返し draining technique.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat noodles are boiled in shared water and the menu is entirely noodle-based, so cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable; no gluten-free preparation is offered.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The chili dipping/seasoning sauce for tsukemen and dandan noodles typically relies on wheat-containing Japanese soy sauce; no wheat-free soy sauce is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Bowls are topped with char siu pork and the sauces are meat/fish-based, so all menu items involve animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny late-night counter ramen shop with a mobile-order system and a Japanese-only menu, so basic Japanese or a translation app helps; the spice level is fully customizable, so it is easy to order something mild.

hiro_delica_celery.gf_detail: The signature dish is a wheat-noodle soupless dan dan men, and the seasoning is built on a miso-and-soy-sauce base (soy sauce normally contains wheat). There is no indication of gluten-free menu items or preparation, so this is not suitable for someone requiring strict gluten avoidance.
hiro_delica_celery.vegan_detail: The dan dan noodles are topped with a miso-seasoned minced-meat base, and the evening menu is bento/izakaya fare; the broth/seasoning uses soy sauce and animal ingredients. No vegan dishes are documented.
hiro_delica_celery.hours_raw: Mon–Fri 11:30–13:30, 18:00–22:00; closed Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays. (Lunch noodle service runs only the two midday hours.)

chef_bio.origin: Hiroshima (originally in the Nakamachi district before relocating to Otemachi)
chef_bio.background: Delica Celery started life as a bento and prepared-foods shop in Nakamachi, where the owner, Yamamoto Hiroyuki, set out roughly 50 large trays of dishes every day, sold by the portion/weight under a punishing sales grind. The relentless workload eventually wore down his health, prompting a move to the present Otemachi location behind Chuden Hospital and a complete reinvention of the business about a dozen years ago.
chef_bio.philosophy: After burning out on the old high-volume deli, Yamamoto rebuilt the shop around a focused, sustainable concept: a short, two-hour lunch service (11:30-13:30) centered on one dish done well. His seasoning is deliberately bold so it doubles as a sauce for rice.
chef_bio.specialty: Soupless dan dan noodles (汁なし担々麺, 650 yen) at lunch, with the shop turning into an izakaya in the evening

anecdotes.text: The miso seasoning is made strong on purpose so it pairs with rice - in the owner's words, 'みその強い味付けにしているのでご飯との相性がいいんです.' The base layers slow-simmered root vegetables, ginger, garlic and aromatics into a soy-sauce broth, then piles on miso minced meat, sesame, crunchy Korean chili and a mountain of green onion, leaving plenty of sauce to finish over self-serve rice (50 yen a bowl, refillable).

The rice habit borders on legend: on one midweek lunch the shop blew through 4.5 measures of cooked rice in two hours and had to cook more, thanks to neighborhood office workers ordering refill after refill to soak up the leftover sauce.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The Chugoku Shimbun feature confirms owner Yamamoto Hiroyuki's Nakamachi bento-shop past, the health-driven move to Otemachi (behind Chuden Hospital) and reinvention ~12 years ago, the 650-yen soupless dandan, the 'miso pairs with rice' quote, 50-yen refillable rice and the 4.5-measure rice rush. The ~50-trays-a-day detail is corroborated by shop-history writeups found via search.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core dish is wheat noodles seasoned with a miso and soy-sauce base, so gluten is integral and there is no documented gluten-free handling.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth/seasoning is built on soy sauce (typically wheat-containing) layered with miso.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Signature noodles are topped with miso-seasoned minced meat; no vegan preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a tiny, cash-only neighborhood spot run by the owner with ordering via ticket machine and little to no English, so basic Japanese and a relaxed attitude will help a foreign student feel at home.

hiro_tsuda_seifudo.gf_detail: Momiji manju are sponge cakes made from wheat flour batter, so the core product is not gluten-free. No gluten-free options are indicated. Not suitable for those avoiding gluten.
hiro_tsuda_seifudo.vegan_detail: Momiji manju batter is a castella-style sponge typically made with eggs and dairy, and flavors include milk chocolate and others with dairy. The seasonal oyster gratin bun (kaki gra-man) contains shellfish and dairy. No vegan offerings are documented.

chef_bio.background: A long-established maple-leaf bun (momiji manju) shop on Miyajima founded in 1908 (Meiji 41) and now run by the third generation of the same family. It sits in the middle of the Omotesando shopping arcade leading toward Itsukushima Shrine, in a nostalgic retro storefront.
chef_bio.philosophy: Rather than chasing novelty, the shop values doing the ordinary things well and keeping the old-fashioned method consistent across generations.
chef_bio.specialty: Traditional koshi-an (smooth red bean) momiji manju baked in the classic style, with varieties such as red bean, milk chocolate, blueberry, and black sesame; from October through March it also sells a distinctive oyster gratin steamed bun (kaki gra-man, made with Shimada Suisan oysters) and offers shaved ice and soft serve in warmer months.

anecdotes.text: The shop has been baking momiji manju in the classic style since 1908 and is now in its third family generation, and invites visitors to sit in its small rest area to enjoy a freshly baked manju with tea.
A beautiful calico cat acts as the shop's signboard mascot and is a popular photo subject for visitors, often appearing on the shop's Instagram.
Its in-shop pamphlet recounts the playful origin legend of momiji manju tied to a remark attributed to Ito Hirobumi about maple-leaf-shaped hands.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: shinise.tv records the 1908 (明治41) founding, third-generation family operation, koshi-an classic-style manju, the small tea rest area, and the Ito Hirobumi maple-leaf-hands legend from the in-shop pamphlet. oyakodetanoshimou.com confirms the calico-cat mascot, the milk-chocolate/blueberry/black-sesame varieties, the October-March oyster-gratin bun (かきグラまん, Shimada Suisan), and on-site shaved ice/soft serve.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The shop's entire core product line is wheat-flour sponge cake baked on the premises, so the environment is flour-heavy with no gluten-free preparation noted.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Manju are baked with batter and offered alongside milk chocolate and dairy items, with the seasonal oyster gratin bun containing shellfish and cream sauce, indicating shared handling of animal-derived ingredients.

positives.text: Momiji manju are hand-made and baked in-shop, and can be eaten fresh in a small seating area.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed walk-up confectionery counter on the main Miyajima arcade; you can point at the maple-leaf cakes and pay easily, though staff likely speak little English so a few words of Japanese or pointing helps.

hiro_wasou_pettara_pottara_ho.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The mochi/rice base is gluten-free in itself, but each piece is glazed and finished with a sweet soy sauce, and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. No gluten-free preparation or separate handling is documented. Celiac travelers should avoid.
hiro_wasou_pettara_pottara_ho.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The only items are grilled mochi-rice topped with oyster (牡蠣) or filled with conger eel (穴子), both finished with a soy-based glaze. There is no plant-based option on the menu.
hiro_wasou_pettara_pottara_ho.notes: [Mom & Pop] 和奏 ぺったらぽったら本舗 is a small independent stall on Miyajima, set along the seaside walking path that leads toward Itsukushima Shrine. Its signature is 'pettara pottara' — a Miyajima specialty of mochi-rice (a blend of glutinous and regular rice) molded into a small oval onig

chef_bio.background: 和奏 ぺったらぽったら本舗 is a small independent stall on Miyajima (Kitanohama, on the seaside walking path that leads toward Itsukushima Shrine, quieter than the main arcade). Its signature is 'pettara pottara' - a Miyajima specialty of mochi-rice (a blend of glutinous and regular rice) molded into a small oval onigiri-like cake, brushed with a sweet-savory soy glaze and grilled until the outside is crisp and caramelized while the inside stays chewy ('crispy outside, chewy inside'). It comes two ways: topped with a plump local oyster, or with conger eel (anago) tucked inside.
chef_bio.specialty: Grilled mochi-rice 'pettara pottara' with either oyster on top or conger eel inside, finished to order with a torch and a brush of sweet soy sauce

anecdotes.text: The name 'pettara pottara' is the shop's own registered trademark and evokes the rhythmic sounds of pressing and shaping the rice; a little in-shop jingle sings the words, and customers say it lodges in your head long after you leave.

Each piece is finished to order with an extra brush of soy and a quick torching, sending up a fragrant aroma of caramelized soy that visitors say you can smell from along the path; one customer warns the glaze drips easily, so mind your clothes when you tilt the wrapper.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 4travel.jp confirms the registered-trademark name and in-store jingle plus the two versions (oyster on top / anago inside) of the grilled mochi-rice cake with sweet-soy glaze. food.onarimon.jp confirms the to-order torching, the caramelized-soy aroma drifting along the path, and the Kitanohama seaside-path location on the way to Itsukushima Shrine.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Each piece is glazed and finished with a sweet soy sauce; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so these items are not gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The only menu items contain oyster or conger eel plus a soy-based glaze, so there is no vegan-safe item to protect from cross-contact.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny walk-up stall on Miyajima's seaside path; you simply point to the oyster or conger-eel version, pay cash, and eat standing, so very little Japanese is needed but no English menu or service should be expected.

hiro_gelateria_baccano.gf_detail: A dedicated gelato shop. The gelato itself (a frozen dairy custard) does not inherently contain wheat, and many fruit and milk-based flavors are naturally gluten-free, but this is not a gluten-free establishment and no gluten-free protocols are documented. Served in a cup avoids the wheat cone. Flavors such as genmaicha (brown rice) are fine, but verify nothing contains barley/wheat-derived additives, and note possible cross-contact from shared scoops/equipment. Ask staff directly about each flavor.
hiro_gelateria_baccano.vegan_detail: The core product is dairy gelato made with local Chichiyasu 'Hiroshima delicious milk', so standard flavors are not vegan. Fruit-based sorbet-style options (e.g. strawberry, pineapple, and the signature Hiroshima/Setoda lemon) appear seasonally and are typically water-and-fruit based, which can be dairy-free — but the shop does not explicitly advertise vegan items, and recipes/equipment may share dairy. A vegan visitor should confirm with staff which sorbets are made without milk.
hiro_gelateria_baccano.hours_raw: 11:00-17:00 (2nd-floor seating until 16:30); the official site lists 10:00-18:00. Closes at 17:00 in winter. Irregular days off.

chef_bio.background: A mother-and-son shop that opened in August 2014 on Miyajima, tucked between the Omotesando shopping arcade and the quieter Machiya-dori lane on the way to Itsukushima Shrine. Etsuko Doi had long dreamed of running her own business; when her son, who had worked in Italian dining, proposed opening a gelateria, they made the dream real together.
chef_bio.philosophy: All gelato is made with no artificial coloring, no artificial flavoring, and no preservatives, so every vivid color in the case comes from the ingredient itself (the pink apple gelato, for instance, gets its hue from red apples cooked with their skins). The shop champions local sourcing, building the base from Chichiyasu's 'Hiroshima delicious milk' and featuring seasonal produce such as strawberries from contracted Miyajima-area farms.
chef_bio.specialty: 無添加の自家製ジェラート。看板はストレート果汁を使った広島・瀬戸田レモン。黒ごま・ピスタチオ・抹茶・ほうじ茶・玄米茶なども人気で、常時約18種類が並ぶ。

anecdotes.text: The name 'BACCANO' means 'revelry' or 'a lively din' in Italian, chosen to express the family's wish that the shop always be bustling with happy customers.
The pink color of the apple gelato is entirely natural, achieved by cooking red apples together with their skins rather than using any coloring.
Around 18 flavors are available daily, with seasonal fruit such as strawberry and pineapple rotating in during the early-summer rainy season.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: japan-stroll.com confirms mother Etsuko Doi and her Italian-dining son opened BACCANO in August 2014 between Omotesando and Machiya-dori, the additive-free (無添加) policy, the naturally pink red-apple-skin gelato, Chichiyasu Hiroshima milk, Setoda-lemon signature and the 'revelry' meaning of BACCANO. hatsumeshi.com confirms ~18 daily flavors with seasonal fruit rotation.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No gluten-free protocol is documented; shared scoops and a common gelato case mean cross-contact between flavors and with any wheat cones is possible. Request a cup and ask staff per flavor.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The gelato base is dairy (Chichiyasu Hiroshima milk); fruit sorbet-style flavors may be dairy-free but are produced in the same kitchen, so cross-contact with milk is possible. Confirm specific flavors with staff.

positives.text: Gelato is made in-house with no artificial coloring, flavoring, or preservatives, and the milk base and many ingredients are locally sourced, which gives clear visibility into what is in each flavor.

cultural_comfort.note: A friendly family-run gelato counter where pointing at the colorful case and a few words of Japanese go a long way; the upstairs tatami room is shoes-off and asks each person to order something.

Fried foods share fryers with battered items. Not suitable for a strict gluten-free diner.

Signature dishes are Hiroshima Bay oysters, conger eel (anago) sashimi and grilled, sashimi platters, senjigara (fried pork offal), lever katsu (liver), and Takamiya brand chicken. Dishes rely on fish, shellfish, meat, and dashi/soy seasonings. No vegan menu or documented plant-based options.

chef_bio.philosophy: The house aims to be a warm, approachable shop 'loved by the local oyaji (regulars),' the kind of place friends say 'let's meet at Tomasu again tonight.' The kitchen emphasizes heartfelt, homemade cooking and seasonal local ingredients at friendly prices.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima Bay oysters (raw, fried, butter-sauteed, sake-steamed, tempura), conger eel/anago prepared as seared sashimi with wasabi-soy or thin-sliced with ponzu, homemade gansu (fish-paste fritter), and homemade senjigara (fried pork offal).

anecdotes.text: The signature anago (conger eel) is offered as seared sashimi dressed with wasabi-soy, or thin-sliced with ponzu, prized for its fatty sweetness and texture.

Gansu, a Kure-area specialty, is made here from white fish paste mixed with vegetables and seasoning, breaded and deep-fried to order for a crisp outside and soft center; senjigara (fried dried pork offal) is also made in-house.

chef_bio.origin: Central Hiroshima (Naka-ku), Setouchi Inland Sea region
chef_bio.background: 肆一饗 (Hoshiimama Ikkyo) is a Japanese izakaya tucked into the Nagarekawa-Yagenbori nightlife quarter of central Hiroshima, opened in December 2019. It is designed as an 'adult hideaway' - a calm, traditionally styled space of dug-in horigotatsu private rooms that can seat anywhere from a couple to a party of around fifty (about 64 seats in total).
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen works directly with producers to source seasonal regional ingredients, pairing local Hiroshima sake and premium nationwide labels with seafood-forward Japanese cooking in an intimate private-room setting.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal Inland Sea seafood and local Hiroshima ingredients: sashimi platters of Setouchi fish, oyster dishes made with Etajima winter-bloom oysters, and local Takamiya-area chicken served as a low-temperature steamed chicken, alongside roughly 40 kinds of sake.

anecdotes.text: The house highlights Etajima winter-bloom oysters and locally raised Takamiya chicken prepared by low-temperature cooking, sourced through direct relationships with producers.
Signature plates include a tuna rare-cutlet, horse-meat sashimi, and grilled beef 'koune', a Hiroshima specialty.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site (ikkyou.owst.jp) and Tabelog confirm the December 2019 opening in the Nagarekawa/Yagenbori quarter, horigotatsu private rooms seating 2 to ~48-50 (about 64 total seats), ~40 kinds of sake, seasonal Setouchi seafood and Hiroshima ingredients, and the signature tuna rare-cutlet, horse-meat sashimi and grilled koune beef.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No gluten-free handling is documented; the menu includes fried items (tuna rare-cutlet), and Japanese izakaya cooking relies on wheat-based soy sauce, so cross-contamination should be assumed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: As a traditional Japanese izakaya, standard soy sauce (wheat-containing) is used across sashimi, simmered and grilled dishes; no wheat-free tamari is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Menu is centered on fish, oysters, anago, chicken, horse and beef, with bonito dashi typical of the cuisine; no vegan preparations are documented.

cultural_comfort.note: This is an evening-only adult izakaya in Hiroshima's nightlife quarter with private tatami-style rooms; basic Japanese helps, reservations are smart for the private rooms, and note it is a smoking venue with no entry for under-18s.

hiro_kiyo_courage.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is documented. This is a course-based French kitchen that bakes its own bread and relies on flour in sauces and pastry, so gluten is present throughout the menu. There is no published information on dedicated equipment or cross-contamination control. A celiac or gluten-sensitive diner must call ahead (082-221-2077) to ask whether a wheat-free course can be arranged; do not assume any dish is safe.
hiro_kiyo_courage.vegan_detail: The restaurant is built around pesticide-free organic vegetables delivered twice weekly from a long-standing grower, and listings report it offers vegetarian and partial vegan options. There is no fixed vegan menu: a meat-free or fully plant-based course is made to order, and reservations are required so the kitchen can prepare it. A classic French kitchen uses butter, cream, eggs and stock, so confirm at booking exactly how strict (vegetarian vs. vegan, dairy/egg-free) your needs are.

chef_bio.background: Chef Sumida Kiyokazu was born in Hiroshima in 1979 and entered the kitchen at nineteen. He spent roughly a decade training between Japan and France before opening his own restaurant at twenty-eight in 2008 in Nobori-cho. After more than sixteen years in the city's center, he moved the restaurant to a new home in Minamisenda-Nishimachi, southern Naka-ku, in May 2025 to pursue his ideal more fully.
chef_bio.philosophy: The aim is to draw out the full, honest character of regional ingredients rather than mask them with technique. Vegetables come from a grower he has worked with for over ten years, delivered twice a week, and dishes are kept deliberately simple so that the produce's natural minerality and freshness carry the plate.
chef_bio.specialty: Natural-style French cooking that lets local ingredients speak for themselves, anchored by pesticide-free organic vegetables and the seafood and mountain produce of the Seto Inland Sea region.

anecdotes.text: A signature spinach purée is described by the chef as quite literally just spinach turned into purée, yet it lands as vividly mineral and alive thanks to the quality of the vegetable.

The vegetables are grown without pesticides using organic fertilizer by a farmer in Yamaguchi Prefecture with whom the restaurant has kept a relationship for more than ten years, with deliveries twice a week.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: gnavi's chef profile confirms Sumida Kiyokazu was born in Hiroshima in 1979, began cooking at 19, trained ~10 years across Japan and France, and opened Kiyo courage at 28 in 2008. The official site (kiyocourage.jp) confirms the May 2025 relocation to 広島市中区南千田西町 after 16+ years in Nobori-cho. syokuki.com documents the 'just spinach' purée and the 10-plus-year relationship with a pesticide-free Yamaguchi grower delivering twice weekly.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Guests are advised to inform staff of vegetarian or vegan preferences before ordering and to reserve in advance so the kitchen can accommodate; specific dairy, egg, and cross-contact details are not published and should be confirmed directly.

positives.text: Vegetarian and partial vegan options can be prepared, and an English menu plus English-speaking staff have been reported, making it possible to discuss dietary needs.
The cooking centers on pesticide-free, organically grown vegetables delivered twice weekly from a trusted long-term grower.

cultural_comfort.note: An English menu and English-speaking staff have been reported, and the kitchen will prepare a vegetarian/vegan course if you tell them when you book, so a foreign student can dine comfortably as long as they reserve ahead and explain their needs.

hiro_shanhai_sohonten.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The signature broth is a tonkotsu (pork-bone) soy base, dishes feature char siu pork, wontons, and meat, and the soy tare contains wheat. No plant-based options are documented.

chef_bio.background: A family ramen shop with roots going back more than 60 years. The lineage began with the grandfather, who started a noodle-making business after returning from Manchuria; that led the father to open the original shop, named simply 上海 (Shanhai), in the Nobori-cho area of central Hiroshima. The business later moved to its current Hatchobori location and became 上海総本店. It has been run by the Fujimoto family across generations, with the third generation now running operations and younger family members working in the shop.
chef_bio.philosophy: Preserving an unbroken flavor across generations. The soy-based tare has been continuously topped up since the shop opened, keeping the taste alive over the decades.
chef_bio.specialty: Old-style Hiroshima chuka-soba (ramen): a rich pork-bone and soy-sauce broth (simmered roughly 6 hours) with medium-thick straight noodles, served with generous toppings of bean sprouts, green onion and menma; the wonton ramen and char siu are longtime favorites.

anecdotes.text: Owner Toshiaki Fujimoto says the flavor hasn't changed since his father's time ('味は店をはじめた親父の頃から何も変えとらん'), and the soy tare has been continuously replenished for over 60 years since founding.

Fujimoto ran the shop alongside his twin brother Eiji (英二) as an inseparable pair for about 40 years, sharing shifts and deliveries, until Eiji's recent retirement - and the two still go fishing together.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: zetsumeshi-hiroshima.jp confirms owner Toshiaki Fujimoto (2nd generation, with the 3rd generation now running the shop), the lineage from a Manchuria-returnee grandfather noodle-maker to the father's original 上海 in Nobori-cho to the Hatchobori 上海総本店, the ~6-hour tonkotsu-shoyu broth, the 60-plus-year continuously-topped tare with the 'nothing has changed since my father' quote, and the twin brother Eiji (英二) who worked alongside him ~40 years until his recent retirement.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are the core of nearly every dish, so a shared noodle-boiling pot and wheat-heavy kitchen make this unsuitable for strict gluten avoidance.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is built on a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare that has been continuously replenished for decades; Japanese soy sauce is wheat-based.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The base broth is pork-bone (tonkotsu) and dishes include char siu pork and wontons, so animal products are integral and unavoidable.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, no-frills neighborhood ramen counter where ordering a bowl in basic Japanese (or by pointing) is enough; no English menu is documented, so a translation app helps but the experience is friendly and approachable.
