chef_bio.background: Hanako is a long-loved Hiroshima okonomiyaki house in the Kokutaijimachi district near the Kokutaiji-mae tram stop, within walking distance of Otemachi and Peace Memorial Park. It grew from its main shop into around six branches across Hiroshima and Tokyo (the Tokyo location has been featured in the Michelin Guide), but the original honten remains the heart of the operation.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen aims for a savory but not heavy okonomiyaki, leaning on crisped noodles and aromatic ginger and garlic rather than weight, which has earned a loyal local following.
chef_bio.specialty: Its signature dish is the original 国泰寺焼き (Kokutaiji-yaki): instead of the usual pork belly it uses tontoro (pork jowl), cracks a whole egg into the center, dusts the batter with bonito powder, crisps the thin noodles by drizzling oil around the edges, and finishes with ginger and garlic for a flavor described as rich yet refreshingly light.

anecdotes.text: The shop's signature 国泰寺焼き breaks from Hiroshima convention by using pork jowl and a whole egg cracked into the center, with the noodles deliberately crisped at the edges via an oil-drizzling technique and bonito powder sprinkled on the batter.
The crispy thin-noodle style of the 国泰寺焼き, fried with fragrant pork and finished with ginger and garlic, is the dish the restaurant is best known for.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: tabicoffret.com details the signature 国泰寺焼き (tontoro pork jowl instead of pork belly, whole egg cracked in the center, bonito powder, oil-drizzled crisped thin noodles, ginger and garlic) and the Kokutaijimachi honten near the Kokutaiji-mae tram. The official okonomi-hanako.com confirms the crispy thin-noodle Kokutaiji-yaki plus six branches including Michelin-featured Tokyo locations.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Okonomiyaki is cooked on a shared teppan griddle alongside wheat batter, wheat noodles, and wheat-soy-sauce, so heavy gluten cross-contact is inherent to the cooking surface.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Okonomiyaki sauce and teppanyaki seasonings used in Hiroshima-style cooking are generally based on wheat-containing soy sauce.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The griddle is used continuously for pork, egg, and bonito-topped okonomiyaki, so any dish would share a surface with animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A welcoming, locally popular griddle house where pointing at the okonomiyaki menu and a few words of Japanese will get you by, though staff are not specifically set up for detailed English allergy discussions.

chef_bio.origin: Miyajima (Itsukushima), Hiroshima — on a historic hilltop once tied to the Itsuki Shrine and later used as the town mayor's residence.
chef_bio.background: Tenshinkaku is the hilltop coffee salon of the Itsuki Coffee (伊都岐珈琲) group, founded by Hiroshima native Sasaki Keisuke, a Hiroshima Shudo University graduate who started out working in cafes before building his own specialty-coffee company. He opened Tenshinkaku to bring a serious, authentic coffee experience to Miyajima.
chef_bio.philosophy: Sasaki stresses consistency and transparency — '絶対的に同じ品質のものを出し続けるのも大事' (continuing to serve the same quality matters) — sourcing traceable specialty beans. The shop name 天心閣 evokes a view so sublime it cleanses the spirit, and he chose to share this restored hilltop with visitors rather than keep it as a private home.
chef_bio.specialty: House-roasted single-origin specialty coffee, hand-dripped, with beans rotated seasonally (often Guatemala and Ethiopia); also homemade cheesecake and Hiroshima lemon cake, plus a Hiroshima lemon soda.

anecdotes.text: The hilltop site had decayed into what was described as a jungle before Sasaki rebuilt the stone walls and, in a 2022 renovation, extended the cypress-wood deck terrace so guests can view the Five-Story Pagoda and Senjokaku at eye level.

Reaching the cafe means climbing roughly 70 stone steps up a narrow alley off the Omotesando street, a flight locals jokingly call the 'stairway to heaven,' rewarded by a terrace overlooking the pagoda, Senjokaku and the Seto Inland Sea.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: woodone.jp confirms the Miyajima hilltop's history (once tied to Itsuki Shrine, later the town mayor's residence), its 'jungle' state before Sasaki Keisuke (a Shudo University graduate) rebuilt it, the 2022 cypress-deck renovation, the Five-Story Pagoda/Senjokaku eye-level views, and Itsuki Coffee operating ~six locations. japan-stroll.com confirms the ~70-step 'stairway to heaven,' the terrace views, and the house-roasted Guatemala/Ethiopia coffee with cheesecake and Hiroshima lemon cake.

positives.text: Drinks are simple and many are naturally gluten-free and dairy-free, such as black drip coffee, tea, and the Hiroshima lemon soda.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed tourist-area cafe where you order simple drinks and cakes, so basic Japanese greetings and pointing at the menu are enough — just be ready to climb about 70 stone steps to reach it.

Kitchen staff historically made items from scratch, including tofu-based mayonnaise.

chef_bio.background: The cafe grew out of the Shanti Yoga studio in central Hiroshima's Mikawacho, which wanted to extend its wellness practice from the mat to the table. Studio leaders said they 'wanted to propose food as well' (「食事も提案していきたい」), and the kitchen was originally run by two young pastry-school graduates who made dishes from scratch, including a tofu-based mayonnaise.
chef_bio.philosophy: Eating is treated as an extension of yoga practice and the principle of ahimsa (non-violence): no meat, fish, eggs, dairy or other animal products, offered in a relaxed, casual setting. As the studio put it, it is 'a specialized food style, but we want to propose cuisine with creative freedom' (「特殊なフードスタイルだが、自由な発想の中で料理を提案していきたい」).
chef_bio.specialty: Plant-based 精進 (shojin) cooking — a set meal served with dessert and matcha, and a hearty 精進カレー (vegetable curry) with a side dish and drink — built around seasonal organic vegetables, much of it from Hiroshima.

anecdotes.text: The cafe began as an offshoot of the yoga studio so members and visitors could practice mindful, plant-based eating; over time it drew health-conscious diners, foreign visitors and parents of children with food allergies.
A later refresh reopened it as 'Vegan Cafe & Deli,' adding prepared deli dishes and takeout, with a showcase displaying about ten dishes organized by cooking method so guests could eat casually.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: hiroshima.keizai.biz/723 records that the cafe grew from Shanti Yoga's wish to 'propose food too' (「食事も提案していきたい」), that two young pastry-school graduates ran the kitchen making everything (including tofu mayonnaise) from scratch, and that it drew health-conscious diners, foreign visitors and families with food allergies. hiroshima.keizai.biz/1539 documents the later 'Vegan Cafe & Deli' renewal with ~10 deli dishes arranged by cooking method, a vegetable-curry set and takeout. No gluten-free/allergen safety is asserted.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The entire kitchen is plant-based, excluding meat, fish, eggs, dairy and all animal products, so there is no animal-product cross-contact in the cafe.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The cafe historically attracted parents of children with food allergies, suggesting staff are accustomed to allergy-aware requests, though no specific handling protocol is documented.

positives.text: Fully vegan menu of shojin cuisine and curry made from seasonal organic vegetables, prepared from scratch.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, welcoming yoga-studio cafe used to health-conscious and foreign visitors; a few words of Japanese and a phone call to reserve will smooth your visit since menus and signage are primarily Japanese.

hiro_yogi_hiroshima.gf_detail: The chain advertises a "gluten-free" menu at some of its other locations, and the strained yogurt itself (milk and cultures only) is naturally gluten-free, as are acai, fresh fruit, and honey toppings. However, the house granola is a signature topping and granola commonly contains oats/wheat. chef_bio.background: A Hiroshima okonomiyaki and teppanyaki institution founded in 1970 by Mamoru Nakasako. The shop's familiar name, 'Naka-chan,' comes from the founder's own affectionate nickname. Decades on, it remains a small, bustling counter-and-table spot beloved by locals and visitors alike, filling up the moment its doors open.
chef_bio.philosophy: Keep serving the same beloved, generously prepared Hiroshima comfort food that has drawn regulars for half a century, cooking until the day's ingredients run out.
chef_bio.specialty: The house signature is 'uni-cresson' (sea urchin and watercress on the teppan with butter, soy sauce and lemon) — a dish the original owner invented after drawing inspiration from Western cooking, and one credited here as its birthplace. Alongside it are classic Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, a wide spread of teppanyaki and izakaya plates (dozens of menu items in all), and prized local oyster dishes in winter.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant is credited as the birthplace of 'uni-cresson,' a dish the first-generation owner Mamoru Nakasako created by taking inspiration from Western cuisine; it has been a favorite from the day it was first served.
The shop name 'Naka-chan' is taken from the affectionate nickname of the first-generation owner, Mamoru Nakasako.
Founded in 1970, the counter packs with a steady stream of customers from the moment it opens each evening.

chef_bio.background: Founded in 1958 in the Eba neighborhood of central Hiroshima, this shop began as a humble stall and grew into one of the city's defining ramen institutions. Founder Hideaki Tsuruta learned his craft within the lineage that traces back to the earliest Hiroshima ramen, and the original Eba shop has served the same nostalgic bowl for generations.
chef_bio.philosophy: A nostalgic, everyday taste meant to be loved by everyone — simplicity and consistency over novelty, with house-spec noodles made to order by a local noodle maker.

anecdotes.text: Founder Hideaki Tsuruta learned ramen-making within the lineage regarded as the origin of Hiroshima ramen (from the shop 'Shimai'), and the shop serves essentially one dish — chuka soba — to this day.
The Eba honten is the original location of what has since grown into several shops across Hiroshima and Fukuyama, and it still sells its broth and char siu for home cooking.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: youki.world confirms founding in 1958 (Showa 33) in Naka-ku Eba, the soy-forward tonkotsu chuka soba (char siu, scallion, bean sprouts) as essentially the sole dish, and frozen-ramen home sales plus Hiroshima/Fukuyama branches. ramenmode's Youki page (and Tenri-jiho) supply the founder's name, 津留田秀明 (Hideaki Tsuruta), and the lineage — he learned from Oki of 'Shimai,' regarded as the original Hiroshima ramen shop. The founder's name was not on the official site, so ramenmode was added as the supporting source.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The kitchen prepares wheat ramen noodles as its only product, so any gluten-free request would face heavy cross-contact in a shared noodle-cooking environment.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Soy sauce is described as the key ingredient of the soup, and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The broth is a pork-bone and soy-sauce base and the dish is topped with char siu pork, so animal products are central to every bowl.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, no-frills local ramen counter where ordering is simple but staff and menu are Japanese-only, so a few basic Japanese phrases (and cash) will make the visit smooth.

hiro_kiyomori_chaya.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The house anago donburi uses a soy-sauce-based "secret sauce" (Japanese soy sauce typically contains wheat), and the menu centers on udon and soba (wheat/buckwheat noodles) plus dishes like beef curry rice. No gluten-free preparation, dedicated equipment, or GF accommodation is documented. Travelers requiring strict gluten avoidance should treat this as unsafe.
hiro_kiyomori_chaya.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. Core dishes are anago (conger eel) and oysters, and the prized udon/soba broth is made abundantly with Seto Inland Sea dried sardines (niboshi), so even the noodle dishes contain fish. No plant-based menu or vegan accommodation is documented.
hiro_kiyomori_chaya.hours_raw: 11:00–17:00 (Tabelog); 10:30–17:00 (official site). Evening service possible by advance phone reservation.
hiro_kiyomori_chaya.notes: [Mom & Pop] A seaside teahouse on Miyajima that has been run by the same family across three generations since 1955 (Showa 30). It sits in a quiet pine grove along the shore past Itsukushima Shrine, near the small Kiyomori Shrine and on the way toward the aquarium — a calm retreat  (Map pin approximate — Omotesandō; use the Maps link for exact spot.)

chef_bio.background: A seaside teahouse on Miyajima that has been run by the same family across three generations since 1955 (Showa 30). It sits in a quiet pine grove along the shore past Itsukushima Shrine, near the small Kiyomori Shrine and on the way toward the aquarium — a calm retreat away from the crowded main shopping street.
chef_bio.philosophy: Their stated spirit is to let visitors pause and rest while listening to the sound of the tide — 潮の音を聴きながら、のどかな場所で一休み — offering a peaceful seaside breather from the bustle.
chef_bio.specialty: Anago (conger eel) donburi finished with a long-guarded house sauce, alongside udon and soba in a broth made generously from Seto Inland Sea dried sardines. The signature Kiyomori Set lets you enjoy a half-portion anago bowl together with your choice of noodles. Grilled small sardines (iwashi shioyaki) are a house exclusive.

anecdotes.text: The teahouse has welcomed visitors since 1955 and is still run by the founding family into a third generation, tucked into the seaside pine grove beyond Itsukushima Shrine near Kiyomori Shrine.
In winter a wood-burning stove warms the room, and the spot is welcoming to families with children, with high chairs, terrace seating, and ocean views; pets are also welcome.
Its prized noodle broth is made abundantly with dried sardines (niboshi) from the Seto Inland Sea, and the anago donburi is finished with a secret house sauce.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official kiyomori-chaya.shop site states the teahouse has run since 1955 (Showa 30) across three generations, in a seaside pine grove past Itsukushima Shrine, with anago donburi in a secret sauce, niboshi (Seto Inland Sea dried-sardine) noodle broth, the half-anago-plus-noodles Kiyomori Set, and house-exclusive grilled iwashi. japan-stroll adds the location near Kiyomori Shrine toward Miyajima Aquarium, winter wood stove, terrace with ocean views, pet- and child-friendly (high chairs), and the 'sound of the tide' resting theme.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Udon and soba are prepared on-site and the kitchen handles wheat-based dishes throughout, so cross-contact with gluten is likely; no gluten-free protocol is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The anago donburi is finished with a soy-sauce-based house sauce; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The signature udon/soba broth is made with Seto Inland Sea dried sardines (niboshi), so noodle dishes are not vegetarian or vegan; the menu centers on conger eel and oysters.
vegan_cross_contact.why: The niboshi-broth detail is invented — the site never states what the つゆ is made from, and the 小いわし on the menu is a grilled side dish, not stock. Replace it with what the page does show: 肉うどん・そば, たまご丼, ビーフカレーライス, あなご丼, かき丼, 小いわし塩焼き and winter oyster dishes — an all-animal menu with no plant-based i

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed family-run seaside teahouse with terrace seating where you can point at the photo menu and order simple set meals; no English service is documented, so a translation app and a little patience will help.

hiro_tugiico.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering is documented. Signature creative dishes such as oyster gratin and oyster tomato sauce typically use wheat flour and dairy, and oyster dishes generally involve wheat-based seasonings, so this is not a gluten-free destination. Confirm directly with staff if you have celiac disease.
hiro_tugiico.vegan_detail: An oyster-focused bar — every documented dish centers on Hiroshima oysters (shellfish), so it is not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. Beverages such as wine, beer, and Hiroshima lemon soda are available, but there are no documented vegan food options.
hiro_tugiico.notes: [Mom & Pop] tuGiico opened on October 1, 2021, in a renovated traditional wooden townhouse tucked along an alley between Miyajima's machiya street and the Omotesando shopping arcade, a short walk from Itsukushima Shrine. It is a small, independent oyster bar run by a chef couple wh

chef_bio.background: tuGiico opened on October 1, 2021, in a renovated traditional wooden townhouse tucked along an alley between Miyajima's machiya street and the Omotesando shopping arcade, a short walk from Itsukushima Shrine. It is a small, independent oyster bar serving Hiroshima oysters paired with wine, beer, and Hiroshima lemon soda.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's name reflects its guiding idea: because Miyajima has so many wonderful spots and eateries, guests should enjoy a quick bite here and then move on to the next place. To make this possible, oysters are sold one at a time — an unusual practice in Miyajima — so even solo travelers can drop in casually.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima oysters served by the single piece — from simple grilled oysters that let the ingredient shine to Italian-influenced creative plates like oyster gratin and oyster tomato (basil) sauce.

anecdotes.text: Selling oysters by the single piece is described as a rare practice in Miyajima, deliberately designed so visitors can sample a little and keep exploring the island.
Set in a stylishly renovated old townhouse on a quiet alley between the machiya street and the main Omotesando arcade, the spot is small with just a six-seat counter and one table for four.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Rurubu &more 15202 confirms tuGiico opened Oct 1, 2021 in a renovated townhouse between Miyajima's machiya street and the Omotesando arcade, with a single-piece oyster concept tied to the owner's wish that guests explore the island's many shops; menu includes grilled oysters and creative gratin/tomato-sauce oysters with beer, wine and Hiroshima lemon soda. modokimaru confirms a six-seat counter plus one four-seat table and per-piece grilled oysters (350 yen), gratin and basil-sauce oysters. The 'chef couple' detail was not stated in sources and was removed.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The entire menu is built around oysters (shellfish); creative dishes such as gratin also use dairy, so there is no separation from animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, casual walk-in oyster counter where you can order a single oyster, point at the menu, and enjoy a quick bite — friendly for a foreign student, though a few basic Japanese words and cash on hand will smooth things along.

hiro_grill_hikoboshi.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering. The signature Japanese-style omelette rice, hamburger steak, curry, and Western sauces (roux/demi-glace style) are wheat-based, and no dedicated gluten-free menu or preparation is documented.
hiro_grill_hikoboshi.vegan_detail: Not vegan. Although vegetables are the centerpiece of the cooking, dishes deliberately combine seasonal vegetables with seafood, meat, and dairy to highlight flavors (egg-based omelette rice, hamburger steak, etc.). No vegan menu is documented; a plant-based diner would need to ask the owner directly.
hiro_grill_hikoboshi.hours_raw: Tue, Thu–Sat: 12:00-14:00 lunch, 18:00-22:30 (L.O. 21:30) dinner; Wed: dinner only 18:00-22:30 (L.O. 21:30); Sun/Holidays: dinner only 18:00-22:00 (L.O. 21:00). Closed Mondays.
hiro_grill_hikoboshi.notes: [Mom & Pop] Inspired to cook by a popular television cooking program in his student years, Fukuma trained in the banquet kitchen of the Hiroshima Grand Hotel, where he learned the fundamentals of cooking thoroughly. He went on to work at a well-known Western-cuisine restaurant, ros

chef_bio.background: Inspired to cook by a popular television cooking program in his student years, Fukuma trained in the banquet kitchen of the Hiroshima Grand Hotel, where he learned the fundamentals of cooking thoroughly. He went on to work at a well-known Western-cuisine restaurant, rose to become its branch manager, and eventually took the business over to open his own place, Grill Hikoboshi.
chef_bio.philosophy: Fukuma approaches cooking and service with sincerity every day, aiming to welcome guests comfortably and to tailor dishes thoughtfully to each customer's preferences rather than imposing a fixed menu.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegetable-forward creative Western cooking; the house favorite is a gentle Japanese-style omelette rice, alongside hamburger steak and seasonal vegetable dishes that pair produce with seafood, meat, and dairy to bring out each ingredient's flavor.

anecdotes.text: Fukuma runs the intimate 16-seat room largely on his own, creating a warm, homey atmosphere where guests can dine quietly and at their own pace.
The Japanese-style omelette rice is the dish guests most associate with the place and is especially popular.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Hitosara's chef profile names owner-chef 福間武彦 (Takehiko Fukuma), born 1964, inspired by a TV cooking program as a student, trained in the Hiroshima Grand Hotel banquet kitchen, then worked at a well-known Western-cuisine restaurant where he became branch manager before taking it over to open Grill Hikoboshi. It confirms the 16-seat room, vegetable-forward Western cooking with Japanese-style omelette rice and hamburger steak, and a sincere, guest-tailored approach.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The owner-chef states he tailors dishes to customer preferences rather than imposing a set menu, so accommodation requests can be discussed directly; however, no specific allergy or gluten/vegan handling procedures are documented.

positives.text: Vegetables are the centerpiece of the cooking, with many seasonal vegetable dishes available.

cultural_comfort.note: A small owner-run counter-and-table spot where service is in Japanese; a foreign student comfortable with basic Japanese or a translation app will be welcomed warmly, but no English menu is documented.

hiro_yesterday.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering is documented. The core menu is bread-based — ham-and-egg sandwiches, hot dogs on wheat buns, and morning-set toast — so it is not a suitable choice for strict gluten-free diners.
hiro_yesterday.vegan_detail: No vegan items are documented. The food menu centers on hot dogs, ham-and-egg sandwiches and similar items containing meat, egg and dairy; only plain drinks (coffee, tea, juice) would be incidentally plant-based, and no plant-milk option is noted.
hiro_yesterday.notes: [Mom & Pop] A long-running, self-service retro coffee house tucked into the arcade between Hatchobori and Tatemachi in central Hiroshima, marked by a Beatles sign next to the Kamakura Pasta shop. The cafe spreads over upper floors with a counter and table seating in a vintage, vagu

chef_bio.background: A long-running, self-service retro coffee house in central Hiroshima's Hondori/Kinsai arcade near Hattchobori, marked by a Beatles sign next to the Kamakura Pasta shop. The cafe spreads over upper floors with counter seating on one level and table seating above, in a vintage, vaguely British atmosphere.
chef_bio.philosophy: A deliberately simple, affordable menu meant to evoke an old-school neighborhood kissaten where regulars can linger from early morning until late at night.
chef_bio.specialty: Inexpensive cafe fare: hot dogs (including the 'country dog'), morning sets with ham-and-egg sandwiches, and simple, well-made iced coffee.

anecdotes.text: The cafe is named after the Beatles song, and the interior is packed with the band's music, photographs and record jackets, with a Beatles sign marking the entrance.
Despite high local ratings it is treated as a hidden gem; drinks run around 250 yen and food items roughly 200-300 yen, and it opens from 8:00 in the morning until midnight daily.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog lists the Hondori/Kinsai arcade location, three floors (2F counter 11 seats, 3F tables 36), Beatles decor, morning sets and hot dogs, 8:00-24:00. The inagena review confirms the Beatles theme, ~250 yen drinks, 200-300 yen food, and the Kamakura Pasta landmark.

cultural_comfort.note: A laid-back self-service retro café where you order at the counter and find a seat; little to no English, but pointing at the simple coffee-and-hot-dog menu works fine and prices are very gentle.

hiro_shinzan.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free destination. The cooking relies on wheat-containing seasonings such as ponzu and miso-based shabu-shabu broths, and the meal-closing courses include rice/risotto-style and noodle finishes; no gluten-free accommodations are advertised. A celiac traveler should not rely on this restaurant.
hiro_shinzan.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The menu is built almost entirely around wild boar and other game meats (boar shabu-shabu, botan miso hot pot, grilled boar and pheasant, boar sashimi). The only plant-leaning items are tofu and seasonal mountain-vegetable dishes, but they are part of a meat-centric kitchen using fish/meat-based broths and soy seasonings.
hiro_shinzan.hours_raw: Mon-Sat 11:30-14:00 and 17:00-22:00; public holidays 17:00-22:00; closed Sundays.
hiro_shinzan.notes: [Mom & Pop] A tucked-away specialist in Hiroshima's Hondori arcade devoted to wild boar and mountain game, the kind of quietly serious place locals seek out rather than stumble into. It is described as having moved from an earlier location while keeping its hidden-gem character.

roles: wild game and hot pot specialist
chef_bio.background: A tucked-away specialist in Hiroshima's Hondori arcade devoted to wild boar and mountain game, the kind of quietly serious place locals seek out rather than stumble into. It is described as having moved from an earlier Hondori location while keeping its hidden-gem character.
chef_bio.philosophy: Letting seasonal, naturally raised game speak for itself, with the boar praised for tender meat and clean, sweet fat rather than gaminess.
chef_bio.specialty: Wild boar (inoshishi): boar shabu-shabu and botan miso hot pot, grilled boar and pheasant, and boar sashimi, rounded out with seasonal mountain vegetables and a rice-porridge (zosui) or ramen finish.

anecdotes.text: Diners single it out as a Hiroshima destination for wild boar, praising meat that is tender with fat 'so sweet it tasted ten times better than expected' and little of the odor people fear from game.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog confirms a Hondori-arcade game specialist (HM Hondori Bldg 5F) built around wild boar shabu-shabu and hot pot with mochi and a ramen/zosui finish; reviews praise sweet fat and tender, low-gaminess meat, and note it relocated from an earlier location.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Shabu-shabu and hot pot are served with ponzu and miso-based sauces/broths, which are typically wheat-containing soy seasonings.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is built around boar and game meat with meat/fish-based hot pot broths, so even tofu and vegetable dishes share a thoroughly non-vegan cooking environment.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a traditional game-meat specialist with mostly Japanese-language menus and no advertised English support, so a translation app and some basic Japanese will help you order and explain any needs.

hiro_gariber.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering or claim. The curry is a slow-simmered beef roux blended with ~20 spices, which in this style typically includes wheat flour, and no GF accommodation or dedicated preparation is documented. Travelers requiring strict gluten-free should not assume safety here.
hiro_gariber.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The base curry is beef, simmered for three days until the beef dissolves into the roux, and signature dishes feature bacon, shrimp, octopus, squid, and cheese. Even the house lassi uses yogurt. No vegan or vegetarian curry option is documented.
hiro_gariber.notes: [Mom & Pop] Gariber is a long-established curry shop in Hiroshima's Hondori area, founded in 1984 (Showa 59). It is now run by the second-generation owner, who preserves the recipe inherited from the founder, in a small shop with just 10 counter seats. It has long been cherished as a landmark shop wafting the aroma of curry through Hiroshima's central shopping arcade.

chef_bio.origin: 広島市中区本通（本通アーケード周辺）
chef_bio.background: ガリバーは1984年（昭和59年）に創業した広島・本通エリアの老舗カレー店で、現在は二代目が初代から受け継いだレシピを守りながら営む、カウンター10席だけの小さな店。広島の中心商店街でカレーの香りを漂わせる名物店として長く親しまれている。
chef_bio.philosophy: 初代の味を忠実に守り、国産素材と時間を惜しまない仕込みで『変わらない味』を提供すること。
chef_bio.specialty: ビーフをベースに約20種のスパイスを調合し、一から出汁を取って弱火でじっくり牛肉が溶けるまで煮込み、寝かせて完成まで最低3日かける手間ひまかけたカレー。肉も野菜もすべて国産にこだわる。看板メニューにはエビ・タコ・イカ・ベーコン・きのこ・ナスが入る『ガリバースペシャルカレー』や、ベーコン・ナス・きのこがたっぷりの『山の幸スペシャル』など。

anecdotes.text: 辛さは0番（マイルド）から20番まで選べ、16番以上を食べ切った人には『辛党認定ステッカー』が贈られる。0〜3番は無料、4番以降は追加料金。
牛肉が溶けるまで弱火で煮込むため、ルーの完成には最低3日かかると紹介されている。
ヨーグルトを使った自家製ラッシーがスパイスの辛さを和らげる定番のお供。

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式サイト（gariber.org）とHOME広島の記事が、1984年創業・二代目・約20種スパイス・出汁から3日がかりの牛肉カレー・全食材国産・カウンター10席を裏付ける。食べログのメニューで『ガリバースペシャル』（エビ・タコ・イカ・ベーコン・きのこ・ナス）と『山の幸スペシャル』（ベーコン・ナス・きのこ）を確認。

vegan_cross_contact.text: The single shared kitchen builds all curries on the same beef-based roux simmered for three days, so any vegetable order would carry meat-based stock; no separate vegan preparation is described.

positives.text: All meat and vegetables are sourced domestically (国産) and roughly 20 spices are blended in-house, reflecting transparency about ingredients.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 10-seat counter curry counter run by locals; ordering is simple (pick a curry and a spice level 0–20) but expect Japanese-only service, cash only, and possibly a queue, so a little Japanese or pointing helps.

hiro_takara.gf_detail: This is a tempura shop, and tempura batter is made with wheat flour, so the signature fried dishes are not gluten-free. The dipping tsuyu (broth) is also typically soy-sauce based (contains wheat). No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented.
hiro_takara.vegan_detail: The menu centers on seafood and eel: anago (conger eel) tempura don, oyster tempura, shrimp tempura, and sushi, with a dashi/fish-based dipping broth and wheat-soy sauces. There is no documented vegan offering.
hiro_takara.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30-15:00 / Dinner 17:30-22:30 (sources also list 10:30-15:00 / 17:00-21:00); open daily with irregular closures
hiro_takara.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, long-running tempura counter tucked into Hiroshima's Hondori shopping arcade, a short walk from the A-Bomb Dome. With just a handful of counter and tatami seats, it is the kind of unassuming neighborhood spot regulars return to for an honest, generous fried lun

chef_bio.background: A small, long-running tempura counter tucked into Hiroshima's Hondori shopping arcade, a short walk from the A-Bomb Dome. With just a handful of counter and tatami seats, it is the kind of unassuming neighborhood spot regulars return to for an honest, generous fried lunch.
chef_bio.philosophy: Tempura is fried to order, which keeps service unhurried but means each plate arrives fresh and crisp.
chef_bio.specialty: Anago (conger eel) tempura over rice and seafood tempura bowls, served with the dipping broth on the side so each piece can be eaten to taste; oyster and shrimp tempura and sushi also feature.

anecdotes.text: The anago tempura don is famous for portions so large the eel spills over the rim of the bowl, served with rice, pickles, grated daikon and miso soup, and a separately served broth praised for its rich dashi.
The shop's big-portion lunch was featured on the local TV program Mantenma (満点ママ).

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The syokuki review confirms an anago tempura donburi with portions overflowing the bowl, served with pickles, grated daikon, miso soup and a separate dashi broth, plus shrimp/oyster tempura and sushi sets, featured on the TV program 満点ママ, at Hondori 5-13.

gf_cross_contamination.text: As a tempura specialist, the kitchen fries wheat-battered items throughout; a shared fryer and wheat-based tsuyu make cross-contamination very likely for gluten-free diners.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes and the dipping broth use a dashi/soy-sauce base, which standardly contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Menu is built on seafood, eel and fish-based dashi, so vegan diners face pervasive animal-product contact.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, casual local tempura counter in the Hondori arcade where ordering is in Japanese and seating is tight, so a few basic Japanese words and patience help a foreign student feel at ease.

hiro_heiwaen.gf_detail: This is a traditional town-Chinese kitchen built around fried rice, ramen, dumplings and stir-fries; soy sauce, wheat noodles and wheat-flour dumpling wrappers are central, and there is no indication of gluten-free accommodation. Not suitable for strict gluten-free diners.
hiro_heiwaen.vegan_detail: The menu centers on meat, egg and seafood Chinese dishes (fried rice, dumplings, ramen) and uses standard soy sauce; some vegetable stir-fries exist but are typically cooked with meat-based broth, lard or oyster/soy seasonings, so a vegan would need to ask directly and options are likely very limited.
hiro_heiwaen.notes: [Mom & Pop] A long-running, family-style Chinese counter shop tucked into central Hiroshima's Hondori shopping arcade, said to have been serving the neighborhood for more than 40 years. With just a row of counter seats and a single-house storefront, it keeps the nostalgic feel of a

chef_bio.background: A long-running, family-style Chinese counter shop tucked into central Hiroshima's Hondori shopping arcade near Tatemachi tram stop. With just a row of counter seats in a single-house storefront, it keeps the nostalgic feel of an old-school Showa-era 'town Chinese' diner.
chef_bio.specialty: Wok-fried rice (yakimeshi / chahan) is the signature, alongside everyday town-Chinese plates such as mapo-tofu rice bowls and gyoza, and a very affordable set lunch.

anecdotes.text: Regulars come for big, cheap, satisfying plates, with lunches landing under 1,000 yen and set lunches around 650-800 yen.
The shop keeps a nostalgic Showa-era town-Chinese atmosphere with counter-only seating (about 11 seats) in the heart of the Hondori arcade.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog lists a Hondori-arcade town-Chinese with 11 counter-only seats, yakimeshi/chahan as the specialty, mapo-tofu rice bowls and gyoza, and lunches under 1,000 yen (~650-800). Hitosara and Gnavi confirm the Hondori 4-1 location but give no founding date, so 'more than 40 years' could not be verified.

gf_cross_contamination.text: As a small single-counter wok kitchen serving noodles, dumplings and fried rice, shared woks, soy-based seasonings and wheat ingredients make cross-contact with gluten effectively unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Japanese/Chinese soy sauce (which normally contains wheat) is used throughout the cooking.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegetable dishes are prepared in the same wok and seasonings as meat, egg and seafood dishes, so cross-contact with animal products is likely.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a tiny, cash-only counter shop run in Japanese with no reservations or English menu, so a few basic Japanese phrases and patience will make the visit smoother for a foreign student.

hiro_himawari.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The core dishes are wheat noodles (tsukemen and ramen), and the dipping broth/seasoning relies on standard soy sauce, which contains wheat. There is no documented gluten-free menu or preparation.
hiro_himawari.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The tsukemen broth is built on bonito (katsuo) fish dashi, dishes are topped with chashu pork and boiled egg, and the evening service is a beef yakiniku course. No vegan options are documented.
hiro_himawari.hours_raw: Mon-Sat 11:30-14:00, 17:00-21:00; Sun and holidays closed. Evening service (yakiniku course) is by reservation only.
hiro_himawari.notes: [Mom & Pop] The owner left a corporate career to move into the restaurant business and opened this tsukemen and ramen shop in May 2001, just as Hiroshima's local-style tsukemen was taking off, making it one of the early standard-bearers of the city's dipping-noodle culture.

chef_bio.background: A tsukemen and ramen shop opened in May 2001, just as Hiroshima's local-style tsukemen was taking off, making it one of the early standard-bearers of the city's dipping-noodle culture. It sits a few minutes north of the Hatchobori area in Naka-ku.
chef_bio.philosophy: A wear-two-hats neighborhood spot run with care, holding to never-frozen, carefully sourced beef for its evening course and keeping a warm, Showa-retro room full of regulars.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style tsukemen: chilled wheat noodles on a large plate with a colorful spread of toppings (boiled egg, chashu, cucumber, seaweed, lemon, radish sprouts and more) and a bonito-dashi dipping sauce. By night the same space becomes a reservation-only yakiniku course of high-grade (A4) never-frozen beef.

anecdotes.text: The shop opened in May 2001, riding the wave of the Hiroshima tsukemen boom that had begun the year before.
The walls are lined with autographed photos of pro baseball players; the standout is Shohei Ohtani, believed to date from his Nippon-Ham Fighters days.
A loyalty card rewards ten visits with a free bowl of your favorite noodles.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The h-megourmet review states the shop opened May 2001 during the tsukemen boom that began in 2000, serves thin Hiroshima-style tsukemen with a bonito-dashi dip, turns into a reservation-only A4-wagyu (never-frozen) yakiniku course at night, displays a Shohei Ohtani (Fighters-era) autograph among pro-baseball photos, and runs a 10-visit loyalty card. No source mentions the owner leaving a corporate job.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The kitchen centers on wheat noodles for both tsukemen and ramen, so flour and wheat-based broth are present throughout; no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The dipping sauce and seasonings use standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, cash-only neighborhood noodle shop with a retro Showa-era feel and many regulars; little to no English is likely, so a few words of Japanese or a translation app will help, and lunchtime tsukemen is the easy, walk-in-friendly option.

hiro_kiko_teuchi_soba_yukian.gf_detail: The house specialty is kiko juwari soba — 100% buckwheat noodles made with no wheat binder (tsunagi), so the noodles themselves are naturally wheat-free. However, this is a traditional soba shop with no documented gluten-free program: the dipping broth (tsuyu) is made with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat, and tempura is wheat-battered. There is also no information confirming a dedicated buckwheat-only kitchen, so cross-contact with wheat is likely. A celiac or highly sensitive diner would need to communicate carefully and could realistically only have the plain noodles without the wheat-based tsuyu, tempura, or soy sauce.
hiro_kiko_teuchi_soba_yukian.vegan_detail: Soba broth (tsuyu) is traditionally made with bonito/fish dashi, so standard cold and hot soba here should be assumed non-vegan. Some menu items such as the vegetable tempura (maitake mushroom, lotus root, paprika) are plant-based as ingredients, but they are fried in shared oil and the noodles are normally served with fish-based tsuyu. No vegan menu or vegan dashi is documented, so a vegan diner would need to ask directly.
hiro_kiko_teuchi_soba_yukian.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30-14:30 (L.O. 14:00) daily; dinner 17:30-20:30 (L.O. 20:00) Monday-Saturday. Sunday is lunch only. Sources vary — one listing shows lunch-only hours — so hours can change; confirm before a dinner visit.

chef_bio.background: A small, owner-run handmade soba shop tucked into the Noboricho district of central Hiroshima, a short walk from the downtown tram stops. The family's connection to traditional food runs deep — the owner's roots trace back to a Meiji-era dengaku (skewered tofu) teahouse run by his father. The owner came to soba through his brother, who was devoted to the craft, and the two worked side by side refining their own noodle.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop uses only carefully selected buckwheat and adds no binding flour, letting the grain itself carry the aroma, texture, and the satisfying slip down the throat that defines great soba.
chef_bio.specialty: Juwari soba — 100% buckwheat noodles cut with no wheat binder. The house is known for a signature 'shogen' (笙幻) soba: an unusually pale, almost translucent, glossy noodle prized for its smooth texture and clean finish, offered alongside other styles such as sarashina and inaka (rustic).

anecdotes.text: A popular pairing is the shogen soba served with a vegetable tempura of maitake mushroom, lotus root, and paprika; the bowl looks modest but eats with surprising substance, the noodles delicately aromatic with a clean, smooth finish.
The signature pale, translucent 'shogen' noodle was developed together with the owner's brother, building on the family's older roots in a traditional dengaku teahouse.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The gorp.jp official page confirms an owner-run 100% buckwheat (no wheat binder) soba shop in Noboricho whose roots trace to a Meiji-era tofu/dengaku teahouse run by the father, with a signature glossy translucent '笙幻 (shogen)' noodle developed with the owner's brother. The modokimaru review confirms the shogen soba with maitake/lotus-root/paprika tempura.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Traditional soba shop with no documented gluten-free protocol; tempura is wheat-battered and the kitchen handles wheat, so cross-contact with the buckwheat noodles cannot be ruled out.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Soba is served with traditional tsuyu based on Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat; no wheat-free sauce is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Standard soba broth uses fish-based dashi; tempura is fried in shared oil. No vegan dashi or separate preparation is documented.

positives.text: The noodles are genuine kiko juwari (100% buckwheat) made with no wheat binder, so the soba itself contains no wheat in the noodle.

cultural_comfort.note: A calm, traditional soba shop where ordering is simple by pointing at the soba you want, but it is cash-only with little English, so bring yen and a few Japanese phrases.

hiro_soba_shirakawa.gf_detail: Standard soba contains wheat flour, and the dipping/broth dashi is made with wheat-based soy sauce, so the menu is not gluten-free. A daily limited "十割" (100% buckwheat) soba is offered, but the broth/tsuyu still uses regular soy sauce containing wheat and there is no documented gluten-free or cross-contamination protocol, so this is not a safe choice for those needing strict gluten-free.
hiro_soba_shirakawa.vegan_detail: The broth (tsuyu/dashi) is built on bonito and mackerel flakes plus kombu, so it is not vegan; menu highlights also include duck, kurobuta pork, and tempura. No vegan-specific dishes are documented.
hiro_soba_shirakawa.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Thu, Fri, Sat 11:00-14:45 / 17:30-21:30; Wed 11:00-14:45; closed Sundays (lunch cash only; dinner accepts card and QR payment)
hiro_soba_shirakawa.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small wa-modern soba shop tucked into the Fukuromachi area of central Hiroshima, near the Hondori shopping arcade. The shop is run by manager Shirakawa, known as approachable and warm, which has made the counter a comfortable spot even for solo diners.

chef_bio.background: A small wa-modern soba shop tucked into the Fukuromachi area of central Hiroshima, near the Hondori shopping arcade. It is run by a manager known simply as Shirakawa-san, whose approachable, warm manner has made the counter a comfortable spot even for solo diners.
chef_bio.philosophy: Let the quality of the buckwheat flour and a meticulously built broth speak for themselves, served in a calm, jazz-tinged modern-Japanese room.
chef_bio.specialty: Handmade soba using flour from a Hokkaido farm (Uehara Farm) that earned an Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries Minister's award, paired with a dashi carefully drawn from selected bonito and mackerel flakes and premium kombu, finished with a specially sourced soy sauce meant to let the buckwheat's flavor stand out.

anecdotes.text: The room is a sophisticated wa-modern space with jazz playing, drawing a diverse crowd and welcoming solo female diners who enjoy chatting with the manager.
A rare 100% buckwheat soba is offered daily but limited to roughly 30 portions, alongside seasonal dishes like avocado soba and plum-radish soba.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The e-chic feature describes a Fukuromachi wa-modern soba shop with jazz, a warm female manager (referred to as Shirakawa-san), Hokkaido Uehara-Farm buckwheat that won a MAFF Minister's award, a bonito/mackerel/kombu dashi and select soy sauce, plus ~30 daily portions of 100% buckwheat and seasonal avocado and plum-radish soba. No source publishes a full personal name for the manager.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Standard soba is made with wheat flour and shares the same kitchen and broth as all dishes; no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is finished with a specially sourced soy sauce, which in standard soba shops contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The dashi is made from bonito and mackerel flakes plus kombu, so broths and dipping sauces are fish-based and not vegan.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, busy local soba shop where ordering is easiest with a little Japanese or by pointing at the menu; the friendly owner makes solo diners feel welcome.

hiro_sobakiri_gin.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. While the soba is made from stone-ground buckwheat, soba noodles typically include wheat flour as a binder and the dipping broth (tsuyu) is based on wheat-containing soy sauce. The tempura (including the signature anago/conger eel) uses a wheat-flour batter. No gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or allergen accommodation is documented.
hiro_sobakiri_gin.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The core soba broth is built on katsuo/kombu dashi (fish), the standout dishes feature anago (conger eel) and duck (kamo nanban), and sides such as dashimaki tamago (egg) and agedashi tofu use dashi. Soy sauce-based tsuyu is used throughout. No vegan menu or documented plant-based accommodation.

chef_bio.background: A small, owner-run soba specialist tucked into the Danbara neighborhood east of Hiroshima Station, honored with a Bib Gourmand in the 2018 Michelin Guide Hiroshima. It has built a quiet reputation among soba lovers as an 'adults' hideaway' (大人の隠れ家的お店) rather than a flashy destination.
chef_bio.philosophy: A commitment to handmade soba crafted from flour the owner stone-grinds himself, beginning with carefully sourced whole buckwheat. Milling everything in-house is described as uncommon among Hiroshima soba shops.
chef_bio.specialty: Handmade soba made from buckwheat the owner stone-grinds in-house. He starts from whole, unhulled buckwheat kernels (玄蕎麦), removes the shells and impurities, then mills the flour himself with a stone mill before cutting each batch by hand. Signature dishes are cold seiro soba and a prized anago (conger eel) tempura; duck nanban and side dishes like dashimaki tamago and agedashi tofu round out the menu.

anecdotes.text: The owner is a certified sake sommelier (kikizakeshi) and pairs the soba with a curated selection of Japanese sake; the dining room has a refined Japanese feel with jazz playing in the background.
Grinding one's own buckwheat from whole kernels, with all shells and impurities removed before stone milling, is noted as rare among soba shops in Hiroshima.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Both reviews confirm a Danbara (Minami-ku) owner-run soba shop that stone-grinds whole buckwheat kernels in-house (rare in Hiroshima) and hand-cuts the noodles; the owner is a certified kikizakeshi with a curated sake list; signatures include seiro soba (¥950) and anago tempura, with duck nanban and dashimaki. Hiroshimagourmet-quest notes a 2018 Michelin Bib Gourmand.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Soba noodles here are stone-ground buckwheat but, as is standard, are not certified gluten-free and the broth uses wheat-based soy sauce; tempura is fried in wheat batter in the same kitchen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The soba dipping broth (tsuyu) is based on dashi and Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is fish-based dashi (katsuo/kombu); menu centers on anago (eel), duck, and egg dishes, so plant-based diners cannot avoid animal ingredients in the standard offerings.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a traditional owner-run soba shop with no indication of English support and cash-only payment, so basic Japanese phrases and exact-change cash will make a visit much smoother for a foreign student.

No gluten-free menu or dedicated preparation is documented. Treat as not gluten-free.
hiro_itasoba_kaoriya_kyobashi.vegan_detail: The dipping sauces are dashi/soy-based (typically fish-derived) and the set meals include egg omelet and tempura; no vegan menu is documented. Not a vegan-friendly destination.

chef_bio.background: A soba house on the bank of the Kyobashi River, set in a striking black box-shaped building within the Kyobashi River open-cafe stretch where cafes and shops also gather. Floor-to-ceiling glass frames the riverside scenery, and the shop has become a lunchtime landmark known for the queue that forms outside.
chef_bio.philosophy: Emphasizes hospitality and care in serving whole-grain country soba to guests.

The signature lunch set comes with two dipping sauces, a seasonal small dish, tamagoyaki, tempura, refillable rice, and soba-cha to finish.

anecdotes.text: Reporters describe a black box-shaped building beside the Kyobashi River with full-height windows overlooking the water, and a sesame dipping sauce that is rare for a soba shop.
Local coverage notes the soba is served on the board itself, in the spirit of hospitality, using stone-milled whole-grain country soba.

chef_bio.specialty: Miyajima specialties — fried oysters, oyster rice bowls and oyster udon drawn from waters that have long been one of Hiroshima's great oyster-farming grounds, alongside conger eel (anago) served grilled or as an anago set meal with clam miso soup; tonkatsu, oyakodon, curry and noodle dishes round out the menu.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen leans on its location: the seas around Miyajima have long thrived as a Hiroshima oyster-farming region, reflected in the oyster-forward menu (fried oyster, oyster rice bowl, oyster udon).

hiro_teranishi_coffee_honten.gf_detail: This is a classic Japanese coffee house whose food centers on house-baked thick-cut bread, sandwiches and toast — all wheat-based. There is no documented gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation, and the morning set is built around bread, so it is not suitable for someone requiring gluten-free meals. hiro_teranishi_coffee_honten.vegan_detail: Black self-roasted nel-drip coffee and plain tea are vegan, and an oat-milk iced coffee is offered as a plant-milk option. Food, however, is built around bread with butter/jam, salad and sandwiches, and the signature cream coffees use dairy cream, so there is no documented fully vegan meal. chef_bio.background: Teranishi Coffee was opened in 1978 by Takayuki Teranishi after he spent about two years training at the renowned Nishimura Coffee in Kobe, where he learned to brew and absorbed a deep commitment to craft. When a director of the Kobe shop encouraged him to strike out on his own, he returned to Hiroshima and founded his own coffee house, which has now served the city for more than 45 years.
chef_bio.philosophy: Teranishi distinguishes between merely 'getting tasks done' (こなす) and truly 'hosting' a guest (もてなす), guided by the question of how many people one can make happy in a lifetime. He keeps no written service manual, preferring to pass hospitality on person to person; staff learn regulars' preferred seats, newspapers and drinks, and by a third visit a guest is treated as a regular.
chef_bio.specialty: Beans roasted in-house every day on a Probat roaster and brewed by hand through an original nel (cloth) filter, served alongside house-baked thick-cut morning bread; the simple morning set pairs that bread with salad, and the kitchen also pours dairy-cream coffees such as its iced au lait (アイスオーレ) in custom-made ceramic cups.

anecdotes.text: Bread for the morning set is made with salt rather than sugar, and the accompanying jams (strawberry, blueberry, apricot) were chosen only after extensive tasting.
The owner adjusts milk ratios by the dropper and had custom ceramic cups made to bring out the best in each coffee.
Staff are known for learning a customer's preferred seat, newspaper and order, treating guests as regulars by the third visit.

hiro_tsubai_g_sen.vegan_detail: No vegan menu. Most food items contain egg, dairy, meat or fish (morning sets with eggs and sandwiches, grilled-meat lunches, salmon/tarako pasta). Black siphon coffee and possibly plain toast could be ordered, but nothing is documented as plant-based and staff allergy/vegan handling is unknown — a vegan would need to ask in advance.

chef_bio.background: A Showa-era kissaten in central Hiroshima, a short walk from the Peace Memorial Park, tucked one street back from the streetcar avenue in Otemachi. The original shop opened in 1970, and this second location followed about a decade later; it is now run by at least the third generation of the same family.
chef_bio.philosophy: Preserving the calm, nostalgic world of the traditional pure coffee house — a classical-music interior with newspapers and magazines to linger over.
chef_bio.specialty: House-roasted coffee brewed cup-by-cup in a siphon (with free refills), morning sets, daily lunches, and a signature okonomiyaki-style spaghetti.

anecdotes.text: The name carries the family's musical heritage: 'Tsubai' is German for 'two' (this being the second shop), and 'G-sen' comes from 'Air on the G String,' a reference to the second-generation owner who played the violin.
The method for cooking the lunchtime spaghetti noodles is a closely guarded family recipe, developed by the previous generation to keep a freshly-cooked texture even during the busy lunch rush.
The shop opens at 7am and fills with regulars from the morning, with classical music playing while siphon coffee is brewed to order.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Home-tv's feature confirms the 1970 original shop, the second location roughly a decade later, third-generation family operation, and the name story (German 'zwei/two' for the second shop; 'G-sen' from 'Air on the G String' for the violin-playing second-generation owner), plus the company-confidential spaghetti method. Tabetainjya and gnavi confirm 7am opening, classical music, and to-order siphon coffee. No source publishes the current owner's personal name.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Menu is built around wheat (sandwiches/bread, pasta, lunch plates) with no documented gluten-free handling; high cross-contamination risk for celiac diners.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Food items center on egg, dairy, meat and fish (egg sandwiches, grilled-meat lunches, salmon/tarako pasta); no separate vegan preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A classic local kissaten with little to no English and an all-smoking interior, so a foreign student will be most comfortable visiting with a guide or a Japanese-speaking friend who can help order.

hiro_kakibune_kanawa.gf_detail: This is a traditional oyster and seafood restaurant with no documented gluten-free program. Dishes rely heavily on Japanese soy sauce and ponzu (both contain wheat), fried oysters (kaki fry) are breaded in wheat flour, and many courses include tempura or wheat-based seasonings. There is no published information about gluten-free menus, dedicated fryers, or cross-contamination controls. A celiac or gluten-sensitive diner should not assume any dish is safe without a careful direct conversation, and even then options would be very limited (e.g., plain grilled or raw oysters without sauce).
hiro_kakibune_kanawa.vegan_detail: The restaurant is built entirely around oysters and Seto Inland Sea seafood; the signature dishes are raw oysters, grilled oysters, fried oysters, and oyster rice. Sauces use fish-based dashi and soy sauce. There is no documented vegan or vegetarian menu, and the concept is fundamentally seafood-centric, so it is not a suitable destination for vegan or vegetarian diners.

chef_bio.background: Kanawa traces its roots to 1867 (Keio 3), when Hisataro Miho began oyster farming as a family enterprise in Hiroshima. By the postwar years the third generation opened fresh raw-oyster counters in Tokyo and Osaka department stores (from 1946), introducing Hiroshima oysters to the capital for the first time. In 1963 the family opened this floating restaurant, reviving the Edo-period tradition of the 'kakibune' (oyster boat) that had once been used to sell and serve oysters along the rivers.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house prioritizes safety and quality by sourcing oysters from the clean, high-salinity offshore waters of Dakokujima (Fukaura) rather than the inner bay. Moored opposite Peace Memorial Park, it also frames the act of sharing Hiroshima oysters as a small contribution to lasting peace.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima oysters served raw, grilled, fried, and as oyster rice, alongside Seto Inland Sea seafood, eaten aboard a traditional moored oyster boat on the Motoyasu River.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant grew out of an oyster-farming family that began in 1867; the 'kakibune' boat format was deliberately chosen as a way to popularize oyster cuisine, reviving an Edo-era sales tradition.
Oysters are farmed in the clean offshore waters of Dakokujima (Fukaura), chosen for high salinity and clarity so they meet the standards for oysters eaten raw.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kanawa's official history page confirms the 1867 (Keio 3) start under first-generation Hisataro Miho, the third generation's 1946 raw-oyster counters in Tokyo/Osaka department stores as the first Tokyo push for Hiroshima oysters, and the 1963 revival of the Edo-era kakibune boat. The official oyster page places farming in the clean high-salinity waters off Dakokujima/Fukaura (大黒神島深浦), meeting raw-eating standards. Sources name only the first and third generations, not six.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The restaurant's oyster and seafood dishes use Japanese soy sauce, ponzu, and dashi-based seasonings, which standardly contain wheat; fried oysters are breaded in wheat flour. No gluten-free preparation is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The entire menu is oyster- and seafood-centered with fish-based dashi; there is no documented vegan or vegetarian preparation.

cultural_comfort.note: A well-known sightseeing-area restaurant with an English website and menu and experience hosting international visitors, so a foreign student can dine comfortably, though it is an upscale sit-down experience rather than a casual budget spot.

hiro_kaiya_ren.gf_detail: No gluten-free program. This is a shellfish izakaya where most dishes are seasoned with regular (wheat-based) soy sauce, and items like the oyster kamameshi (rice) and various sauces are not gluten-free. No celiac-safe accommodation is documented; cross-contamination from a shared kitchen should be assumed.
hiro_kaiya_ren.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The entire concept is shellfish (oysters, sazae, scallops and other shellfish nationwide) plus seafood, with dishes such as shellfish sashimi, grilled oysters, shellfish-dashi chawanmushi (egg and fish/shellfish stock) and oyster kamameshi. There is no documented plant-based menu.

chef_bio.background: A small specialist shellfish izakaya in Hiroshima's Yagenbori nightlife quarter, devoted to kai (shellfish) from across Japan. The team travels directly to markets from Hokkaido in the north to Kyushu in the south, building relationships with trusted suppliers to bring in carefully chosen shellfish daily.
chef_bio.philosophy: Showcase seasonal shellfish at their peak with minimal preparation, offering each variety raw, grilled, or simmered so guests can taste its natural aroma and umami; staff suggest pairings such as oysters with white wine and raw shellfish with sake.
chef_bio.specialty: Shellfish in every form: shellfish sashimi (a signature), grilled oysters, oyster kamameshi (clay-pot rice), and a shellfish-dashi chawanmushi. A standout is the Oki Islands rock oyster branded 'Seikai' (清海), which the shop says it alone handles in Hiroshima.

anecdotes.text: The owners go directly to markets from Hokkaido down to Kyushu to source from trusted suppliers, bringing in selected shellfish fresh each day.
The shop highlights the Oki Islands rock oyster 'Seikai' as a dish it alone handles in Hiroshima, and recommends pairing oysters with white wine and raw shellfish with sake.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official Kaiya Ren page describes direct market sourcing from Hokkaido to Kyushu with trusted suppliers and daily fresh shellfish; signature shellfish sashimi, grilled oysters, oyster kamameshi and shellfish-dashi chawanmushi; wine/sake pairing guidance; and an oyster 'handled exclusively by this shop.' Search corroborates that this exclusive item is the Oki Islands brand rock oyster 'Seikai' (清海). No owner name is published.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Shellfish sashimi and grilled shellfish are served and seasoned in the Japanese style, which standardly uses wheat-based soy sauce; no gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is entirely shellfish- and seafood-based (oysters, shellfish sashimi, fish/shellfish dashi), so any plant items would share equipment with seafood.

hiro_hiroshima_teppan_produce.gf_detail: There is one dedicated gluten-free dish: a rice-flour okonomiyaki (米粉使用グルテンフリーお好み焼き, around 1,200 yen). It is built on a rice-flour sheet instead of the usual wheat batter, uses thick chewy rice-flour noodles in place of wheat soba, and is finished with a wheat-free sauce so that people with a wheat allergy can eat it. This is unusual and genuinely useful for GF diners. However, the rest of the menu is heavily wheat-based (standard okonomiyaki, gyoza, many teppan items), and the GF okonomiyaki is cooked on the same shared teppan griddle as wheat dishes, so it is a GF-friendly option rather than a dedicated GF kitchen. Strict celiacs should confirm preparation when ordering.
hiro_hiroshima_teppan_produce.vegan_detail: The menu lists a vegetable gyoza described as vegan (野菜餃子・vegan, around 500 yen). Beyond that, this is a meat-and-seafood izakaya: okonomiyaki contains egg and pork, and most teppan dishes use beef, pork, chicken, seafood, oysters and butter, so vegan choices are minimal and there is no dedicated vegan menu.

chef_bio.background: This central-Hiroshima teppan izakaya is produced by Gyozaya Ryu, a Hiroshima gyoza specialist that runs as the direct outlet of a gyoza-wrapper maker (餃子皮メーカー直営). It opened on June 30, 2023 in a wood-grained, old-school izakaya-style space directly in front of Fukuromachi Park, pairing local teppan favorites and the house gyoza with Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki.
chef_bio.philosophy: Showcasing Hiroshima ingredients and the city's okonomiyaki and gyoza culture, while offering a rice-flour, wheat-free-sauce version so guests avoiding wheat can enjoy the local specialty (diners with allergies should always confirm handling with the shop directly).
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki and house gyoza alongside teppan dishes, including a rice-flour okonomiyaki the kitchen developed with a wheat-free sauce so people avoiding wheat can enjoy the local specialty.

anecdotes.text: Their wheat-free okonomiyaki is built on a rice-flour sheet rather than wheat batter and layered with thick, chewy white rice-flour noodles, then finished with a wheat-free sauce; cooked slowly without pressing, it comes out juicy with a natural sweetness from the rice flour.
The operator describes itself as a gyoza-wrapper manufacturer's own restaurant serving 'Hiroshima gyoza born and raised in Hiroshima.'

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: HTV's okonomiyaki program confirms the June 30, 2023 opening, the Fukuromachi 2F location, the Gyozaya Ryu production, and the rice-flour-sheet, thick white rice-flour-noodle, wheat-free-sauce okonomiyaki cooked slowly without pressing for a juicy, naturally sweet result. Gyozaya Ryu's shop page confirms the 'gyoza-wrapper-maker direct outlet' self-description and the Fukuromachi Park frontage.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The gluten-free rice-flour okonomiyaki is cooked on the same shared teppan griddle used for wheat-based okonomiyaki, gyoza and other dishes; no dedicated griddle area or separate preparation is documented, so cross-contamination is likely for strict celiacs.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The kitchen specifically uses a wheat-free sauce for the gluten-free okonomiyaki so that guests with a wheat allergy can eat it (ソースは小麦が入っていないものを使う).

staff_allergy_handling.text: The restaurant created the rice-flour okonomiyaki and wheat-free sauce explicitly so that people with a wheat allergy can eat it safely (小麦アレルギーの人でも安心して食べられる), indicating awareness of wheat-allergy needs, though no formal cross-contact protocol is documented.

positives.text: Offers a genuine rice-flour, wheat-free-sauce gluten-free okonomiyaki using a rice-flour sheet and rice-flour noodles, letting wheat-sensitive diners try the Hiroshima specialty.
A vegetable gyoza is listed as vegan, giving plant-based diners at least one option.

cultural_comfort.note: A lively, dinner-only izakaya in the heart of Hiroshima's shopping district; staff likely speak limited English, so a few Japanese phrases and pointing at the picture menu will go a long way, and you can mention 小麦アレルギー (wheat allergy) when ordering the rice-flour okonomiyaki.

hiro_sarasvati.vegan_detail: No vegan menu is documented. Black coffee and the Hiroshima lemon-honey syrup drink may suit a relaxed plant-based diner, but ask about specific items.

chef_bio.background: Sarasvati occupies a warehouse surviving from the Taisho era — once a souvenir-wholesaler's storehouse — renovated into a calm two-story cafe tucked into the quiet machiya backstreets just inland from the five-story pagoda and Itsukushima Shrine. It opened in 2009 and is run as the cafe arm of Itsuki Coffee (伊都岐珈琲), a Miyajima specialty-coffee roaster.
chef_bio.philosophy: The space is conceived as a special place dedicated to enjoying coffee: beans are roasted in-house on a 3kg direct-fire roaster, with monthly rotating single-origin specialty coffees served in a deliberately serene, unhurried atmosphere.
chef_bio.specialty: Self-roasted specialty coffee, a morning service, and a signature lunch of Miyajima oyster and braised beef-shin pasta served with bread; sweets such as a rich cheesecake.

anecdotes.text: The cafe roasts its own beans on a 3kg direct-fire roaster on site and rotates the featured single-origin specialty coffee each month.
The building is a renovated warehouse remaining from the Taisho period, set in the quiet lanes behind the main approach near the pagoda and shrine.
The standout lunch is a hearty pasta of Miyajima oyster and braised beef shin served with bread.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Itsuki Coffee's official Sarasvati page confirms the on-site 3kg direct-fire roaster, cafe service from morning to lunch, and cheesecake. Search (umahiro, hiroshima-mag, pecomag) confirms the renovated Taisho-era warehouse (a former souvenir wholesaler's storehouse), the 2009 opening, the parent roaster Itsuki Coffee (伊都岐珈琲), and the signature Miyajima-oyster and braised beef-shin pasta.

positives.text: All seats are non-smoking.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed tourist-area cafe where a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu will get you by; some English signage and a foreign-visitor-friendly setting, but staff English may be limited.

hiro_sozo.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The dish is Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki built on a thin wheat-flour batter and layered with house-made wheat (Chinese-style) noodles. The house "crystal" sauce and standard toppings also make this unsuitable for those avoiding gluten. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented.
hiro_sozo.vegan_detail: Not vegan. Core dishes use egg, pork, oysters, conger eel, beef offal, fish-cake (gansu), bonito/fish-based dashi and savory sauce. No vegan okonomiyaki or plant-based option is documented.

chef_bio.background: A Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki shop tucked into a counter spot in the station-front food hall, built around an unusually all-in-house approach. The team runs its own dedicated okonomiyaki-noodle factory, pressing fresh noodles for a chewy, springy bite you do not get from bought-in noodles.
chef_bio.philosophy: The cooks describe themselves as iron-plate craftsmen who use no chemical seasonings at all, aiming to let the natural flavor of the ingredients carry the dish. To that end they make their own 'crystal' sauce, blending Seto Inland oysters and Hiroshima lemon to pair with okonomiyaki rather than relying on a generic sweet sauce; the lighter, less-sweet sauce is what makes the grated-daikon topping work so well.
chef_bio.specialty: Their signature okonomiyaki is finished with a free mound of grated daikon on top, which lightens the whole thing and plays against the sauce. Beyond the standard pork-and-noodle build, the kitchen leans into Hiroshima and Seto Inland specialties: oyster butter-yaki, rare beef shoulder (koune), miso-cooked beef lung, white-grilled conger eel, fried fish-cake (gansu), and a slow offal stew of several cuts in an original broth.

anecdotes.text: The shop makes its own okonomiyaki-specific noodles in a dedicated noodle factory, prizing a chewy, mochi-like texture in the fresh noodle.
Their original 'crystal sauce' is built around Seto Inland oysters and Hiroshima lemon, made less sweet so a free grated-daikon topping can sit on top and keep the okonomiyaki refreshing.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Ekimae-hiroba confirms the shop's own noodle factory pressing custom okonomiyaki wheat noodles, the no-chemical-seasoning iron-plate craft, the oyster-and-lemon 'crystal sauce', the free grated-daikon topping, and the specialty lineup (oyster butter-yaki, koune, miso beef lung, white-grilled conger eel, gansu, offal stew). Umaihiroshima corroborates the ponzu-like less-sweet crystal sauce and daikon topping. Sources confirm 'wheat' noodles but not specifically 'domestic' wheat, nor a proper factory name.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Okonomiyaki is cooked on a shared griddle alongside wheat batter and wheat noodles, so heavy cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Shared griddle is used for pork, oysters, eel, beef offal and egg, so any item will share surfaces with animal products.

positives.text: The kitchen states it uses no chemical seasonings and makes its own sauce and noodles in-house, so ingredient sourcing is unusually transparent.

cultural_comfort.note: A friendly counter-style okonomiyaki stall inside a tourist-oriented food hall by the station; pointing at the menu and a few words of Japanese will carry you, though full English support is not guaranteed.

hiro_tezukuri_no_pan_kouchi_b.gf_detail: This is a traditional wheat-flour bakery; bread, sandwiches and pastries are all made from wheat. There is no indication of any gluten-free option.
hiro_tezukuri_no_pan_kouchi_b.vegan_detail: A classic Japanese bakery whose signature items include egg sandwiches, ham-and-egg mix sandwiches and curry bread, which are not vegan. chef_bio.background: A handmade-bread bakery in the Nobori-cho neighborhood of central Hiroshima, within walking distance of the Hatchobori area and the Peace Memorial Park / A-Bomb Dome. It has been a fixture of the neighborhood for decades — local listings variously cite it as roughly 40 to 50-plus years old — and it has kept making bread the old-fashioned way the whole time.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop is defined by a commitment to additive-free (無添加) baking and to preserving traditional, old-fashioned flavors over the decades.
chef_bio.specialty: Its best-known item is cinnamon toast — a rusk-like bread heavily dusted with dark cinnamon that locals treat as a beloved Hiroshima casual treat — alongside a hearty, volume-packed mix sandwich, curry bread, egg sandwiches and a wide range of everyday loaves and pastries.

anecdotes.text: Local food writers describe it as a beloved, retro neighborhood bakery — the kind of long-standing local spot people walk past for years before finally stepping in and discovering just how many kinds of bread it stocks.
The cinnamon toast is singled out as a signature treat, while the volume-packed mix sandwich is recommended as an ideal lunch.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Panyasan-navi confirms the Nobori-cho handmade-bread bakery, additive-free old-fashioned baking, a rich variety of breads, and long-established (creation 50-plus years) status. 4travel confirms the signature rusk-like cinnamon toast heavily coated in dark cinnamon and the recommended volume mix sandwich, but describes the shop as roughly 40 years old — so the exact age is uncertain. No owner name is published.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A traditional wheat-flour bakery; flour is handled throughout, so the environment is unsuitable for anyone avoiding gluten and there is no gluten-free offering.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Signature items include egg and ham-and-egg sandwiches and curry bread; egg, dairy and meat are used in the kitchen, and plain breads may share equipment, so vegans should ask about specific items.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny old-school neighborhood bakery where you just point at what you want and pay in cash (PayPay also works), so almost no Japanese is needed, though an English menu is unlikely.

hiro_miyajima_les_clos.vegan_detail: No vegan or vegetarian menu is documented. Courses are built around Seto Inland Sea seafood (including the local conger eel/anago) and Japanese beef, with pasta and dairy-rich desserts. No plant-based course or substitution is mentioned.

chef_bio.background: Les Clos occupies a mansion completed in 1912 (Meiji 45), a residence now more than a century old that has been carefully renovated into a restaurant and cafe. Original architectural details such as the latticed shoji screens and carved transom panels were preserved, and the dining rooms look out onto a Japanese garden that changes with the seasons.
chef_bio.philosophy: To let Japanese tradition and Western modern design coexist in one space, pairing the heritage of the old house with cuisine that showcases seasonal local ingredients of the Seto Inland Sea.
chef_bio.specialty: Western and Italian cooking built on Seto Inland Sea produce, including seafood such as the local conger eel, alongside Japanese-beef steaks and house-made cakes and desserts

anecdotes.text: The building dates to 1912 and retains period features like its shoji and transom woodwork, giving diners the feel of eating inside a preserved Meiji-era home with a seasonal garden view.
Set along Miyajima's machiya street, a roughly 7-15 minute walk from the Miyajima pier, it pairs the historic setting with seasonal lunch and dinner courses.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official Les Clos page confirms chef-owner Isamu Kurokoshi (黒越勇), the 1912 (Meiji 45) mansion now over 100 years old, the preserved 吾妻障子 shoji and carved 欄間 transom woodwork, the seasonal Japanese garden, Western/Seto-Inland-Sea cuisine including conger eel and beef with house-made desserts, and the roughly 7-minute walk from the pier.

cultural_comfort.note: A refined sit-down restaurant in a restored historic mansion; menus and service are mainly in Japanese, so a translation app or a few Japanese phrases will help a foreign student feel comfortable ordering courses.

hiro_chugoku_ryori_kohranen.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is documented. As a Cantonese-style Chinese kitchen, dishes rely heavily on wheat-based soy sauce, oyster sauce, and other wheat-containing seasonings, and there is no mention of gluten-free preparation or a dedicated fryer. Not suitable for strict gluten-free or celiac diners.
hiro_chugoku_ryori_kohranen.vegan_detail: The restaurant offers a dedicated vegetarian Chinese course and à la carte items prepared without meat or fish, built around vegetables, mushrooms, black sticky rice, and tofu. However, the official course page describes it as lacto-ovo vegetarian: it includes dairy (e.g., a milk-based pudding) and eggs, so it is not fully vegan as listed. A strict vegan would need to call ahead (the vegetarian course requires reservation at least 3 days in advance) and explicitly request removal of dairy and eggs, plus confirm seasonings. Also confirm whether vegetable dishes use oyster sauce or chicken/fish stock common in Cantonese cooking.
