chef_bio.background: 煌蘭苑 is the Chinese restaurant on the second floor of Hotel Granvia Hiroshima, directly connected to Hiroshima Station so guests can reach it without stepping outside even on rainy days. It serves Cantonese-style Chinese cuisine in a setting that ranges from open dining to private rooms of several sizes, geared toward family meals and formal entertaining alike.
chef_bio.philosophy: Head chef Daiji Yamamoto cooks around the ancient idea that food and medicine come from the same source (医食同源), building well-balanced dishes meant to bring diners health and joy suited to the occasion.
chef_bio.specialty: Cantonese cuisine guided by the principle of 医食同源 ("food and medicine share the same origin"), with carefully balanced menus that combine a wide range of ingredients. Hong Kong-style clay-pot (煲仔) dishes are a signature, alongside multi-course menus and à la carte selections.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen prepares a dedicated vegetarian Chinese course without meat or fish, centered on vegetables, mushrooms, black sticky rice, and tofu, so that guests with dietary preferences can still enjoy authentic Chinese cooking when they reserve ahead.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The hotel's Kohranen page confirms head chef 山本大治 (Yamamoto)'s 医食同源 philosophy, the Cantonese base, the Hong Kong-favored clay-pot (煲仔/ボウジャイ) signature, the 2F station-connected location, and private rooms of varying sizes. The plan page confirms the reserve-ahead lacto-ovo-vegetarian course of vegetables, mushrooms, black sticky rice and tofu.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Cantonese-style Chinese cooking at this restaurant relies on standard Chinese seasonings such as soy sauce and oyster sauce, which contain wheat; no gluten-free preparation is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The vegetarian course is lacto-ovo: it explicitly contains no meat or fish but does include dairy (a milk-based pudding) and eggs, so it is not vegan without modification.

staff_allergy_handling.text: A dedicated meat-and-fish-free vegetarian course is offered with a required reservation at least three days in advance, indicating the kitchen accommodates dietary requests arranged ahead of time.

positives.text: Offers a dedicated vegetarian course and à la carte vegetarian items free of meat and fish, built on vegetables, mushrooms, tofu, and black sticky rice.

cultural_comfort.note: As the restaurant inside Hotel Granvia Hiroshima (directly connected to Hiroshima Station), staff are used to international hotel guests and can handle English and special dietary requests made in advance, so a foreign student should feel comfortable here.

hiro_bakery_roti.gf_detail: This is a wheat-flour bakery, so essentially all products contain gluten. No gluten-free options or dedicated gluten-free handling are documented; not suitable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.
hiro_bakery_roti.vegan_detail: No vegan-specific information is documented. This is a conventional Japanese bakery whose breads typically contain egg, milk, and butter, and signature items (cheeseburger bread, snow-crab cream, BLT dog, French toast, cinnamon rolls) clearly include dairy, egg, meat, and seafood. A vegan visitor would need to ask item-by-item and should not assume any product is plant-based.
hiro_bakery_roti.hours_raw: 7:00–19:00, closed Wednesdays (per local blog and news coverage). One platform listing alternatively shows 7:00–18:30 and Tue–Wed closed; confirm directly with the shop.

chef_bio.background: A small, owner-run neighborhood bakery in Hiroshima's Sakaimachi district, a short walk west of the downtown Hondori shopping street and the Peace Memorial Park. Open since 2009, it has become a quietly beloved local fixture, filling the shop each morning with the smell of freshly baked bread.
chef_bio.specialty: Known for an unusually wide and playful range of savory filled breads — a Japanese-style cheeseburger bun finished with grated-daikon (おろしだれ) sauce, a BLT hot dog, karaage (fried chicken) dog, and creative fillings like smoked cheese with potato salad and Sicilian-style caponata — alongside sweet options such as French toast and cinnamon rolls.

anecdotes.text: The owner recommends coming before noon, when the full lineup of breads is on display, reflecting a hands-on, made-fresh-daily approach.
The interior is described as a warm, calming space with bread arranged in the center and along the windows, plus a small eat-in corner so you can enjoy a roll on the spot.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Good-tomorrow confirms the Sakaimachi (堺町) owner-run bakery, 7:00-19:00 hours (closed Wednesdays), the eat-in corner, the before-noon full lineup, and the savory breads (cheeseburger, BLT, karaage dog, smoked-cheese potato salad, Sicilian caponata) plus French toast and cinnamon rolls. Search confirms the 2009 opening and that the cheeseburger is finished Japanese-style with a grated-daikon sauce (おろしだれ). No owner name is published.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A wheat-flour bakery; flour is handled openly throughout, so airborne and surface gluten cross-contact is unavoidable. No gluten-free production documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Breads and fillings include dairy, egg, meat, and seafood; no separation from animal ingredients is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed self-service neighborhood bakery where you pick up bread on a tray and pay at the counter, so very little Japanese is needed, though staff likely speak little English.

hiro_teppanyaki_x_fuchuyaki_a.gf_detail: This is an okonomiyaki/Fuchu-yaki house. The batter and the layered noodles are wheat-based, and the savory sauce typically contains wheat, so the core dishes are not gluten-free. No gluten-free accommodation is documented.
hiro_teppanyaki_x_fuchuyaki_a.vegan_detail: The signature Fuchu-yaki is built on crispy minced beef, and other dishes feature pork, squid and egg, plus a sauce that is generally not vegan. No vegan menu or accommodation is documented.
hiro_teppanyaki_x_fuchuyaki_a.hours_raw: Tue–Sun 11:30–13:15, 17:00–21:15; closed Monday (per Tabelog). One secondary listing shows 11:00–14:30 / 17:00–22:00 with irregular closures, so confirm before visiting.
hiro_teppanyaki_x_fuchuyaki_a.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small second-floor okonomiyaki and teppanyaki shop that opened in central Hiroshima's Tatemachi district in November 2023, a short walk from the Hondori shopping arcade.

chef_bio.origin: Hiroshima, specializing in Fuchu-yaki, the minced-meat style of okonomiyaki that originated in the city of Fuchu.
chef_bio.background: A small second-floor okonomiyaki and teppanyaki shop that opened in central Hiroshima's Tatemachi district on November 17, 2023, a short walk from the Hondori shopping arcade.
chef_bio.specialty: Fuchu-yaki: instead of sliced pork, the cook uses 100% beef mince griddled until crisp, layered with noodles fried until crackly-crunchy. A house favorite is the Acchan Special, combining pork, shiso (perilla) leaf, fresh squid and plenty of green onion for a mix of crispy noodles and snappy scallions.

anecdotes.text: The shop's draw is as much the cook as the food: he is known for a big, funny personality, and regulars say you fall for the manager before you even taste the okonomiyaki.
The Fuchu-yaki is made with 100% beef mince griddled crisp, giving the noodles a signature crackly texture.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The mypl new-open article confirms the Tatemachi 2F location near Hondori, the Fuchu-yaki made with crisp-griddled minced meat and crackly noodles, the Acchan Special (pork, shiso, squid, green onion), and the manager's big, entertaining personality. Tabelog records the opening date as November 17, 2023. No owner name is published.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, lively counter shop where the cook chats with guests; a little conversational Japanese or a translation app will make ordering and the back-and-forth much smoother for a foreign student.

hiro_teppanya_ganga.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. The core menu is okonomiyaki (wheat-flour batter and wheat noodles), yakisoba, and teppanyaki served with standard Japanese sauces (okonomi/soy sauces typically contain wheat). No gluten-free menu or accommodations are documented.
hiro_teppanya_ganga.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The menu centers on meat (1-pound steak, Hiroshima wagyu, hormone), seafood (local oysters, uni-and-spinach 'uni-horen'), and egg/pork-based okonomiyaki. No vegan dishes are documented.
hiro_teppanya_ganga.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30-14:00 (some sources 11:30-13:30); Dinner Mon-Thu 17:30-23:00, Fri & days before holidays 17:30-24:00, Sat 17:30-24:00 (L.O. 23:00). Sources disagree on the closed day (one lists Wed, others Sun/holidays, others irregular).

The counter sits right at the grill, so guests take in the taste,

chef_bio.background: A small, independently run teppanyaki and okonomiyaki spot on Tachimachi (立町) in central Hiroshima, beside the Nakanotana shopping street and a short walk from the Hondori arcade and the Peace Memorial Park. The counter sits right at the grill, so guests take in the taste, the sizzle, and the aroma of Hiroshima ingredients cooked in front of them.
chef_bio.philosophy: Showcasing Hiroshima regional ingredients on the teppan in a relaxed, neighborhood setting suited to everything from after-work drinks to small gatherings.
chef_bio.specialty: House '我んが焼 (Ganga-yaki)' okonomiyaki, the hearty value-priced 1-pound steak, fried local oysters (from Eba/江波), and a uni-and-spinach teppan dish (uni-horen / ウニホーレン); a brothless (no-soup) dandan noodle is offered for takeout. Local sake and wine are paired with the grill dishes.

anecdotes.text: The shop bills itself around tasting Hiroshima's local gourmet on the teppan, with the counter described as a place to enjoy taste, sound, and aroma all at once.
Signature items highlighted by the shop include the popular value-priced 1-pound steak, the house 'Ganga-yaki' okonomiyaki, fried Eba oysters, and a uni-and-spinach dish.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The Nakanotana mall page and Gnavi listing describe 我んが as a Tachimachi teppanyaki/okonomiyaki spot built on Hiroshima ingredients, with counter seats billed for enjoying taste, sound and aroma at once; signatures include the 1-pound steak, 我んが焼, ウニホーレン and カキフライ (Eba oysters), plus a takeout-only 汁なし担々麺. Address 中区立町3-23.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat-based okonomiyaki batter and wheat noodles are cooked on a shared teppan grill alongside other dishes; no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes use standard okonomiyaki/soy-style sauces, which typically contain wheat; no wheat-free sauce is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Menu is built on meat and seafood (steak, oysters, uni) cooked on a shared grill; no vegan preparation or separation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A friendly small local teppanyaki-izakaya where counter seats put you right by the grill; little to no English is documented, so a few Japanese phrases or a translation app will help, but the casual atmosphere is welcoming to visitors.

hiro_tetsujin_chuka_kimura.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. The menu centers on Chinese dishes using soy sauce, XO sauce and other wheat-based seasonings, plus noodles (ramen) and fried rice; mapo tofu and stir-fries rely on soy/wheat-containing sauces. No gluten-free accommodation is documented.
hiro_tetsujin_chuka_kimura.vegan_detail: Not vegan. Signature dishes are meat- and seafood-heavy (chicken, shrimp, squid; mapo tofu and mapo eggplant typically contain minced pork) and rely on animal-based and fermented sauces (XO sauce, soy sauce). No documented plant-based options.
hiro_tetsujin_chuka_kimura.notes: [Mom & Pop] The owner-chef, nicknamed the "Tetsujin" (Iron Man), trained at well-regarded Sichuan and Cantonese restaurants before opening his own counter-style place in central Hiroshima.

chef_bio.background: The owner-chef — whose shop name 鉄人 (Iron Man) nods to his command of the wok — trained at well-regarded Sichuan and Cantonese restaurants before opening his own counter-style place in Hiroshima's Kanayama-cho (銀山町).
chef_bio.philosophy: He makes his seasonings by hand from scratch — the Sichuan pepper and the sauces — and pursues ingredient quality, down to shrimp peeled one by one, serving authentic, handmade Chinese food in a casual, reasonably priced setting.
chef_bio.specialty: Sichuan-Cantonese Chinese cooking, with a mapo tofu (麻辣豆腐) served bubbling-hot and heavy on Sichuan pepper that has become a local favorite; other signatures include mapo eggplant (麻婆ナス), ebi chili (shrimp in chili sauce), and cuttlefish stir-fried in XO sauce.

anecdotes.text: The counter seats are the recommended spot because diners get a front-row "live" view of the chef working the wok.
When a local food blogger polled their Instagram followers for the best mapo tofu in town, this shop placed third.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog states the owner trained at renowned Sichuan/Cantonese restaurants and hand-makes his sansho and sauces and hand-peels shrimp; the modokimaru blog (Jan 2025) confirms the 麻辣豆腐, 麻婆ナス, ebi chili and XO cuttlefish, recommends the counter for watching the wok, and notes the shop placed 3rd in the blogger's Instagram mapo-tofu poll. Counter-focused, ~18 seats, 中区銀山町11-23.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes use soy sauce, XO sauce and other Chinese seasonings that are typically wheat-containing, and the menu includes ramen and fried rice.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Kitchen is meat- and seafood-forward (chicken, shrimp, squid; pork-based mapo dishes), so heavy shared-equipment animal cross-contact is expected.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, lively counter-style Chinese izakaya run by one chef; basic Japanese helps for ordering and casual conversation, and there is no indication of an English menu.

hiro_yakitori_kakehashi_kanay.gf_detail: This is a charcoal yakitori and chicken-hotpot izakaya. The grilled skewers are basted in tare and seasonings built on regular (wheat-based) soy sauce, and fried/marinated items and the hotpot broth also rely on standard soy-based seasonings. There is no documented gluten-free menu, no dedicated fryer information, and no indication that wheat can be avoided across the menu. Gluten-free travelers should treat this as unsafe unless they can confirm specifics directly with the kitchen in Japanese.
hiro_yakitori_kakehashi_kanay.vegan_detail: A specialist chicken restaurant with no documented plant-based options.
hiro_yakitori_kakehashi_kanay.hours_raw: Mon-Sat & holidays: 18:00-23:00 (food L.O. 22:00 / drinks L.O. 22:30, last entry 21:30). Closed Sundays.
hiro_yakitori_kakehashi_kanay.notes: [Mom & Pop] A compact charcoal-yakitori and chicken-hotpot spot tucked away in Hiroshima's Ginzan-cho nightlife district, a few minutes' walk from the Ginzan-cho tram stop. It opened in 2024 as a sister to a nearby Nagarekawa chicken restaurant under the same Kakehashi name.

chef_bio.background: A compact charcoal-yakitori and chicken-hotpot spot tucked into Hiroshima's Kanayama-cho (銀山町) nightlife district, about a three-minute walk from the Kanayama-cho tram stop. It opened on 30 May 2024 when the original 地鶏かけはし in Horikawa-cho split into two shops — a main shop and this Kanayama branch under the same Kakehashi name.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen leans on Tosa binchotan charcoal to draw out the true character of each chicken breed, crisping the surface while keeping the inside juicy, and frames itself as an artisanal, sophisticated hideaway.
chef_bio.specialty: Skewers of carefully selected heritage-breed jidori chicken grilled over Tosa binchotan charcoal, plus a rich chicken water-hotpot (mizutaki) featuring Miyazaki jidori.

anecdotes.text: The menu showcases distinct regional breeds chosen for different roles, including Akita's Hinai-jidori, Mie's Kumano-jidori, and Ehime's Himekko-jidori on the grill, with Miyazaki jidori starring in the hotpot.
A local food blogger covered the shop as a newly opened yakitori spot (opened 30 May 2024) that split off from the Horikawa-cho 地鶏かけはし.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The gorp page confirms Tosa-binchotan grilling and the breeds (秋田比内地鶏, 三重熊野地鶏, 愛媛媛っこ地鶏 for skewers; みやざき地頭鶏 for the water-hotpot) at 中区銀山町11-23 西川ビル2F; the kingofchem ameblo dates the opening to 30 May 2024 as a split of the Horikawa-cho 地鶏かけはし into a main shop and this Kanayama branch (~18 seats).

gf_cross_contamination.text: As a yakitori and izakaya kitchen, grilled skewers, fried items, and the hotpot share seasonings and surfaces built on wheat-containing soy sauce and tare; no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tare and dipping/seasoning sauces for the grilled chicken are based on standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is built entirely around chicken, with broths and seasonings of animal/soy origin, so plant-based dishes would share equipment and stocks with meat.

hiro_setouchi_ryori_zassouan_.gf_detail: No gluten-free program. As a Setouchi izakaya the cooking relies on wheat-based Japanese soy sauce and dashi-based sauces, plus tempura (octopus tempura) and other battered/fried items, so cross-contact with wheat is pervasive. No documented gluten-free menu or accommodation.
hiro_setouchi_ryori_zassouan_.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The entire concept centers on local Seto Inland Sea seafood — oysters (including year-round raw oysters), conger eel, sea bream, octopus, small sardines — plus regional pork. Dashi (fish stock) and wheat-soy-based seasonings run through the menu. No documented vegan dishes.
hiro_setouchi_ryori_zassouan_.hours_raw: 18:00–24:00 (L.O. 23:30); some listings show extended Fri/Sat hours to ~02:00. Closed Sundays.
hiro_setouchi_ryori_zassouan_.notes: Zassouan is a Hiroshima dining group with roughly a quarter-century of history, built on a simple ambition: to make a restaurant that represents Hiroshima using only Hiroshima ingredients and Hiroshima sake. The Seto (銀山町) branch carries that idea into the Nagarekawa ni

chef_bio.background: Zassouan is a Hiroshima dining group that describes roughly a quarter-century of history built on a simple ambition: to make a restaurant that represents Hiroshima using only Hiroshima ingredients and Hiroshima sake. The Seto (銀山町) branch carries that idea into the Nagarekawa/Yakugenbori nightlife district, serving the bounty of the Seto Inland Sea in an intimate setting.
chef_bio.philosophy: Local production for local consumption (地産地消) — the kitchen set out to champion Hiroshima's own ingredients and rice wines before the farm-to-table idea became fashionable, so that transplants and out-of-town guests can taste and understand Hiroshima's food culture in one sitting.
chef_bio.specialty: Setouchi local cuisine: oysters, conger eel (anago — the conger eel rice, anago-meshi, is the signature #1 favorite), sea bream, octopus, small sardines, and regional pork, paired with Hiroshima local sake.

anecdotes.text: Through ongoing research and testing with oyster producers, the restaurant secured a supply of sterilized oysters that lets it serve raw oysters all year round — a distinction it shares with only one dedicated oyster specialist in the city.

The house aims to be a place where newcomers to the region can grasp Hiroshima's food culture, presenting marine fare alongside mountain produce such as Momiji pork, Akitsu potatoes, and pickled Hiroshima greens.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: hiroshima-ouen.com states 穴子めし is the #1 dish and that, through testing with oyster producers, the shop serves 無菌 (sterile) raw oysters year-round — one of only two places in Hiroshima city (with one oyster specialist) to do so. koune and nagarekawa pages confirm the Seto-Inland-Sea/Hiroshima focus and local sake, Momiji pork, Akitsu potatoes and Hiroshima greens. The ~quarter-century, only-Hiroshima-ingredients concept is reported across listings (zassouan.net is now offline).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Menu includes tempura (e.g., octopus tempura) and other fried items, indicating shared frying and battering with wheat flour.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Seasonal Setouchi seafood dishes are seasoned in the standard Japanese izakaya manner, relying on wheat-based soy sauce and dashi.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is built around fish, shellfish (oysters), and meat, with fish-based dashi throughout; no separation for plant-only diets is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A traditional Hiroshima izakaya where menus and service are primarily in Japanese; a little Japanese or a translation app will make ordering the local seafood dishes much smoother for a foreign student.

hiro_yamamura_chaya.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering. The core dishes rely on wheat: anagomeshi and the various rice bowls are seasoned with standard Japanese soy sauce (which contains wheat), omurice is made with wheat-containing seasonings, and udon noodles are wheat. There is no indication of gluten-free preparation, dedicated equipment, or allergy accommodation.
hiro_yamamura_chaya.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The menu centers on animal products: conger eel (anago), oysters, eggs (omurice, tamago-don, kaki-tama), and dishes seasoned with fish-based dashi and soy sauce. No documented plant-based or vegetarian set meals.
hiro_yamamura_chaya.notes: [Mom & Pop] Tucked inside a small park on Miyajima island, a short walk from Itsukushima Shrine and the Momijidani Park ropeway area, Yamamura Chaya is the kind of unassuming neighborhood eatery that islanders themselves drop into. While most of Miyajima's dining caters to day-trip (Map pin approximate — Omotesandō; use the Maps link for exact spot.)

chef_bio.background: Tucked inside a small park (Fujinno-dana) on Miyajima island, a walk downhill from the Momijidani ropeway area and near Itsukushima Shrine, Yamamura Chaya is the kind of unassuming neighborhood eatery that islanders themselves drop into. While most of Miyajima's dining caters to day-trippers, this is a genuine old-fashioned shokudo (everyday diner) serving honest, affordable home-style lunches.
chef_bio.philosophy: An ordinary, comforting lunch over casual conversation rather than a tourist showpiece; the appeal is the warm, lived-in atmosphere of a real island teahouse.
chef_bio.specialty: Conger eel over rice (anagomeshi) alongside everyday comfort plates the locals order most: a fluffy omurice, oyster rice bowls, egg rice bowls, fried rice, and udon.

anecdotes.text: A diner who went looking for somewhere genuinely local rather than tourist-facing described it as the place 'where Miyajima residents come to eat in a cozy atmosphere,' valuing the comfort and the offhand conversation with the staff, and noted the omurice as the most popular item among islanders.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The Tabelog review describes 山村茶屋 as a local Miyajima shokudo where residents eat in a relaxed atmosphere; omurice (¥700) is the islanders' most popular order, fried rice (¥600) is 'plainly delicious', and anago dishes are available. It sits in Fujinno-dana Park, downhill ~10 min from the ropeway.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Anagomeshi and the rice bowls are seasoned with standard Japanese soy sauce/tare, which contains wheat; udon is also wheat-based.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Kitchen centers on conger eel, oysters, eggs, and fish-based dashi, so cross-contact with animal products is unavoidable across the menu.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a relaxed local spot where residents chat casually with the staff, so a little basic Japanese and an easygoing attitude will help you feel welcome; English support is unlikely.

hiro_okonomiyaki_yocchan.gf_detail: This is a Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki shop. The dish is built on a wheat-flour crepe batter and layered with wheat noodles (soba/udon) and finished with okonomiyaki sauce, so the core menu is not gluten-free. No gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or accommodations are documented, and everything is cooked on a single shared griddle. Not suitable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.
hiro_okonomiyaki_yocchan.vegan_detail: Every okonomiyaki here includes pork and egg as standard, and the signature dishes use them plus optional squid, shrimp, and other animal toppings. The sauce and griddle are shared with meat. No vegan or vegetarian options are documented. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
hiro_okonomiyaki_yocchan.hours_raw: Mon-Fri 11:00-14:30 / Sat & holidays 11:00-14:00 / closed Sundays (lunchtime only)
hiro_okonomiyaki_yocchan.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small counter-style Hiroshima-okonomiyaki shop tucked into the basement of an office building right next to the Hiroshima Prefectural Government, founded by owner Hidenori Yoshiyama in 1990 and run as a beloved weekday-lunch spot for local office workers.

chef_bio.background: A small counter-style Hiroshima-okonomiyaki shop tucked into the basement of an office building in the Motomachi/Kamiyacho district next to the Hiroshima Prefectural Government, founded by owner Hidenori Yoshiyama in 1990 and run as a beloved weekday-lunch spot for local office workers.
chef_bio.philosophy: Yoshiyama believes great okonomiyaki comes from reading the griddle: 'a person who understands the griddle's feelings can make delicious okonomiyaki.' He steams the cabbage gently to coax out its natural sweetness for a light, fluffy texture rather than a dense one, and holds to a simple standard of cheap prices, generous portions, and good taste.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, with the most popular order being the soba nikutama (noodles layered with pork and egg). The owner sources fresh noodles from a local maker (Isono Seimen) and finishes the dish with Mouri Brewing's Carp Sauce from Miyoshi, which uses vegetable-based natural sweetness rather than artificial sweeteners.

anecdotes.text: The owner carefully controls cooking time and the cabbage's position on the griddle to bring out its natural sweetness, aiming for a fluffy texture instead of a hard one.
He chooses Mouri Brewing's Carp Sauce because it has no artificial sweeteners, so when brushed onto the hot okonomiyaki it gives off an appetizing aroma.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Chugoku Shimbun's okonomiyaki feature profiles owner 吉山英典 (est. 1990): he gently steams cabbage to draw out sweetness for a fluffy texture, holds to 'cheap, generous, tasty', uses Isono Seimen (磯野製麺) fresh noodles and Mouri Brewing's Carp Sauce (Miyoshi/三次) with no artificial sweeteners. Tabelog lists the shop basement in Motomachi/Kamiyacho, 肉玉 the signature.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Single shared teppan griddle on which wheat-based okonomiyaki and noodles are cooked together; no separation documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Finished with okonomiyaki/Carp brand sauce (Mouri Brewing), which is wheat-containing and not gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All okonomiyaki are made with pork and egg as standard and cooked on a shared griddle with other meat and seafood toppings.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a tiny, cash-only lunchtime counter shop in an office-building basement frequented by local workers, so come ready to order in Japanese (or by pointing) and don't expect English menus or card payment.

hiro_karada_ni_yasashii_sosak.gf_detail: According to several reservation-information sites, the menu using local ingredients can be customized to gluten-free on request. However, there is no mention of a dedicated cooking line, and as a Japanese restaurant the standard menu likely uses wheat-containing seasonings (soy sauce, miso, etc.). For gluten-free requests, advance consultation and confirmation by phone (082-246-7721) is necessary. Safety assessment: not reliably safe for celiacs; gluten-free is offered as an on-request customization with no dedicated line, and wheat-based seasonings are likely in standard dishes.
hiro_karada_ni_yasashii_sosak.vegan_detail: The restaurant's signature is "body-friendly" obanzai centered on vegetable dishes, and it states explicitly that a vegetarian menu is available. According to reservation-information sites, vegan customization is also possible on request. However, because the standard obanzai and the dashi often use animal-derived ingredients such as seafood and bonito dashi, those wanting fully vegan should consult at the time of advance reservation. Safety assessment: vegetarian-friendly and vegan-possible on request, but the default dashi is often animal-based, so advance consultation is needed for strict vegan.
hiro_karada_ni_yasashii_sosak.hours_raw: Mon-Sat & holidays: 11:00-15:00 (L.O. 14:00), 17:00-22:00 (L.O. 21:00) / Sun: 17:00-22:00 (some sources say closed Sun). Takeout/delivery 11:00-18:00. Irregular days off during private bookings or large catering jobs.
hiro_karada_ni_yasashii_sosak.notes: She obtained her cook's license in 1979 and graduated from the Faculty of Letters of Hiroshima Jogakuin University in 1980. After marrying she devoted herself to homemaking, but prompted by her husband's illness she opened the soup and obanzai shop "Kitchen Potluck" in 2000. In October 2010 she relocated to Fukuromachi/Nakamachi in Naka-ku and opened the natural-food restaurant "AGRI." She serves as a director of Slow Food Hiroshima and is involved in efforts to promote rice flour, as well as being active in many fields such as cooking segments on TV and radio and lectures at her alma mater, Hiroshima Jogakuin University.

chef_bio.origin: 広島市出身（1956年生まれ）。実家は魚屋兼仕出し業を営んでいた。
chef_bio.background: 1979年に調理師免許を取得、1980年に広島女学院大学文学部を卒業。結婚後は家事に専念していたが、夫の病気をきっかけに2000年にスープとおばんざいの店『キッチンポットラック』を開業。2010年に中区袋町へ移転して自然派の店『AGRI』をオープンした（現在は中町）。スローフード広島の理事を務め、広島市の米粉推進委員として米粉普及にも関わるほか、テレビ・ラジオの料理コーナーや2013年からの母校・広島女学院大学での講義など、多方面で活動している。
chef_bio.philosophy: 『野菜の力を創り出す』『食と人をつないで新しい価値を創り出す』をコンセプトに、体にやさしい料理で食卓を豊かにすることを目指す。2020年には減塩レシピ本『魔女の幸せ100年レシピ』を著すなど、減塩・健康志向の食を発信している。
chef_bio.specialty: 季節の野菜をたっぷり使い、20種類以上の食材を一皿に盛り込む『おばんざいランチ』。広島県産の米や玄米を用い、塩分2g以下に抑えた『減塩ランチ』も看板。

anecdotes.text: 実家が魚屋兼仕出し業という食の環境で育ち、夫の病気を機に2000年に自身の店を開いたことが料理研究家としての出発点となった。
広島の減塩サミット(2012年・2014年)に出展し、瀬戸内ブランド認定を受けた『まるごと広島レモンケーキ』など地域食材を生かした商品開発にも取り組んでいる。

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Japanese Wikipedia gives her bio: born 1956 in Hiroshima to a family running a fish shop/caterer, cook's license 1979, graduated 広島女学院大学文学部 1980, opened キッチンポットラック in 2000 after her husband's illness, moved to Fukuromachi and opened AGRI in 2010; Slow Food Hiroshima director, Hiroshima city rice-flour committee, university lecturer from 2013. The AGRI site/HotPepper confirm the 20+-ingredient おばんざいランチ with 玄米, the 塩分2g以下 減塩ランチ, the 減塩サミット (2012/2014) and the Setouchi-brand まるごと広島レモンケーキ.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: 和食・おばんざいの店であり、醤油・味噌など小麦を含む調味料が通常使われているとみられる(出汁・味付けの基本)。グルテンフリー希望は事前相談が必要。

vegan_cross_contact.text: おばんざいや出汁には魚介・かつお出汁など動物性食材が使われることが多く、完全ヴィーガンには事前のカスタマイズ相談が前提。

staff_allergy_handling.text: 地元食材を使ったメニューはリクエストに応じてヴィーガン・グルテンフリーにカスタマイズ可能と案内されている。

positives.text: 野菜料理にこだわり、ベジタリアンメニューがあると明記。塩分2g以下の減塩ランチなど健康配慮メニューが充実。
料理研究家が営む個人店で、玄米(美人玄米)や20品目以上の食材を使った体にやさしいおばんざいが看板。

cultural_comfort.note: 料理研究家のオーナーが営む個人店で、英語メニューや英語対応の記載は確認できないため、基本的な日本語(または翻訳アプリ)があると安心して食事と食事制限の相談ができます。

hiro_shofuku_miyajima.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free destination. Core dishes rely on Japanese soy sauce and dashi-based seasonings (which typically contain wheat), and grilled/glazed anago and oyster rice use soy-based sauces. Onigiri and rice bowls are rice-based but the seasonings are not gluten-free, and no gluten-free preparation or labeling is documented. A celiac traveler should not rely on this spot.
hiro_shofuku_miyajima.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The entire menu is built around oysters (raw and grilled), anago (conger eel), scallops and other seafood, with dashi and fish-based seasonings throughout. There are no documented plant-based main dishes.
hiro_shofuku_miyajima.hours_raw: 10:30-20:00 daily (primary listing). A separate listing shows 10:30-18:00 with Tuesdays closed, so closing time and a possible Tuesday rest day can vary seasonally.
hiro_shofuku_miyajima.notes: [Mom & Pop] Shofuku opened in 2017, with its main shop in Hiroshima city's Horikawa-cho district; the Miyajima shop is its second location, set right in front of the ferry terminal at the entrance to the Omotesando approach. It is a small independent operation rather than a chain. (Map pin approximate — Omotesandō; use the Maps link for exact spot.)

chef_bio.origin: Hiroshima city (Horikawa-cho main shop), expanding onto Miyajima island.
chef_bio.background: Shofuku opened in 2017, with its main shop in Hiroshima city's Horikawa-cho district; the Miyajima shop is its second location, set right in front of the ferry terminal at the entrance to the Omotesando approach. It is a small independent operation rather than a chain.
chef_bio.philosophy: A focus on fresh, carefully handled local oysters and anago, served in both sit-down and grab-and-go formats so visitors can taste Miyajima's signature seafood while strolling.
chef_bio.specialty: Local oysters served raw and grilled, including large, plump oysters prized for sweetness and umami, plus oyster rice and fresh anago (conger eel) dishes. The shop leans on oysters that are described as non-frozen and not treated with chlorinated water, prized for clean, clear flavor.

anecdotes.text: Diners highlight the friendly, knowledgeable hospitality, with staff happy to share local tips alongside the seafood.
The shop is praised for fresh oysters that are not frozen and not disinfected with chlorinated water, giving them a notably clean, transparent taste.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog confirms 笑福 opened 2017 with its main shop in Horikawa-cho and the Miyajima shop as the 2nd location in front of the ferry terminal at the Omotesando entrance; it serves local oysters raw and grilled, oyster rice and anago, and prides itself on non-frozen oysters not treated with chlorinated water for a clean, clear taste (24 seats, no reservations). Hitosara notes friendly, knowledgeable service.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes such as glazed/grilled anago, oyster rice and onigiri rely on Japanese soy- and dashi-based seasonings, which conventionally contain wheat; no gluten-free soy sauce is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The menu is entirely seafood-based (oysters, anago, scallops) with dashi seasonings, so cross-contact with animal products is unavoidable across the whole operation.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual walk-up oyster and anago shop right by the ferry where you can point at what you want and eat on the go, so a few words of Japanese and a smile go a long way even if no English menu is guaranteed.

hiro_kura_vitto.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation is documented. Signature dishes are wheat-based: the Hiroshima oyster margherita pizza and the daily-changing pasta both contain wheat. Tapas and light fare are not described as gluten-free, and no gluten-free menu or preparation is mentioned anywhere. A celiac or gluten-sensitive diner should treat this venue as unsuitable unless they confirm specific options directly.
hiro_kura_vitto.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The menu centers on oysters (oyster pizza), and the documented tapas include low-temperature salmon and roast beef; pizza and pasta typically use cheese and dairy. No vegan dishes or plant-based options are documented. The draw is local Hiroshima sake, shochu, wine, and craft beer paired with seafood and meat small plates.
hiro_kura_vitto.hours_raw: 9:00-23:00 (food L.O. 22:00 / drinks L.O. 22:30); lunch from around 11:30

chef_bio.origin: Miyajima island, Hiroshima — set just inside the main entrance of Hotel Miyajima Besso, a short walk from the ferry pier
chef_bio.background: 蔵VITTO is the bar of Hotel Miyajima Besso, a modern property produced by Kinsuikan, a long-running Miyajima hot-spring inn founded in 1902. The name plays on 蔵 (kura, a sake brewery storehouse), a nod to the idea that you have arrived at the gateway of Miyajima with Hiroshima's celebrated local brews waiting for you.
chef_bio.philosophy: Celebrating Hiroshima as one of Japan's great sake regions and pairing local craft drinks with cuisine built on fresh regional produce — an everyday oasis for grown-ups that welcomes both hotel guests and passing travelers.
chef_bio.specialty: A relaxed adult bal showcasing Hiroshima's drink culture alongside small plates such as a generous Hiroshima oyster pizza and rotating daily tapas from the hotel chef, served from morning (9:00) through late evening.

anecdotes.text: The bar pours Sakurao Gin distilled in nearby Sakurao (Hatsukaichi) and local Miyajima craft beer, with signature cocktails like a Miyajima Gin Tonic and Hiroshima Spumoni developed under bartender Shingo Noma.
You can enjoy fresh bread bought from the hotel's own bakery, Shimaumai PAN (島旨PAN), right at the bar counter.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The Hotel Miyajima Besso 蔵VITTO bar page confirms the bar is produced by Kinsuikan (founded 1902), pours Sakurao Gin (Hatsukaichi), Miyoshi-winery wine and Miyajima/Hiroshima craft beer from 9:00, offers signature cocktails Miyajima Gin Tonic and Hiroshima Spumoni under Shingo Noma, an oyster pizza and tapas, and bread from its Shimaumai PAN (島旨PAN) bakery. The mrs.living reporter article covers the same bar.

cultural_comfort.note: As a stylish bar inside a hotel right by the Miyajima ferry pier, it's used to receiving travelers, so a friendly konnichiwa and pointing at the menu will get you a warm welcome even with limited Japanese.

hiro_okonomiyaki_matochan.gf_detail: This is a Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki house. The okonomiyaki batter and crepe layer are made from wheat flour, the layered noodles (そば) are wheat, the signature あげおこ is deep-fried battered okonomiyaki, and dishes are finished with wheat-based okonomiyaki/Otafuku sauce and soy-sauce-based seasonings. The fried oysters (牡蠣フライ) use wheat breadcrumbs. No gluten-free menu, preparation, or accommodation is documented anywhere. Not suitable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.
hiro_okonomiyaki_matochan.vegan_detail: The menu centers on egg-and-pork okonomiyaki, oysters (Miyajima brand 牡蠣), squid, shrimp, and bonito/fish-based dashi and toppings, with sauces that are not vegan. The closest non-meat item documented is an oven-baked potato-salad-and-cheese dish (ポテサラチーズ焼, dairy, not vegan). No vegan or fully vegetarian options are documented, and no vegan accommodation is mentioned. Not suitable for vegans.
hiro_okonomiyaki_matochan.hours_raw: Mon, Wed, Thu (and holidays): 11:00-16:00 (L.O. 15:00). Fri, Sat, Sun: 11:00-16:00 (L.O. 15:00) and 17:00-21:00 (L.O. 20:00). Closed Tuesdays. May close early when sold out.
hiro_okonomiyaki_matochan.notes: [Mom & Pop] Tucked into a quiet alley just steps from the exit of Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima, this Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki shop occupies a converted house more than twenty years old, giving it a calm, lived-in feel away from the bustle of the main shopping street. (Map pin approximate — Omotesandō; use the Maps link for exact spot.)

chef_bio.background: Tucked into a quiet alley just steps from the exit of Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima, this Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki shop occupies a converted house more than twenty years old, giving it a calm, lived-in feel away from the bustle of the main shopping street.
chef_bio.philosophy: Pairing honest, classic Hiroshima okonomiyaki with the best local Miyajima oysters, so the place works equally for a quick walking snack and for diners who come specifically for the oysters.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki and Miyajima oysters. The standout is あげおこ, a deep-fried okonomiyaki made for eating on the move, offered in soba, squid, oyster, and cheese versions. The kitchen also leans hard into local oysters, using the premium Hiroshima 'Gokusen (極選)' brand for dishes like the oyster special (five large oysters piled on the okonomiyaki) and oyster ponzu with a house-blended ponzu.

anecdotes.text: The owner's own favorite build is an okonomiyaki with shrimp, squid, shiso (oba), and squid tempura bits, and he personally recommends the seseri (chicken neck) served with grated-radish and ponzu.
あげおこ (deep-fried okonomiyaki) has a crisp texture unlike ordinary okonomiyaki and is made for eating on the move — a popular grab-and-go for shrine visitors.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shop's own site confirms まとちゃん occupies a converted 20+-year-old house near the Itsukushima Shrine exit; signatures are あげおこ (crispy deep-fried okonomiyaki for eating on the move, in soba/squid/oyster/cheese versions), premium Gokusen-brand oysters (oyster special = five large oysters; oyster ponzu with house-blended ponzu), the owner's shrimp-squid-shiso-tempura build, and seseri (chicken neck) with grated-radish ponzu.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core dishes (okonomiyaki batter, layered wheat noodles, deep-fried あげおこ, and breaded fried oysters) are all wheat-based and cooked on shared teppan/fryer surfaces; no gluten-free preparation is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes are finished with wheat-based okonomiyaki/Otafuku sauce and soy-sauce-based seasonings (e.g., ponzu), which typically contain wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The menu is built around egg, pork, oysters, squid, shrimp, and fish-based dashi/toppings cooked on a shared griddle; no vegan preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, casual family-run okonomiyaki spot in a converted old house just off the Itsukushima Shrine path; English is not advertised, but pointing at the picture menu and a friendly konnichiwa will get a foreign student through comfortably.

hiro_miyajima_sushi_tensen.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. This is a traditional sushi counter built around soy sauce (the kitchen pairs sushi with four soy-sauce styles including tamari and a tsuyu/dashi-soy blend, all conventional wheat-containing or dashi-based seasonings), plus dishes like seared Hiroshima beef and oyster soup. No gluten-free menu or wheat-free soy sauce is documented, and there is no dedicated fryer or GF handling on record.
hiro_miyajima_sushi_tensen.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The entire menu centers on raw and grilled Seto Inland Sea fish, Miyajima oysters, and Hiroshima beef, with fish-based dashi and soy sauces throughout. No vegan or vegetarian course is documented; meals are chef's-choice omakase.
hiro_miyajima_sushi_tensen.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30-14:00 (last entry 13:00, L.O. 13:30); Dinner 17:00-22:00 (last entry 20:30, L.O. 21:30). Closed Wednesdays, and the 1st and 3rd Tuesday of each month.
hiro_miyajima_sushi_tensen.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small hideaway-style sushi counter tucked into a quiet alley just off Miyajima's Omotesando shopping street, a short walk from the Miyajima ferry pier. It opened in 2017 and seats guests at an intimate counter where the chef serves an omakase progression. (Map pin approximate — Omotesandō; use the Maps link for exact spot.)

chef_bio.background: A small hideaway-style sushi counter tucked into a quiet alley just off Miyajima's Omotesando shopping street, a short walk (about five minutes) from the Miyajima ferry pier. It opened in 2017 and seats guests at an intimate counter where the chef serves an omakase progression.
chef_bio.philosophy: A devotion to local sourcing: the seasonal Seto Inland Sea fish, the wasabi, the rice, and the sake are all from Hiroshima Prefecture. The sushi rice is seasoned with a blend of rice vinegar and red vinegar, and rather than one all-purpose soy sauce the counter pairs each piece with one of four styles - sudachi soy, Tosa soy, tamari, and a tsuyu-style blend - chosen to match the ingredient.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal fish of the Seto Inland Sea, served as nigiri and small plates, alongside signature local items such as seared Hiroshima beef and a soup made with Miyajima oysters.

anecdotes.text: Seasonal menus rotate with the catch; a winter lineup featured yellowtail, sea cucumber, oysters, and Japanese jack mackerel.
The kitchen deliberately switches between four different soy sauces - sudachi, Tosa, tamari, and a tsuyu blend - depending on which fish is being served.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Hatsukaichi-concierge confirms 天扇 opened 2017, ~5 min from the ferry, a counter omakase using Seto-Inland-Sea fish, wasabi, rice and sake all from Hiroshima Prefecture; the shari blends rice and red vinegar; four soy sauces (sudachi, Tosa, tamari, tsuyu blend) are matched to each piece; specialties include seared Hiroshima beef and Miyajima oyster soup; a winter lineup featured yellowtail, sea cucumber, oysters and jack mackerel.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The restaurant pairs sushi with four soy-sauce styles (sudachi, Tosa, tamari, and a tsuyu/dashi-soy blend); these are conventional Japanese soy-based and dashi-based seasonings, none documented as gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Menu is entirely fish-, shellfish-, and meat-based (Seto Inland Sea fish, Miyajima oysters, Hiroshima beef) with fish dashi, so no separation from animal products is possible.

cultural_comfort.note: A reservation-only counter sushi-ya where the chef serves omakase course by course; a little Japanese and an understanding of sushi-counter etiquette will help, though staff are used to visitors to Miyajima.

hiro_hiroshima_tsukemen_buchi.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The core dish is tsukemen — wheat-flour noodles dipped in a sauce built on soy sauce (which contains wheat). There are no documented gluten-free options.
hiro_hiroshima_tsukemen_buchi.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The dipping broth is a three-blend of chicken-and-pork bone (鶏ガラ豚骨) with seafood (魚介) and tomato, and the dish is served with chashu (roast pork). The wheat noodles and soy-sauce-based dare make this unsuitable for vegans or vegetarians.
hiro_hiroshima_tsukemen_buchi.notes: [Mom & Pop] A Hiroshima-style tsukemen specialist tucked into the Wing Building on Tatemachi, a short walk from the Hatchobori and Hondori shopping districts and just steps from Tatemachi tram stop. It is reported to be the Hiroshima arrival of a well-known Tokyo tsukemen name, bri

chef_bio.background: A Hiroshima-style tsukemen specialist tucked into the Wing Building on Tatemachi, a short walk from the Hatchobori and Hondori shopping districts and just steps from the Tatemachi tram stop. By night the same space becomes the restaurant Pul Dil Mare, so the tsukemen runs chiefly as a daytime operation.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style spicy tsukemen: chewy wheat noodles served with a dipping sauce blending pork-bone richness, seafood umami, and tomato, topped with juicy chashu, with diner-selectable chili heat.

anecdotes.text: The signature is a dipping sauce combining pork-bone richness with seafood umami and tomato, paired with juicy chashu, with spice levels customizable to the diner's preference.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog describes ぶちうま as an independent Hiroshima-style tsukemen shop (not a chain) in the Wing Building on Tatemachi (立町, ~116m from the tram stop) whose space becomes 'Pul Dil Mare' at night; the つけ麺 (¥1,100) has a 豚骨 (pork-bone) + seafood + tomato dipping sauce with customizable heat and chashu. Gnavi confirms the 中区立町6-1 ウイングビル1F address.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A wheat-noodle tsukemen shop with soy-sauce-based dipping broth; gluten is central to the menu and there is no indication of gluten-free handling or separation.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The dipping sauce is soy-sauce based (standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat); the broth is a chicken-pork-bone, seafood and tomato blend.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is animal-based (chicken-pork bone plus seafood) and the dish is topped with pork chashu; no vegan or vegetarian preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny lunch-only counter noodle shop where ordering is simple (point to the tsukemen and tell them your spice level); a few words of Japanese and a friendly konnichiwa will carry you through with no English expected.

hiro_toriiya.gf_detail: No gluten-free options. The signature momiji croissant ("Momikuro") is made from wheat croissant dough, and momiji manju are wheat-and-egg sponge cakes. Local dishes such as anago-don (conger eel rice) and oyster dishes are served with standard wheat-based soy sauce and sauces. No dedicated gluten-free items or accommodations are documented.
hiro_toriiya.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. Sweets contain dairy and egg (cream, cheese, chocolate croissant varieties; momiji manju use egg). Savory menu centers on conger eel (anago) and oysters, which are not vegan, and uses fish/wheat-soy-based seasonings. No documented plant-based options.
hiro_toriiya.hours_raw: 8:30-17:00 (shop). The dining area is roughly 10:30-16:00. Hours vary during busy seasons (April-June, September-November).

chef_bio.background: Toriiya sits right on Miyajima's Omotesando shopping arcade, on the lively path that runs from the ferry pier toward the great torii and Itsukushima Shrine. It works as a tourism center (観光センター): the ground floor is a souvenir shop where momiji manju (maple-leaf-shaped cakes) are sold, while the 2nd and 3rd floors host dining rooms for groups, with the in-house eatery serving Hiroshima specialties such as anago-don.
chef_bio.philosophy: The 'momiji croissant' is made as a hand-held food-walk (tabe-aruki) snack to enjoy while strolling the arcade, and its fillings are built on the shop's own house-made an (sweet bean paste) rather than bought-in paste.
chef_bio.specialty: The shop is best known for the 'momiji croissant' nicknamed 'Momikuro' (もみクロ), sold at its storefront for snacking as you stroll. A square of crisp croissant dough frames a soft maple-leaf-shaped center, offered in six standing varieties — red bean, cream/custard, apple, chocolate, cheese, and one rotating seasonal flavor — with the recommended tsubu-an using the shop's house-made anko.

anecdotes.text: The Momikuro is a media-featured 'new specialty' of the shop and is described as palm-sized (手のひらサイズ), so it satisfies without filling you up before other island treats.
It comes in six standard flavors, and the shop's own house-made anko is used for its recommended red-bean (tsubu-an) filling, setting it apart from ordinary momiji manju.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Official site and Tabetainjya food-walk blog: Toriiya is a Miyajima tourism center (souvenirs + upstairs group dining serving anago-don); its Momikuro momiji croissant comes in six flavors (red bean, cream, apple, chocolate, cheese, seasonal), palm-sized, with house-made anko in the recommended red-bean version.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Savory island dishes such as anago-don and oyster dishes are served with standard Japanese seasonings, which typically include wheat-based soy sauce.

cultural_comfort.note: A busy, tourist-friendly arcade shop where you can simply point at a croissant and pay at the counter, so a few words of Japanese and a smile are all you need to enjoy a food-walk snack.

chef_bio.background: Founded in 1933, Kimuraya Honten is a family-run momiji manju shop standing on a prominent corner right where the Omotesando shopping street begins on the approach to Itsukushima Shrine. For generations it has made its maple-leaf cakes by hand, and visitors can watch the manju being baked right at the storefront.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop deliberately keeps its original formulation and traditional dough, making its momiji manju without emulsifiers or additives — reportedly one of the only makers on Miyajima to do so, which appeals to families and additive-conscious visitors.
chef_bio.specialty: Momiji manju with a notably firm, chewy dough that sets it apart from the softer versions sold elsewhere on the island, filled with a sweet, sticky adzuki bean paste made to the original recipe. Beyond the classic red-bean version, the shop offers fillings such as soy-milk cream, cheese, raisin, pumpkin, and chestnut.

anecdotes.text: The proprietor describes keeping the recipe unchanged: making the manju with the traditional dough and without emulsifiers ('配合を変えず昔ながらの生地にこだわり、乳化剤等を使用せず製造').
The firm dough and unchanged-since-opening sweet bean paste give the cakes a distinctly old-fashioned Miyajima character, best enjoyed with green tea.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Oyakode-tanoshimou blog: Kimuraya Honten, est. 1933, corner shop at the start of Omotesando; firm chewy dough, emulsifier/additive-free (reportedly the only such maker on Miyajima), fillings include soy-milk cream, cheese, raisin, pumpkin, chestnut.

chef_bio.background: Sakamoto Kashiho is a family-run sweets shop on Miyajima that has been baking momiji-manju since 1955, more than seventy years of single-family craft. It sits a block off the bustling Omotesando arcade, a quieter spot where visitors can step away from the crowds about ten minutes from Itsukushima Shrine.
chef_bio.philosophy: Rather than buying in pre-made fillings, the shop makes everything by hand: the father personally crafts both the bean paste and the castella sponge, carefully removing the skins of the azuki beans to produce a refined paste with a gentle sweetness and smooth texture.
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-baked momiji-manju with house-made azuki bean paste, and a signature filling-free salted-butter momiji.

anecdotes.text: The signature salted-butter momiji breaks from tradition with no anko at all, instead kneading French sea salt and New Zealand butter into the fluffy castella sponge for an entirely different flavor; it is the shop's most popular (No.1) item.
Seasonal momiji rotate through the year: cherry-leaf-scented sakura anko in spring, Uji matcha with whole azuki in summer, chestnut-cream Mont Blanc in fall, and roasted sweet-potato paste in winter.
A small tea space (about 14 seats) lets guests eat the momiji fresh from the oven, warm and fluffy, with complimentary self-serve tea.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Japan-stroll gourmet blog: Sakamoto Kashiho, est. 1955, off Omotesando (~10 min from the shrine); father hand-makes bean paste and castella, peeling azuki skins; No.1 salted-butter momiji (French salt, NZ butter, no filling); seasonal flavors; ~14-seat space with free self-serve tea.

cultural_comfort.note: A small family-run sweets shop tucked off the main arcade; a friendly greeting and pointing at the freshly baked momiji you want will carry you through, though detailed allergy questions may be hard without some Japanese.

chef_bio.background: Karabu (辛部) is one of the standard-bearers of Hiroshima-style tsukemen, the city's spicy cold dipping-noodle dish. Though it arrived after the genre's pioneers, it won a following on the strength of its noodles and broth and grew into a small chain with several Hiroshima locations; the Tokaichi shop is the original main store (十日市本店).
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima tsukemen: firm, springy wheat noodles served cold alongside a clean, spicy dipping broth, dressed with cabbage, cucumber, negi, nori or bonito, and chashu, with a customizable heat scale.

anecdotes.text: The spice level is set on a wide scale from 0 up to around 30, with a signature stick-style heat gauge; locals note that even '10' lands only just short of medium-hot.
The noodles are described as firm with a crunchy bite and the broth as simple and clean enough to drink down, drawing many female customers and strong local support.
Regarded as one of the representative Hiroshima tsukemen names, comparable in recognition and scale to other major local specialists, having expanded to multiple branches across the city.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Modokimaru and Syokuki blogs: Karabu is a representative Hiroshima tsukemen shop, the Tokaichi location being the honten; spice runs 0-30 on a stick gauge; firm crunchy noodles and a clean drinkable broth; many female customers; expanded to roughly six branches across Hiroshima.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat noodles are the core product, so flour and wheat are pervasive in the kitchen; no GF preparation is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The dipping broth is seasoned with soy sauce, which in this style is typically wheat-based; no gluten-free soy alternative is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes are built on meat/fish broth and topped with pork chashu and bonito, so shared cookware and broth make vegan service impractical.

cultural_comfort.note: Ordering is by ticket machine and the menu is mostly in Japanese, so glance at the posted menu outside and learn the spice scale before stepping up to order.

hiro_wakabatei.gf_detail: This is a tsukemen shop: the noodles are wheat and the spicy dipping broth uses soy sauce (wheat-based) and fish dashi, so the core dishes are not gluten-free. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented.
hiro_wakabatei.vegan_detail: The signature spicy dipping broth is built on bonito/seafood (fish) dashi, so the tsukemen is not vegan. No vegan or vegetarian options are documented; vegetable toppings exist but the broth itself contains fish.

chef_bio.background: A small counter-only tsukemen shop tucked into the Takanobashi shopping street in central Hiroshima, opened as Hiroshima-style spicy dipping noodles grew in popularity. It is run as a family operation by a couple, with the proprietress tending the broth and a partner helping with service; the room is an L-shaped counter of about ten seats.
chef_bio.philosophy: A restrained, seafood-forward dipping broth with the spice dialed exactly to the diner's request, served in an intimate counter setting.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style tsukemen: thin wheat noodles served with a cold, seafood-and-bonito dipping broth that you can order at a customizable heat, from no spice up to eye-watering challenge levels.

anecdotes.text: The shop is famous for its escalating spice levels; diners who conquer the most extreme heat have their names posted in the shop, and a 'Hell Ramen' at the top spice level (with multiplier challenges reaching 150x and 200x) is offered as a challenge even regulars find brutal.
The broth leans on bonito dashi with restrained acidity, and the noodles are noticeably thinner than at rival Hiroshima tsukemen shops.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Oomin77 blog: Wakabatei on Takanobashi shopping street, L-shaped counter (~10 seats) run by a couple; famous for escalating spice with conquerors' names posted, a 'Hell Ramen' and 150x/200x multiplier challenges; bonito-forward broth with restrained acidity; noodles thinner than rivals.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core dishes are wheat noodles boiled in shared water and a soy-sauce-based dipping broth, so cross-contamination with gluten is unavoidable; no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Hiroshima tsukemen dipping broth is soy-sauce based, and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The dipping broth is made with fish/bonito and seafood dashi, so all tsukemen contains animal-derived stock.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 12-seat counter shop run by the owners; ordering is simple but staff likely speak little English, so knowing a few Japanese words for ordering and your desired spice level helps.

hiro_indo_ryori_roopali_wakak.gf_detail: No documented gluten-free program. Naan and the breads are wheat-based, and the popular set lunches center on naan, so they are not gluten-free. Turmeric/saffron rice with a curry could be a starting point, but Indian curries here may use wheat-thickened or dairy bases and no celiac-safe handling is stated. A coeliac should phone ahead (082-264-1333) and confirm dish by dish; assume cross-contact in a busy shared kitchen.
hiro_indo_ryori_roopali_wakak.vegan_detail: As a North Indian restaurant it carries genuine meat-free items: vegetable salad with beans, vegetable pakora (Indian-style vegetable tempura), and vegetable/chickpea-style curries. However these are not certified vegan — paneer (cheese) pakora is on the menu, and curries and naan commonly use ghee, butter, cream, yogurt or milk. Ask for a fully plant-based vegetable or dal curry without dairy, and pair with plain rice rather than naan (naan often contains milk/yogurt). Vegetarian is easy here; strict vegan requires asking the staff to omit dairy.
hiro_indo_ryori_roopali_wakak.notes: A long-running Indian restaurant a short walk from Hiroshima Station, where much of the kitchen and floor staff are from India, giving the food and the room an authentic feel. chef_bio.background: A long-running Indian restaurant a short walk from Hiroshima Station (Wakakusacho, Higashi-ku), where much of the kitchen and floor staff are from India, giving the food and the room an authentic feel. It has become a neighborhood fixture, especially at lunch, when a queue often forms for its generous curry sets.
chef_bio.specialty: North Indian curries cooked with Indian spices, served with freshly baked naan and rice. The set lunches let you choose from several curries (including the Roopali Special Set with tandoori items) with free refills of naan and rice.

anecdotes.text: At lunchtime a line forms outside for the choose-your-curry sets, a sign of how the spot has been embraced locally.
Diners pick their favorites from several curries and the naan and rice can be refilled, which is part of its everyday appeal.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Syokuki and Tabelog: Roopali Wakakusacho honten near Hiroshima Station; lunchtime queues for choose-your-curry sets; Roopali Special Set pairs curry with naan, rice and tandoori items; North Indian curries with freshly baked naan; open 11:00-14:30 / 17:00-21:30.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Naan and the bread-based sets are wheat; in a shared Indian kitchen with flour and fried items, cross-contact with wheat is likely and no gluten-free handling is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegetable pakora is fried alongside paneer (cheese) pakora, and curries/naan commonly use ghee, butter, cream or yogurt, so plant-based dishes may share oil and dairy unless you ask staff to omit them.

positives.text: Genuine meat-free items exist, including vegetable salad with beans, vegetable pakora, and vegetable/chickpea-style curries, so vegetarians have real choices.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, foreigner-friendly Indian restaurant where much of the staff is from India and English is often understood, so a foreign student can order easily; a few words of Japanese or simple English both work fine.

hiro_graffity.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free destination. Core dishes (burritos, soft tacos, enchiladas, chimichangas) are built on wheat-flour tortillas; fried items like fish tacos and chimichangas use battered/deep-fried components, and there is no documented dedicated fryer or gluten-free protocol. No gluten-free menu or claims found on any source. Corn-tortilla or naturally GF options may be possible to ask about in person, but cross-contact cannot be assumed safe.
hiro_graffity.vegan_detail: An omnivore, meat-forward diner (beef, chicken, catfish), but it carries several vegetarian dishes and staff have said they can make them vegan on request. There is no dedicated vegan menu, so vegans should communicate clearly when ordering and confirm no animal products (cheese, sour cream, lard) are used.

chef_bio.background: Graffity is a San Diego-inspired Mexican and California-style diner in central Hiroshima's Fukuromachi, run by two brothers and going strong since it opened in October 2009 (around 17 years). Chef Kai developed his Mexican and Tex-Mex cooking during five years working in the San Diego area before bringing that style home to Hiroshima.
chef_bio.philosophy: A from-scratch kitchen: every dish and condiment is made in-house so the flavors are as full and fresh as they should be, exemplified by the super-fresh salsa and guacamole.
chef_bio.specialty: Burritos, enchiladas and soft tacos with grilled chicken or beef, fish tacos and Cajun-grilled catfish, alongside the kitchen's own fresh salsa and guacamole

anecdotes.text: Chef Kai picked up his ideas about Mexican and Tex-Mex food during five years working in the San Diego area, and makes every dish and condiment from scratch.
The restaurant is run by two friendly brothers and has been a popular, expat-loved spot, with a fun casual space, sofas by the windows, and counter seating.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: GetHiroshima and Hiroshima Keizai Shimbun: Graffity is a brothers-run Mexican/American (California-style) diner in Fukuromachi, opened Oct 2009; the chef learned his craft over five years in the San Diego area and makes everything from scratch (fresh salsa and guacamole).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Signature dishes are built on wheat-flour tortillas (burritos, soft tacos, enchiladas) and several items are battered and deep-fried (fish tacos, chimichangas), so gluten exposure and shared-fryer cross-contact are likely; no gluten-free protocol is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegetarian dishes can reportedly be made vegan on request, but Mexican dishes here commonly include cheese and sour cream and the kitchen is meat/fish-heavy, so confirm omission of dairy and animal fats when ordering.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Staff are described as very friendly and have indicated they can adapt vegetarian dishes to vegan, suggesting willingness to accommodate requests communicated at the table.

positives.text: Everything is made from scratch in-house, including the fresh salsa and guacamole, which makes plant-based customization easier to request.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, expat-friendly Mexican diner where the staff are known to be very welcoming and English is workable, so a foreign student can order comfortably and ask about vegetarian or vegan adaptations.

hiro_okonomiyaki_teppan_kushi.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. No gluten-free batter, noodle, or sauce alternatives are documented, and there is no indication of a dedicated gluten-free preparation area.
hiro_okonomiyaki_teppan_kushi.vegan_detail: Largely not vegan. Core dishes use egg, pork, beef, chicken, and local oysters, and okonomiyaki includes egg plus likely fish/bonito-derived sauce. hiro_okonomiyaki_teppan_kushi.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small independent teppan izakaya that opened in 2018, tucked into an alley behind the Edion main-store west building and about a minute on foot from the Kamiyachō-nishi tram stop, a short walk from the Peace Memorial Park.

chef_bio.background: A small independent teppan izakaya that opened in December 2018 in Hiroshima's Otemachi district, near the Edion main store and a short walk from the Kamiyachō-nishi tram stop and the Peace Memorial Park. Owner-chef Junji Yamada trained for about seven years at a well-known okonomiyaki restaurant before striking out on his own.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen emphasizes its own touches on the classics, using fresh noodles seasoned with an original paitan (chicken-bone) broth that are meant to stand up well to okonomiyaki sauce.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki paired with a wide range of teppan-grilled skewers, letting guests enjoy two of the city's signature ways of cooking on the iron griddle in one sitting.

anecdotes.text: The house okonomiyaki, やまだ焼き, layers in squid tempura, shiso (perilla) leaf, and green onion, with deluxe and special versions adding cheese, garlic chips, kimchi, and scallion.

Skewers run from shiso-wrapped pork and chicken-cheese to beef harami and ponzu-dressed gizzard, and a casual 'choi-nomi' set pairs a drink with a small dish and three skewers for easy after-work grazing.

chef_bio.background: A long-standing, family-run okonomiyaki and steak-house counter in central Hiroshima's Teppocho, just a short walk from the Hatchobori district. It is run as a small team built around the owner.
chef_bio.philosophy: A minimal, ingredient-forward approach described as okonomiyaki 'made with the eater in mind' rather than relying on heavy technique.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki cooked with a distinctive light touch: a slightly thick batter is laid down and topped with plenty of fish powder, cabbage, salt and pepper, tenkasu, rinsed bean sprouts, and two slices of pork belly. The cook uses no binding agents, spreads lard onto the griddle rather than over the food, and does not press the okonomiyaki down with the spatula, instead letting high heat steam it so it stays voluminous and never squeezed dry. The fresh noodles (from Isono Seimen) are seasoned right on the griddle with dashi, salt, and garlic powder rather than being pre-sauced.

anecdotes.text: The shop is known as a place former Prime Minister Fumio Kishida frequents when in Hiroshima, and his visits have been featured on national news.

Reviewers note the okonomiyaki is never pressed flat with the spatula, leaving it light and full-bodied rather than dense (high heat steams it), and the griddled Isono Seimen noodles are seasoned with dashi, salt, and garlic powder instead of sauce.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Isono Seimen shop directory confirms YUBU is a Kishida haunt aired on national news; Oomin77 blog details the light-touch method — no binding agents, lard on the griddle, no pressing (steamed by high heat), Isono Seimen noodles seasoned on the griddle with dashi, salt and garlic powder, layered with fish powder, cabbage, tenkasu, rinsed bean sprouts and two pork-belly slices.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Single shared teppan griddle used for wheat-batter okonomiyaki, wheat noodles, and tenkasu (fried wheat bits), creating heavy gluten cross-contact.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Okonomiyaki uses fish powder, pork belly, and egg, and the noodles are seasoned with dashi on the same griddle, so no dish is free of animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, cash-only, no-reservation local counter shop with limited open days and no English menu noted, so some basic Japanese and flexibility with the short hours will make a foreign student's visit much smoother.

chef_bio.background: The shop began in 1945 as a nameless stall a couple opened in the black market in front of Hiroshima Station right after the atomic bombing. After an eviction it moved to the Nagarekawa entertainment district, and after a fire it settled at its current location, where it has now run for about 41 years. Third-generation owner Kono Noriaki (河野憲昭) worked as a banker until 55, then took early retirement to carry on the family business, standing at the counter twelve hours a day except Sundays.
chef_bio.philosophy: Old-fashioned home cooking with simple seasoning that never tires the palate, so regulars keep returning; about forty pre-made side dishes are served instantly, a style born from early customers who were rushed taxi drivers and nightlife workers.
chef_bio.specialty: Kare-jiru (curry soup): a light, soothing thinned curry simmered with potato, onion, carrot, beef and beef tendon, finished with a house dashi of kombu, sardine and bonito.

anecdotes.text: The curry soup was born about forty years ago when the owner's brother-in-law, a heavy drinker, asked for curry thinned out because curry rice was too heavy; the owner's sister Tomoko recalled a school-lunch curry soup and finished it by thinning with dashi. Turmeric is added generously as a hangover soother for the late-night drinking crowd.

The kitchen effectively runs around the clock: the owner's sister Tomoko preps from 6 a.m. to evening, then hands off to Kono for the 6 p.m.-6 a.m. service, with clientele shifting from salarymen to bar staff to small-business owners through the night.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Hiroshima Home-TV feature: Shinkyo began 1945 as a nameless black-market stall by Hiroshima Station, moved to Nagarekawa after eviction, then its current site (~41 yrs); third-gen owner 河野憲昭 (ex-banker to 55) works 6pm-6am; kare-jiru created by sister Tomoko (school-lunch memory, dashi-thinned, half spicy/half mild roux, turmeric for hangovers), homemade kombu/sardine/bonito dashi; near-24h operation.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Home-style braised side dishes and dashi-based dishes are seasoned with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The signature curry soup contains beef and beef tendon and a fish-based dashi (kombu, iriko, katsuo), so it is not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.

cultural_comfort.note: A deep-night counter spot run by an elderly proprietor where regulars order in Japanese by pointing at rows of pre-made side dishes; manageable by pointing but a very local, no-English atmosphere.

chef_bio.origin: Opened March 29, 2018 at the ekie commercial complex inside JR Hiroshima Station, on the first floor.
chef_bio.background: The restaurant is part of the みのりみのるプロジェクト (Minori Minoru Project), launched in 2010 by JA Zennoh, the national federation of Japan's agricultural cooperatives, with its first shops opening that September at Ginza Mitsukoshi in Tokyo. The Hiroshima ekie location is the seventh in the series. The project was created so that producers and consumers could connect through food and farming, showcasing domestic, seasonal regional produce.
chef_bio.philosophy: Built on the idea of 'producers and consumers thinking of one another through food and agriculture,' emphasizing local-production-for-local-consumption (地産地消) and regional revitalization, here highlighting Hiroshima and the broader Chugoku and Shikoku regions.
chef_bio.specialty: Teishoku set meals built around local ingredients — the signature みのる定食 lets diners choose two mains from a rotating lineup, served with rice and miso soup. Standout dishes include a Hiroshima wagyu-and-pork hamburg developed with JA Zennoh Meat Foods and steak/rice bowls featuring Hiroshima wagyu branded 'Motonari'.

anecdotes.text: When the Hiroshima location opened in 2018, the concept was to start with Hiroshima Prefecture ingredients and progressively expand to feature products from across the Chugoku and Shikoku regions.
The flagship みのる定食 is a build-your-own set: pick two mains from a lineup that mixes everyday staples with seasonal specials, paired with rice and miso soup.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, easy-to-enter set-meal restaurant inside the Hiroshima Station ekie complex with picture-friendly teishoku menus, so a foreign student can manage with basic Japanese greetings and pointing, though staff English may be limited.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual local set-meal counter where you order at a touch-panel ticket machine and pay cash, so a foreign student can manage with minimal Japanese, but staff communication is in Japanese and there is no English menu, so bringing a translation app or this guide helps.

chef_bio.background: A small, family-feeling okonomiyaki shop tucked one block off Miyajima's busy Omotesando shopping street, on quieter Machiya-dori. It is run day to day by two women, described as the proprietress and her daughter, and keeps the relaxed, unhurried feel of a neighborhood place rather than a tourist counter.
chef_bio.philosophy: A homey spot where you can eat at a leisurely pace; the owners chat casually with guests and the place is built around regulars and an easygoing local atmosphere.
chef_bio.specialty: Authentic Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki; the standard niku-tama-soba (pork, egg, cabbage, bean sprouts and noodles) is the house favorite, cooked slowly for a fluffy rather than crisp-edged result, and finished with sweet Otafuku sauce against crunchy vegetables.

anecdotes.text: The shop is run by two women, described as the okami and her daughter, who keep an at-home, leisurely atmosphere and chat casually with customers.
Because most shops on Miyajima close by early evening, Kishibe's weekday hours running later in the evening make it a handy option for a meal at the end of a day on the island.
The okonomiyaki is cooked slowly for a fluffy texture rather than pressed to crisp edges, with generous cabbage, bean sprouts, green onion and seafood toppings available.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Everything is cooked on a single shared teppan griddle where wheat-batter okonomiyaki and wheat noodles are prepared, so cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes are finished with sweet Otafuku-style okonomiyaki sauce, which is wheat-based.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The shared griddle and dishes routinely involve pork, egg and seafood, so vegan cross-contact cannot be avoided.

cultural_comfort.note: An English menu is available and the two women who run the shop are used to foreign visitors, so a student with no Japanese can order comfortably here.

chef_bio.background: A small, hidden-gem eatery tucked into a quiet side street off the bustling Omotesando approach to Itsukushima Shrine, near the island's post office. Set on the upper floor of a traditional folk-house-style building, it has an intimate, calm room with just six counter seats and three tables and warm indirect lighting.
chef_bio.specialty: Braised conger eel (anago) over rice, including an anago-and-grated-yam (tororo) rice set, and fried local oysters. Unlike the grilled anago common elsewhere on the island, the kitchen here slow-braises the eel until it is soft and tender.

anecdotes.text: A visitor described it as a quiet hidden find off the crowded main approach, praising the soft braised anago over rice and noting the lunch sets run well under 2,000 yen, roughly half what comparable Miyajima specialty restaurants charge for similar dishes.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Fried oysters are breaded in wheat flour and deep-fried; no information indicates a separate gluten-free frying setup.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Signature anago dishes use a soy-sauce-based braising/seasoning sauce, which typically contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Menu is built around conger eel and oysters with fish-based stocks; no vegan-safe preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 9-seat counter-style local spot where a few words of Japanese and a relaxed, polite manner go a long way; English support is uncertain, so pointing at the set menu works well.

hiro_cafe_lente.notes: [Miyajima] An ocean-view cafe making use of an old private house, standing in a quiet corner a little away from the bustling shopping street, right near Miyajima's Itsukushima Shrine. In an atmospheric space that retains old beams and pillars, it arranges antique furniture, sofas, and refined tables, and the grand torii gate and the Seto Inland Sea can be seen from every seat. The 1st floor is the cafe and the 2nd floor operates as a two-room lodging, "private inn lente."

chef_bio.background: 宮島・厳島神社のすぐ近く、賑わう商店街から少し離れた静かな一角に建つ古民家を生かしたオーシャンビューのカフェ。古い梁や柱を残した趣ある空間に、アンティーク家具やソファ、洗練されたテーブルを配し、全席から大鳥居や瀬戸内の海を望める。1階がカフェ、2階は2室の宿泊施設『private inn lente』として営まれている。
chef_bio.philosophy: 席間隔を広く取り、世界遺産の島の風景を眺めながらゆったり寛いでほしいという思いで運営されている。
chef_bio.specialty: オーガニックのオリジナルブレンドコーヒーと、パルメザン・クリームチーズを使い自家製ブルーベリーソースを添えた自家製チーズケーキ。軽食では鶏もも肉とマッシュルームのトマトカレーや、赤米・ほうれん草・豆乳・味噌・オリーブオイルを使ったリゾットが知られる。

anecdotes.text: 赤米とほうれん草の豆乳リゾットはグルテンフリーで、ベジタリアン・ヴィーガンの人でも食べられるとして外国人観光客に人気を集めていると紹介されている。
商店街の喧騒から離れた静かな場所にあり、全席から厳島神社の大鳥居を望めるのが魅力と紹介されている。

positives.text: 赤米とほうれん草の豆乳リゾットはグルテンフリーで、ベジタリアン・ヴィーガンの人でも食べられると複数媒体で紹介されている。
野菜をたっぷり使った健康志向のメニューで、外国人観光客にも人気と記載されている。
